preguntas.subtema: What makes an exposure worse · CPT D1 1H k33 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k123 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.a · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Which circumstances raise the chance that a needlestick from an HIV-positive patient transmits the virus?
opciones: A visibly bloody device, a needle that was in a vein or artery, and a deep injury
A solid needle, a superficial scratch, and contact limited to intact skin
A small-bore needle, a source on treatment, and a splash onto the forearm
A used lancet, a gloved hand, and a source patient with a low viral load
preguntas.explicacion: The average risk after a percutaneous injury with HIV-infected blood is about 0.3 percent, but it is not the same for every injury. A case-control study found the risk higher when the worker met a larger quantity of blood, which showed up as a visibly bloody device, a procedure that put the needle in a vein or an artery, or a deep injury. Large-bore hollow needles and a source with a high viral load point the same way; intact skin carries no meaningful risk at all.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Does Pneumatic Tube System Transport Contribute to Hemolysis in ED Blood Samples?" (West J Emerg Med 2016, PMC5017839), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.D.4 · CCMA 3E k144 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: After installing a longer, faster pneumatic tube route, a laboratory sees more hemolysed samples. Which change in how tubes are sent is supported by the literature as reducing transport hemolysis?
opciones: Using padded inserts inside the carriers, gel tubes and properly filled tubes
Sending tubes uncapped so that pressure changes do not build up inside them
Sending each tube in its own carrier at the highest speed to shorten travel time
Loading each carrier to full capacity so the tubes cannot shift during accelerations
preguntas.explicacion: Variables shown to increase hemolysis during transport are rapid accelerations and decelerations, greater length of travel and high speeds; variables shown to reduce it are gel tubes, properly filled tubes and padded inserts within the canisters. Higher speed works in the wrong direction, and neither uncapping the tubes nor packing the carrier full appears among the variables the study lists.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Refusal of Care", section Definition/Introduction
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2F k43 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.a (both outlines) · RMA I.C.1.a · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: A patient's right to refuse care is founded on which ethical principle?
opciones: Autonomy, the right to make informed decisions about one's own care
Beneficence, which asks that actions be taken for the patient's benefit
Non-maleficence, which requires steps be taken so no one is harmed
Justice, which spreads benefits and risks evenly and without bias
preguntas.explicacion: Refusal of care rests on autonomy: a person may make informed decisions about their own health care, and staff are not to push their own beliefs, or their own decisions, onto the patient. Beneficence, non-maleficence and justice stand alongside autonomy and guide the same difficult situations, but the refusal itself does not rest on them.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.502(a)(1) and (a)(2), Permitted and required disclosures; and HHS, Office for Civil Rights, Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule
preguntas.subtema: Required disclosures · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k220 · CMA II.E.1.c · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3C k36
preguntas.pregunta: In which two situations is a covered entity REQUIRED, rather than merely permitted, to disclose protected health information?
opciones: To the individual who requests access or an accounting, and to HHS investigating compliance
To law enforcement on request, and to the patient's employer for workers' compensation
To any treating provider, and to the health plan paying the claim, on request
To public health authorities, and to a coroner or medical examiner determining cause of death
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.502(a)(2) names only two required disclosures: to the individual when requested under the right of access or the right to an accounting of disclosures, and to the Secretary of HHS when required to investigate or determine the entity's compliance. Everything else in the rule, treatment, payment, operations, public health, law enforcement, coroners and workers' compensation, is permitted under conditions but not compelled by HIPAA itself, although other laws may require some of those reports.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.520(b)(1), Required elements of the notice
preguntas.subtema: Content of the notice · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k33
preguntas.pregunta: Which statement must appear prominently at the top of a notice of privacy practices?
opciones: A header stating how medical information may be used and disclosed and how to access it
The names of every business associate that may receive the patient's information during care
The civil penalty amounts for HIPAA violations, from $100 up to $50,000 per violation
A list of the 18 identifiers that turn health information into protected information
preguntas.explicacion: The notice must be written in plain language and open with a prominently displayed header telling the reader that it describes how medical information about them may be used and disclosed and how they can get access to it, and asking them to review it carefully. It then describes uses for treatment, payment and operations with examples, the other permitted purposes, the uses that require authorization, the individual's rights, the entity's duties, how to complain without retaliation, a contact person and the effective date. Business associate names, penalty tables and identifier lists are not required elements.

preguntas.pregunta: To open the pre-draw interview, which question follows the principle of open-ended questioning first?
opciones: 'How have blood draws gone for you in the past?'
'Have you ever fainted during a blood draw?'
'You're not scared of needles, are you?'
'Did you fast for twelve hours like the doctor said?'
preguntas.explicacion: The technique table says to begin with open-ended questions that allow a free-flowing account, and to move to closed-ended questions afterwards. The other three are closed or leading: the fainting question is a legitimate item from the WHO Annex C interview, but it invites a yes or no, and the leading question about needles steers the answer.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Blood Donation", section Complications
preguntas.subtema: Donor reactions · CPT D4 4D perform phlebotomy for blood donations
preguntas.pregunta: A donor turns pale and sweaty and her blood pressure and pulse fall during collection. What is happening, and what helps?
opciones: Syncope: stop the donation, support her, and keep her reclined a few minutes
Syncope: finish the unit quickly, then sit her upright and offer fluids
A hematoma: release the needle, apply ice, and watch the site closely
Citrate toxicity: slow the return line and give oral calcium at once
preguntas.explicacion: Syncope is the second most common adverse effect of donation, often vasovagal or related to low volume, and shows as a fall in systolic pressure and pulse with weakness, sweating, dizziness or pallor. The donation is paused or stopped and supportive measures begin; keeping the donor reclined a few minutes and moving her upright gradually lowers the risk. Hematoma is the most common effect, and citrate toxicity belongs to apheresis.

preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical error · CPT D3 k9 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(d) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A citrate tube for a prothrombin time is put in the specimen refrigerator to await pick-up. Why is that the wrong choice?
opciones: Whole blood for these assays is held at room temperature, not chilled
Whole blood for these assays is held frozen, and chilling is not enough
Refrigeration bursts the red cells and haemolyses the whole specimen
Refrigeration hardens the gel barrier and traps the plasma underneath
preguntas.explicacion: Whole blood drawn for clotting tests is kept at room temperature, roughly eighteen to twenty-four degrees, and refrigeration is avoided because cold can activate factor VII. Chilling whole blood also lowers factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, which can imitate a bleeding disorder.

preguntas.pregunta: How many percutaneous injuries, needlesticks among them, did Congress estimate happen each year among U.S. healthcare workers when it passed the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act?
opciones: 6 to 8 million
380,000 in all settings
preguntas.explicacion: Section 2 of the Act cites CDC estimates published in March 2000: over 380,000 percutaneous injuries a year from contaminated sharps in U.S. hospital settings alone, and between 600,000 and 800,000 such injuries, needlesticks among them, once every healthcare setting is counted. The same findings put at 62 to 88 percent the share of sharps injuries that safer devices could prevent. StatPearls lands nearby, about 600,000 a year, and adds that close to half are never reported.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Informed Consent", sections Introduction and Other Issues (Human Clinical Studies)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2F k43 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.a (both outlines) · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: 'If you don't let me draw this, the doctor is going to be very upset with you.' Which requirement of valid consent does this remark violate?
opciones: Voluntariness: the decision must be made free of coercion
Disclosure: the risks of the procedure were never fully listed
Capacity: the patient's understanding was never assessed
Documentation: the consent form was never signed
preguntas.explicacion: Valid consent requires a patient competent to make a voluntary decision, and clinicians must avoid creating any sense of coercion toward their recommendation; the research-consent list names the voluntary nature of the decision as one of three elements. Pressure through a third party's displeasure attacks that element directly, whatever was disclosed or signed.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Local Anesthetics in Children", section Toxicity
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4B pediatric collection, D2 k49 age considerations · PBT II.B age-specific needs, II.I considerations
preguntas.pregunta: Why is EMLA cream a special concern in a 6-week-old infant?
opciones: Prilocaine can bring on methemoglobinemia, above all in a baby under 3 months old
Its ester component is broken down poorly when pseudocholinesterase is lacking
The occlusive dressing brings on hypothermia in infants under 3 months of age
Neonatal skin takes the cream up so fast that it peaks within 15 to 30 minutes
preguntas.explicacion: Prilocaine, on its own or inside EMLA cream, can bring on methemoglobinemia, and newborns and babies under three months are the ones most at risk; drugs such as acetaminophen, dapsone, phenytoin and phenobarbital push that risk higher. The ester answer fails on the chemistry: EMLA is 2.5 percent lidocaine with 2.5 percent prilocaine, and both belong to the amide family, so the pseudocholinesterase problem of the esters never arises. Peak plasma levels under an occlusive dressing arrive hours later, not in the first half hour.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, Section 5: Fire-Fighting Measures

preguntas.pregunta: Which safety data sheet section tells you which extinguishing agent is right for a fire involving that chemical, and which is not?
opciones: Section 5, which also warns about products given off as it burns
Section 6, which also covers containment and cleanup after a spill
Section 9, which also gives the flash point and the boiling range
Section 7, which also covers safe storage and incompatible products
preguntas.explicacion: Section 5 is written for the fire: which extinguishing equipment is suitable and which is not appropriate for a given situation, the specific hazards the chemical develops while burning, such as hazardous combustion products, and any special protection or precautions for the people fighting it. The flash point in section 9 tells you the chemical can burn; section 5 tells you what to do about it, and section 6 begins where the release has not caught fire.

preguntas.subtema: Go now, not tomorrow · CPT D1 1H k33 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k123 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.b · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist is stuck at the end of her shift and says she will go to occupational health tomorrow. What is the recommendation?
opciones: Be seen at once, rather than waiting twelve to seventy-two hours for a visit
Be seen within seven days, the deadline that applies to hepatitis B treatment
Be seen at the end of the shift, once the incident report has been written
Be seen within ninety days, while the baseline sample is being preserved
preguntas.explicacion: Follow-up with occupational health should be immediate rather than delayed by twelve to seventy-two hours, because the decisions that depend on it are time-sensitive: baseline testing, hepatitis B immune globulin within about a day, and antiretroviral prophylaxis started preferably within hours. The ninety days is how long a baseline sample is preserved when the employee does not consent to HIV testing on the spot, not a period in which to be seen.

preguntas.pregunta: What is recommended for a device whose sharp sits recessed inside a fixed housing?
opciones: The housing extends past the sharp and keeps fingers out
The housing retracts on activation and exposes the used sharp
The housing is removed before disposal so the bin fills slowly
The housing is colored orange to match an insulin syringe hub
preguntas.explicacion: For a fixed recessed needle the housing has to reach past the sharp, covering it completely and keeping fingers off. Color is a separate recommendation: it should serve a definite purpose, such as telling models or sizes apart, and follow conventions users already know.

preguntas.pregunta: A 16 G needle is used on a small forearm vein and a large hematoma forms. According to WHO Chapter 3, what is the effect of a needle that is too large, and of one that is too small?
opciones: Too large tears the vein and causes bleeding; too small damages the cells and invalidates whole-cell tests
Too large damages the blood cells and invalidates the tests; too small tears the vein and causes a hematoma
Too large slows the draw so the sample clots in the tube; too small lets air into the tubing of the set
Too large causes haemoconcentration of the sample; too small causes the tube to lose its vacuum early
preguntas.explicacion: Section 3.1.1 says that a needle too large for the vein will tear it and cause bleeding, a hematoma, while a needle too small damages the blood cells as the sample is taken and invalidates tests that need whole cells, hemoglobin or free plasma. It adds that transfusion collection needs a larger gauge than blood drawing, and Table 3.1 reserves 16 to 18 G for blood donation.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Fainting, section Home Care
preguntas.subtema: Responses to complications · CPT D3 3K k69 · D1 1M k37 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.B.9.l / 2027 I.B.8.l · RMA III.I · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: A patient faints in a crowded corridor where there is no room to lie down. What is the alternative position?
opciones: Seated forward, with the head between the knees
Seated upright, with the chin lifted and eyes closed
Standing, leaning back against the corridor wall
Seated backwards, with both legs stretched out flat
preguntas.explicacion: The person is normally kept lying down for at least ten to fifteen minutes, ideally somewhere cool and quiet. Where that cannot be arranged, the alternative given is to sit the person forward with the head between the knees; tight clothing round the neck is loosened either way.

preguntas.fuente: NIA, Talking With Your Older Patients, Compensating for visual deficits
preguntas.pregunta: An older patient with poor sight is about to be handed the printed fasting instructions. Which check does the guidance put on the person handing them over?
opciones: That she brought her glasses or contact lenses and has them on before she starts to read
That she can read the top line of the sheet aloud before the phlebotomist lets her keep it
That a relative able to read the sheet for her is present in the room while it is explained
That the sheet has been read to her aloud first, because print alone is not enough at her age
preguntas.explicacion: The measures for a visual deficit are practical and go in order. Light the room well, with light on your own face and as little glare as possible; check that the person actually brought the glasses or lenses she needs and is wearing them; make handwriting clear and keep printed type big enough in an easy face. Nothing there asks the patient to prove she can read, or puts a relative in charge of reading for her. Reading everything aloud belongs to low vision, where print has stopped working at any size.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Granular Leukocytes and Agranular Leukocytes
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k4 (applied D5) · PBT I.B.4 · CCMA 3E k122 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: A differential on a patient with a bacterial infection shows 80 percent of one leukocyte type. Which type is normally the most common and rises with bacterial infection?
opciones: Neutrophils, normally 50 to 70 percent of leukocytes
Lymphocytes, normally 20 to 30 percent of leukocytes
Monocytes, normally 2 to 8 percent of leukocytes
Eosinophils, normally 2 to 4 percent of leukocytes
preguntas.explicacion: Neutrophils are the most common leukocyte at 50 to 70 percent of the count; they respond fast to infection, prefer bacteria, and high counts point to bacterial infection or inflammation, as well as burns and stress. Lymphocytes are second at 20 to 30 percent and rise with viral infections; monocytes are 2 to 8 percent and eosinophils 2 to 4 percent, rising with allergies and parasitic worms.

preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2C k42 · PBT II.A · CCMA 3E2 k124 · RMA III.C.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: A ward asks for a fourth identical panel in two days. Which consideration does the ordering guidance raise?
opciones: Repeat testing is kept for cases likely to yield new or useful information
Repeat testing is capped at three panels for any single admitted patient
Repeat panels are drawn only when the earlier tubes were rejected as unfit
Repeat panels cost little, since testing is under 5% of health spending
preguntas.explicacion: A test earns its place by bearing on the diagnostic hypothesis; timing and necessity ask whether a change in the patient's condition justifies doing it, or doing it again, and a repeat is kept for the case where it will probably turn up something new or useful. Testing is indeed under 5% of health spending, yet 25% to 30% of repeat testing is reported as unnecessary.

preguntas.pregunta: A waived site's refrigerator has a digital data logger with an alarm. How often should staff still check and record its temperature?
opciones: Daily, and the testing room's temperature before the room is used
Weekly, since the logger records continuously and alarms on excursions
Only when the alarm sounds or a control result falls out of range
Monthly, when the QC records are reviewed for shifts and trends
preguntas.explicacion: Refrigerator, freezer and storage-room temperatures are checked and recorded daily, and the testing room's temperature before the room is used, regardless of whether the unit has an alarm, a chart recorder, a data logger or a continuous monitoring system. The log is one of the records a site keeps; refrigerator or freezer failure is a problem to document, report to the person overseeing testing, and correct.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Glucose screening tests during pregnancy (007562), How the Test will Feel; MedlinePlus, Glucose tolerance test (003466), How the Test will Feel; StatPearls, "Glucose Tolerance Test", section Testing Procedures
preguntas.subtema: Tolerance test patient care · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.B patient interaction · CCMA 3E k139 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: Twenty minutes after drinking the glucose solution, a pregnant patient says she feels nauseated, sweaty and lightheaded. What is the appropriate response?
opciones: Reassure her: those reactions are known, and serious effects are very uncommon
Stop the test and report it to the provider as a failed glucose screen
Offer her a light snack to settle her stomach before the next blood draw
Have her drink the glucose solution again, since some may not have stayed down
preguntas.explicacion: Most patients come through the glucose tolerance test with no side effects at all; a few turn sweaty, lightheaded or nauseated once the solution is down, and anything serious is very uncommon. The patient stays seated throughout and does not eat while the test runs. What she is asked beforehand is whether blood tests or medical procedures have brought on such symptoms before, which the provider is told; repeating the drink is no part of any of these protocols.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Disorders of Clotting; and Plasma Anticoagulants
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k8 (applied D3 k74 post-procedural bleeding) · PBT I.C · CMA I.C.6.h(4) (2027: I.C.6.g(4)) · RMA I.A.2.a · NCMA 1.1 EKB 1
preguntas.pregunta: A patient on daily low-dose aspirin keeps bleeding at the puncture site longer than expected. What does aspirin do to hemostasis?
opciones: It is an antiplatelet; it inhibits the aggregation of platelets
It is a thrombolytic; it converts plasminogen into plasmin
It inactivates factor X, in the same way antithrombin does
It blocks vitamin K, so the liver makes fewer clotting factors
preguntas.explicacion: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that is very effective at inhibiting platelet aggregation, which is why it is given during heart attacks and strokes and sometimes daily at low dose to people at cardiovascular risk. Thrombolytics such as tissue plasminogen activator work on plasminogen instead, and antithrombin works on factor X and on the conversion of prothrombin.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Cortisol Test, section What happens during a cortisol test
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K k45 · PBT II.D II.G · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: For a blood cortisol test, when are the samples usually drawn?
opciones: Once in the morning and again around 4 p.m. on the same day
Once at midnight, when cortisol is normally at its peak
Once in the morning only, after a strict 12-hour overnight fast
Every hour for 2 to 3 hours after a sugary glucose drink
preguntas.explicacion: Blood samples are usually taken twice in one day: in the morning, when cortisol is normally highest, and again around 4 p.m., when it is normally much lower, which is why the patient needs two appointments. The physiology matches: peak near awakening, lowest at night. A 12-hour morning fast describes iron, and hourly samples describe the tolerance test.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient's order calls for every tube on the chart. Which one is filled ninth?
opciones: The pale yellow tube used for tissue typing and DNA work
The purple top tube used for hematology and cross-match
The light gray top tube used for glucose determinations
The light green tube used for chemistry panels on plasma
preguntas.explicacion: Position 9 belongs to the pale yellow acid-citrate-dextrose tube, whose listed uses are HLA tissue typing, paternity testing and DNA studies. preguntas.pregunta: A relay call comes through 7-1-1 to book a fasting draw. How must the front desk handle it?
opciones: Accept it and treat it exactly like any other telephone call
Ask the caller to attend in person, since relay is not private
Transfer it to the interpreter line before a booking is made
Take the booking only once a hearing relative confirms it
preguntas.explicacion: The telecommunications relay service, free and nationwide, is reached by dialling 7-1-1 and puts communications assistants in the middle for people with hearing or speech disabilities. A covered entity is required to accept calls placed through relay and video relay services, and whoever answers treats them exactly like other calls; the assistant explains how the system works.

preguntas.pregunta: A 4-year-old needs a finger-prick. Which puncture depth is recommended for that age?
opciones: 1.5 mm, the depth for a child over 6 months and under 8 years
2.4 mm, the depth for a child over 6 months and under 8 years
0.85 mm, the depth for any child who has not reached school age

preguntas.explicacion: Two finger-prick depths are given for children: 1.5 mm between 6 months and 8 years, and 2.4 mm from 8 years on. The 0.85 mm lancet is the length kept for premature babies, and 2.2 mm is the longest lancet in normal use on an adult finger, since a finger puncture is not to pass 2.4 mm.

preguntas.subtema: Shared glucometers · CPT D1 1K k10 · PBT VI.G.4.e · CCMA 3C5 k104 · CMA I.B.5 / 2027 I.B.4 · RMA III.A.4 · NCMA 2A.2
preguntas.pregunta: A glucometer and its lancet platform are used for several inpatients during a round. What does best practice require?
opciones: Dedicate it to one patient, or clean and disinfect it between uses
Change the lancet and wipe the platform with a dry gauze pad
Rinse the platform under running water at the end of the round
Keep it in a clean bag between patients, which avoids contact
preguntas.explicacion: For small quantities of capillary blood the equipment is single-use: a lancet, or a retractable one, and a platform or glucometer either dedicated to a single patient for the whole stay or, between patients, wiped free of every visible trace of dirt and then disinfected with alcohol. The reason is on the record: hepatitis has reached patients where a glucometer or its platform was passed from one person to the next without that reprocessing.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Critical Limits of Laboratory Results for Urgent Clinician Notification" (EJIFCC 2003, PMC6178782), introduction
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5G 5I · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3D9 k117 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A glucose drawn from the arm carrying a glucose infusion comes back far above the critical limit, and the patient looks well. What clears the picture?
opciones: Testing a second specimen collected properly from another site
Repeating the measurement twice on the same tube and averaging
Reporting the figure and letting the clinician judge the context
Diluting the specimen and correcting for the dilution factor used
preguntas.explicacion: Preanalytical influences are named outright as a frequent source of results that only look critical, and the example given is a glucose drawn through a venous catheter that had been used for a glucose infusion. Cases like that are normally settled by testing another, properly collected specimen; repeating the same contaminated tube only confirms the contamination.

preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical error: haemolysis · CPT D3 k9 k59 · PBT II.F II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory rejects a sample as hemolyzed. Which collection practices are recognized causes of hemolysis?
opciones: Pressing the syringe plunger, shaking the tube, and a short draw in the gray tube
Leaving the tourniquet on for more than one minute, and drawing the tubes in the wrong sequence
Using a 21 G needle in an adult, and inverting the citrate tube three to six times
Preparing the skin with povidone iodine, and labeling the tubes away from the patient
preguntas.explicacion: Pressing the plunger raises the risk of hemolysis, Table 2.3 warns that a short draw in the fluoride tube may cause hemolysis, and vigorous shaking or overmixing of the tube produces hemolysis. A long tourniquet causes hemoconcentration, the wrong sequence causes additive carry-over, iodine raises potassium, and three to six gentle inversions is the correct handling of the citrate tube.

preguntas.pregunta: Which device helps locate the dorsal hand veins and antecubital veins of a small child?
opciones: A transilluminator or a small pocket pen light
A tourniquet left in place for three minutes
A warm compress applied for a fixed 10 minutes
An ultrasound probe operated by the phlebotomist
preguntas.explicacion: To make a pediatric venepuncture easier, a transilluminator or a pen light from the pocket is used to bring up the veins on the back of the hand and those of the antecubital fossa. Before that the child is kept warm, which can multiply the flow by seven, and warm cloths on the site widen the vessels.

preguntas.subtema: Complications: haematoma · CPT D3 3Q 3L k70 k74 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E9 k133 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: A hematoma forms at a site where the technique looked correct throughout. Which omission is the likely explanation?
opciones: Pressure was not kept up during and after the needle came out
Pressure was kept up too long after the needle had come out
The tourniquet was released before the needle was withdrawn
The site was cleaned with alcohol rather than povidone iodine
preguntas.explicacion: A hematoma can form when too little pressure is kept up during the draw and after it, which is why the gauze is taped down to give continuous pressure. Releasing the band before the needle comes out is the correct order, and alcohol is the preferred antiseptic for a routine draw.

preguntas.subtema: Equipment quality checks · CPT D3 3B k58 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E3 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: A box of evacuated tubes is found to be past its expiration date. What two problems do expired tubes present?
opciones: Reduced ability to draw blood in, and additives that may have degraded
Loss of sterility of the stopper, and a gel that no longer separates serum
A higher risk of hemolysis, and colors that no longer match the order of draw
Cracks in the plastic, and an anticoagulant that turns plasma into serum
preguntas.explicacion: Expiration dates matter because expired vacuum tubes have a decreased capacity to aspirate blood and their additives may be degraded, so even small deviations can affect the results. The other options mix real problems from the tube collection review, such as a missing anticoagulant or a lost vacuum after uncapping, with effects the chapter does not attribute to expiry.

preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K k46 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: A patient with diabetes fasted 14 hours for a hemoglobin A1C 'to be safe'. Which statement is correct?
opciones: Fasting was not needed; the A1C reflects average glucose over about 3 months
Fasting was needed; the A1C requires no caloric intake for at least 8 full hours
Fasting was needed; samples are drawn before and after a sugary drink
Fasting was harmful; the A1C result will now read falsely low
preguntas.explicacion: The hemoglobin A1C test uses one sample, needs no fasting, and reports average blood glucose over the past 3 months. The 8-hour rule with no caloric intake applies to the fasting plasma glucose, and the drink-then-resample sequence is the tolerance test. Fasting is simply not part of the A1C's preparation.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, introduction and Section 9
preguntas.subtema: Nothing left blank · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k106 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: What must a safety data sheet do when its preparer finds no information for a required element?
opciones: Say that no applicable information was found for that element
Leave that element blank, which is read as not applicable
Copy the entry from a sheet for a similar product in the family
Move the element to section 16 with the other information
preguntas.explicacion: Silence is not allowed. Where the preparer finds no relevant information for a required element, the sheet must say outright that nothing applicable was found, and section 9 repeats the rule for the physical and chemical properties: an item that is not relevant, or not available, carries a note saying so for that property. A blank leaves the reader unable to tell an absent hazard from an unresearched one.

preguntas.fuente: SAMHSA, Urine Specimen Collection Handbook for Federal Agency Workplace Drug Testing Programs (2024), Chapter 7 preparation step 3 and collection step 13
preguntas.subtema: Drug screen procedure · CPT D4 4J k86 · PBT V.C.5 · CCMA 3E k127 witness · RMA III.C.4.a.i · CMA I.C.7.a(2)(f)
preguntas.pregunta: How is the donor's hand washing handled in a federal workplace drug test collection?
opciones: The donor washes under the collector's direct observation before the void
The donor washes in private, since observing would violate the donor's dignity
The donor washes only after handing over the specimen container
The donor uses gloves instead, because soap can adulterate the specimen
preguntas.explicacion: The collector gives the donor a way to wash their hands and watches while they do it; where the collection area has no sink, a waterless cleanser or a moist towelette stands in. Soap, cleanser and disinfectant are cleared out of the restroom as possible adulterants, which is why the washing happens beforehand and under the collector's eye. Once the specimen has changed hands the donor may usually wash again.

preguntas.fuente: SAMHSA, Urine Specimen Collection Handbook for Federal Agency Workplace Drug Testing Programs (2024)
preguntas.subtema: Specimen transport · CPT D4 4J k86 · PBT V.C.5 chain-of-custody · CCMA 3D k121 transport and storage · RMA III.C.4.a.i urine drug screen
preguntas.pregunta: When must a sealed federal drug test specimen package be shipped, and what if it cannot go out that fast?
opciones: Within 24 hours or the next business day, in secure refrigerated storage meanwhile
Within 24 hours or the next business day, at room temperature in a locked room
Within 4 hours of the collection, on cold packs, with no storage permitted
Within one week, provided the tamper-evident seals stay unbroken
preguntas.explicacion: The package reaches the testing facility, or a laboratory certified by HHS, inside 24 hours of collection or on the next business day; one collected on a Friday for Monday shipment waits in secure refrigerated storage. Until pick-up the collector is answerable for protecting it from tampering, damage and theft. A bottle seal found broken after the donor has left cancels the collection.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Antiepileptic Drug Monitoring", section Other Issues, Trough Versus Free Levels
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k45 · PBT II.D II.K · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e
preguntas.pregunta: A patient with severe systemic illness has a phenytoin level ordered as a free level. Why a free level?
opciones: Altered protein binding makes the total level an unreliable indicator
A free level may be drawn at any hour, whenever the last dose fell
A free level takes the place of the trough for short half-life drugs
A free level is measured whenever two antiepileptics are combined
preguntas.explicacion: Free levels give the unbound, pharmacologically active fraction, and measuring them becomes crucial where protein binding may be altered, as in severe systemic illness or with drug interactions. Altered binding can render the total concentration an unreliable indicator of activity and lead to inappropriate dosage adjustments.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3636, Hazard Communication Standard: Labels and Pictograms, Precautionary Statements
preguntas.subtema: Precautionary statements · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k107 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: What are the four types of precautionary statements found on a Hazard Communication label?
opciones: Prevention, response, storage and disposal
Physical, health, environmental and unclassified
Identification, composition, handling and transport
Danger, warning, caution and notice
preguntas.explicacion: Precautionary statements describe the measures recommended to minimize or prevent harm from exposure, storage or handling, and they come in four types: prevention, to limit exposure; response, for spills, emergencies and first aid; storage; and disposal. Physical, health and environmental are the three hazard groups of the GHS; identification, composition, handling and transport are SDS section titles; and Danger and Warning are the only two signal words, so caution and notice do not exist in this system.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Urine collection - infants (003417), How the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Infant bag collection · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.1 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(2)(e) · RMA III.C.4.a.i · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A mother is sent home to collect urine from her 6-month-old with an adhesive bag. Which instruction is correct?
opciones: Wash the genital area, apply the bag, put a diaper over it, check the baby often and remove the bag once urine collects
Apply the bag over the unwashed skin so the adhesive holds better, and leave it in place until the next diaper change
Wash the genital area, apply the bag without a diaper so it is visible, and leave it on for exactly 24 hours
Wash the genital area with an antiseptic, pass a small catheter into the bladder and drain the urine into the bag
preguntas.explicacion: The area around the urethra is washed with the soap or wipes the provider recommends, the bag is opened and stuck on (the whole penis inside it, or over the labia), a diaper goes on over the bag, and the baby is checked often. Active infants can displace the bag, so extra bags are useful. The urine is emptied into the container without touching its inside and, at home, kept in a plastic bag in the refrigerator. Catheterization is done by a provider.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Test!: Actions for Invalid or Questionable Test Results; Recording Results
preguntas.subtema: Result beyond reportable range · CPT D5 5G · PBT IV.B.1 · CCMA 3D3 / 3D9 · CMA I.C.9.a · RMA III.C.3.a
preguntas.pregunta: A glucose meter displays 'HI' instead of a number for a patient who looks unwell. What is the correct handling of this result?
opciones: Treat it as a value beyond the reportable range and follow the manufacturer's steps for such results; a number is not reported
Record 600 mg/dL, the top of the meter's range, as the patient's result and notify the provider of a critical glucose
Record 'HI' as the final result in the log and file it, since the meter has already interpreted the reading correctly
Treat the display as a meter malfunction, switch to a second meter and report whichever numeric value it produces
preguntas.explicacion: When a quantitative result is above or below the reportable range of the instrument, or the system prevents the display of a result, the test is repeated, which may require a new sample; the manufacturer's instructions describe how to handle values that cannot be measured accurately, and results are reported only after the problem is identified and resolved. A display like 'HI' is not a number to transcribe, and an invalid or unacceptable first result is still recorded before retesting.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Blood Culture Contamination: An Overview for Infection Control and Antibiotic Stewardship Programs (2022), section 6 Phlebotomy Teams and Education
preguntas.subtema: Blood culture quality · CPT D4 4A · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139
preguntas.pregunta: A hospital wants to lower its blood culture contamination rate. Which staffing measure does the CDC associate with fewer contaminated cultures?
opciones: Having dedicated phlebotomy teams collect the cultures
Rotating culture collection among all nursing staff on each unit
Having the ordering physician collect the cultures personally
Collecting cultures only through existing vascular access devices
preguntas.explicacion: In hospitals, cultures taken by a phlebotomy team contaminate less often than those collected by staff who do not draw blood for a living, and the CDC lists phlebotomy teams and training in proper technique among its prevention measures, next to skin antisepsis, bottle-top disinfection, hand hygiene, feedback on rates and diversion devices. Drawing through an existing catheter pushes contamination up, not down.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1242(a)(3), Standard: Specimen submission, handling, and referral
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.B · CCMA 3D4 · NCMA 2C.14 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.a
preguntas.pregunta: A swab reaches the laboratory carrying the patient's name and ID number, but nothing on it says where on the body it came from. Under CLIA's specimen labeling policy element, what is missing?
opciones: The specimen source, which must appear on the label when appropriate
The test requested, which must be written on every specimen container
The collector's signature, which is required on all microbiology specimens
The date of birth, which is mandatory on the label for every specimen
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR 493.1242(a)(3) requires the laboratory's labeling procedure to cover the patient's name or unique identifier and, when appropriate, the specimen source; for a swab the site is exactly that appropriate case. The regulation does not put the test name, the collector's signature or the date of birth on the container itself, although the requisition must carry the sex and the age or date of birth.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(e)(2)(ii)(M), Special practices
preguntas.subtema: The biosafety manual · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G · CCMA 3C2 k109 · CMA I.B.8.a / 2027 I.B.7.a · RMA III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.9
preguntas.pregunta: In a laboratory that works with concentrated HIV or HBV, what does the standard require of the biosafety manual?
opciones: It is reviewed and updated at least yearly, and staff must read and follow it
It is written once at start-up and kept for the duration of employment
It is posted at the door with the name and phone of the laboratory director
It takes the place of the exposure control plan for employees in that area
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (e)(2)(ii)(M) asks for a biosafety manual to be prepared or adopted, then reviewed and updated periodically, at least once a year and more often if needed. It also puts a duty on the staff: they are advised of the potential hazards, and they have to read the practices and procedures they are given and then follow them. What goes on the door is the warning sign of (g)(1)(ii)(A). All of this sits on top of the exposure control plan, which paragraph (c) still demands.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5F k89 · PBT III.B · CCMA 3E12 · NCMA 2C.14 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: Before a sample is accepted, the accessioning clerk checks the two identifiers on the tube. What second check does the emergency laboratory in the rejection study also require?
opciones: That the sample and the requested tests match each other correctly
That the tube was drawn by a phlebotomist rather than by a nurse
That the barcode was printed within the last 30 minutes
That the hemolysis index was measured before the sample was accessioned
preguntas.explicacion: In that laboratory the secretary verifies that the minimum two identification criteria, name and surname plus patient ID, are present, and additionally checks that the sample and the test requests match; with these controls the misidentification rate was 0.3 %. Serum indices are measured after acceptance, and neither the collector's role nor the barcode print time is an acceptance criterion.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Fainting, overview
preguntas.subtema: Complications: syncope · CPT D3 k68 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: How long does a fainting episode usually last, and what is the typical recovery?
opciones: Usually less than a couple of minutes, with quick recovery
Usually 10 to 15 minutes, with gradual recovery over an hour
Usually a few seconds, with confusion for several minutes afterwards
Usually 5 to 10 minutes, with weakness for the rest of the day
preguntas.explicacion: Fainting is a brief loss of consciousness from a drop in blood flow to the brain, most often lasting less than a couple of minutes, with quick recovery; the medical name is syncope. Ten to fifteen minutes is how long the person is kept lying down afterwards, and confusion on waking points to a seizure rather than syncope.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Veins", section Structure and Function
preguntas.subtema: Antecubital anatomy · CPT D3 3F k61 k62 · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: Blood in an arm vein drains toward the heart against gravity. Which feature of the vein keeps it from running back down?
opciones: One-way valves set inside the lumen of the vein
A thicker muscular coat than the artery beside it
The perforating branches that reach the deep veins
The venae comitantes that travel with the artery
preguntas.explicacion: Veins carry one-way valves in the lumen, and their job is to stop the blood draining backwards on its way up to the heart. The wall holds less muscle than an artery, which is why a vein stretches and acts as a reservoir. Perforating veins link the superficial system to the deep one, and the venae comitantes are the paired veins that run with the forearm arteries.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Streptococcal Pharyngitis", Evaluation
preguntas.subtema: Rapid strep testing · CPT D4 4G · PBT V.C.1 · CCMA 3D k117 · CMA I.C.10.d.(2) · RMA III.C.4.b
preguntas.pregunta: A child scores in the intermediate range on a clinical decision rule for sore throat. What testing follows?
opciones: Rapid antigen detection testing, the primary diagnostic tool for group A streptococcus
A sputum culture with Gram stain, the primary diagnostic tool for a pharyngeal infection
No testing at all, since an intermediate score is treated the same as a low-risk score
Blood cultures drawn from two sites, the primary diagnostic tool for streptococcal disease
preguntas.explicacion: History and examination alone cannot diagnose group A streptococcal pharyngitis, so a clinical decision rule goes together with rapid antigen detection, which is highly specific. Patients at intermediate or high risk get the rapid test; those at low risk need nothing further. The rapid test may be skipped under age 3, since both the infection and rheumatic fever are rare that young.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Equipment
preguntas.subtema: Tourniquet · CPT D3 k60 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k133 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: What does a tourniquet do that makes venipuncture easier?
opciones: It presses on the limb and blocks the venous return for a while, so the veins show up
It stops arterial inflow so that the veins below it empty and become straighter
It disinfects the skin above the site, so the alcohol contact time can be shortened
It keeps the blood from clotting in the tubing of a winged collection set
preguntas.explicacion: The tourniquet puts a passing pressure on the limb and blocks the flow artificially, which helps the phlebotomist find the veins, and cites studies showing the veins dilate and gain surface area right after a tightly placed tourniquet. It must not stop arterial flow, it has no antiseptic role, and it has nothing to do with the air in butterfly tubing.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.502(g)(1), (g)(3) and (g)(5), Personal representatives
preguntas.subtema: Personal representatives · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k220 · CMA II.E.3.c · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3C k36
preguntas.pregunta: A parent asks for the lab results of their 8-year-old child. How does HIPAA treat the parent?
opciones: As the child's personal representative, acting as the individual for that PHI
As a third party who needs the child's own signed authorization first
As a family member entitled only to a verbal summary at the visit
As a personal representative only after a court has appointed the parent as guardian
preguntas.explicacion: Under section 164.502(g) a personal representative is treated as if they were the individual. For an unemancipated minor that representative is the parent, the guardian or a person acting in loco parentis who holds authority under applicable law to make health care decisions, and it covers the PHI relevant to that role, with no court appointment needed. The exceptions are services the minor may lawfully consent to alone, and situations of abuse or endangerment where the entity may refuse to treat the person as representative; state law can widen or narrow parental access.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.404(a), (b) and (d), Notification to individuals
preguntas.subtema: Breach notification deadline · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.b · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3E k33
preguntas.pregunta: A breach of unsecured PHI has just been discovered. How fast must the covered entity notify the individuals affected?
opciones: No more than 60 calendar days after discovery, and without unreasonable delay
Within 30 days after discovery, matching the right-of-access deadline
Within 90 days after discovery, the period a substitute web notice stays posted
By the end of the calendar year, regardless of the number of individuals
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.404 requires notice to every individual whose unsecured PHI was accessed, acquired, used or disclosed, or is reasonably believed to have been. Two limits apply at once: no unreasonable delay, and 60 calendar days from discovery as the outer edge. A breach counts as discovered the first day it is known, or would have been known with reasonable diligence, to any workforce member other than the one who caused it. Written notice travels by first-class mail, or by e-mail if the person agreed to that; where contact details are missing for 10 or more people, a substitute posting on the website or a media notice runs for 90 days.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)(xiii)(B) and (C), specimen containers
preguntas.subtema: Specimens that can puncture · CPT D1 1G k32 · PBT VI.G.4.d · CCMA 3C8 k108 · CMA I.B.6.a / 2027 I.B.5.a · RMA III.A.2.c III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A specimen stiff enough to puncture its primary container is being shipped to a reference laboratory. What does the standard add?
opciones: A secondary container that resists puncture as well as leakage, and is labeled
A secondary container that closes and holds fluids, with no puncture requirement
A red bag around the primary container, which substitutes for the outer label
A label stating which portion of the primary container remains contaminated
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (d)(2)(xiii) builds up in three steps. The specimen goes in a container that will not leak. If the outside of that container becomes contaminated, subparagraph (B) puts it inside a second leakproof container that is labeled or color-coded. And subparagraph (C) adds the extra requirement here: when the specimen itself could puncture the primary container, the secondary one must be puncture-resistant on top of everything else. The label naming the contaminated portion is for equipment being serviced, under (g)(1)(i)(H).

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Sections 7.1.2 and 7.1.4
preguntas.subtema: CPT D3 k74 complications · PBT II.I complications · CCMA 3E13 · NCMA 2C.10
preguntas.pregunta: A heel-prick that goes too deep in a neonate can infect which structure?
opciones: The heel bone (calcaneus), causing osteomyelitis
The tibial artery, causing septic arteritis
The plantar fascia, causing chronic fasciitis
The posterior tibial tendon, causing tendinitis
preguntas.explicacion: Osteomyelitis of the heel bone, the calcaneus, is one of the complications of capillary sampling the WHO names. The depth rules exist to avoid it: no heel-prick beyond 2.4 mm, avoid the posterior heel where skin to bone is 2.33 mm in a 3 kg baby, and use the medial or lateral plantar surface where the distance is 3.32 mm. The tibial artery risk is laceration, not infection.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), section 2.2.3 Step 5 Disinfect the entry site
preguntas.subtema: Skin preparation for cultures · CPT D4 4A k75 · PBT II.F technique · CCMA 3E k139 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: In the WHO's venipuncture steps, the routine skin prep is a 70% alcohol swab for 30 seconds. Which collection is explicitly excluded from that routine prep?
opciones: A blood culture, which uses a different site preparation
A draw for potassium or uric acid, which uses povidone-iodine
A capillary puncture of the heel in a newborn
A draw from a patient who has an IV line in the other arm
preguntas.explicacion: Step 5 of the WHO procedure applies the 70% alcohol swab for 30 seconds, followed by 30 seconds of drying, unless the collector is drawing blood cultures or preparing for a blood collection, which have their own skin preparation. The same step notes that alcohol is preferred over povidone-iodine precisely because iodine contamination can falsely raise potassium, phosphorus and uric acid, so those tests are not an exception.

preguntas.fuente: ADA.gov, ADA Requirements: Effective Communication, Use of Accompanying Adults or Children as Interpreters
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k16 · PBT II.B · CCMA 6D k195 · CMA F.1.c(2)(4) / 2027 F.1.d(1)(3) · RMA I.D.1.c · NCMA 2B.2
preguntas.pregunta: A deaf patient who uses sign language comes for a draw without an interpreter. Under the ADA effective-communication rules, what may the clinic NOT do?
opciones: Require the patient to supply her own interpreter, family or friend
Offer video remote interpreting, if the connection meets the standards
Exchange written notes for a short, simple question at the counter
Let a companion interpret when the patient asks and the companion agrees
preguntas.explicacion: The ADA puts the duty of effective communication, interpreters included, on the covered entity, and the entity may not tell a patient to bring somebody along to interpret. VRI is an allowed choice where it works, notes will do for simple exchanges, and a companion may interpret in two situations only: an emergency with an imminent threat, or where the patient asks for it, the adult agrees and it is appropriate.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(3)(iii); OSHA, Hospitals eTool, Hospital-wide Hazards: Latex Allergy
preguntas.subtema: Latex allergy and glove alternatives · CPT D1 1J k36 · PBT VI.G.4.g · CCMA 3C3 k100 · CMA I.B.4.b / 2027 I.B.3.b · RMA III.A.3.a.ii · NCMA 2A.4
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist develops hives after wearing the gloves supplied at work. What must the employer provide?
opciones: Glove liners, powderless or hypoallergenic gloves, or a similar alternative, readily accessible
A prescription antihistamine and a return to the same gloves once the hives have settled
A respirator, because latex protein becomes airborne when powdered gloves are removed
A transfer to duties without patient contact until the allergy has been evaluated
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (d)(3)(iii) wants PPE in the right sizes readily accessible, and specifically that a worker allergic to the gloves normally supplied find within reach glove liners, powderless gloves, hypoallergenic gloves or an equivalent alternative. OSHA's latex allergy page warns against assuming those alternatives are latex-free, and among the options it lists gloves that are synthetic, low in protein or free of powder; it also notes that washing the hands once the gloves come off removes powder and latex left on the skin. The glove exception of (d)(3)(ix)(D) belongs to volunteer blood donation centers alone.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Critical Limits of Laboratory Results for Urgent Clinician Notification" (EJIFCC 2003, PMC6178782), introduction
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5G k93 · PBT VI.A · CCMA 3E13 · NCMA 2C.15
preguntas.pregunta: Two clinics served by the same laboratory ask for different critical limit lists, and one of them wants far fewer parameters. Is that legitimate?
opciones: Yes; the list is agreed with the treating physicians and follows local case mix
No; the limits are fixed nationally and apply to every clinic alike
No; the limits belong to the analyser manufacturer's package insert
Yes, but only where the second clinic performs waived testing alone
preguntas.explicacion: For a critical result to be reported at all, the treating physician and the laboratory have to agree beforehand on what counts as one, and the parameters chosen and the limits set depend on the disease prevalence expected in that clinic or practice. The same idea appears in the quality standard, which leaves the definition of critical results to local agreement with the clinicians who use them.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure (Blood Specimens)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3D5 k121 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.b
preguntas.pregunta: A wound specimen for culture reaches the laboratory in a non-sterile cup that barely covers the bottom. Which two requirements did the collection miss?
opciones: A sterile leak-proof container, and enough material for the full microbiological and serological work
A sterile leak-proof container, and a fixative to hold the organisms until the plates are poured
A tightly lidded transport container, and enough material for the full biochemical work-up
A sterile leak-proof container, and a site chosen away from where the organism is most likely to be
preguntas.explicacion: Specimens for culture belong in sterile, leak-proof containers, and the quantity has to be enough for the whole microbiological and serological examination, not just the first plate. The site is chosen from the clinical picture and from where the causative organism is most likely to be found. A fixative would defeat the purpose, since the organisms have to stay alive.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Stool ova and parasites exam (003756), How the Test is Performed; and MedlinePlus, Lab Tests: Ova and Parasite Test, What happens during an ova and parasite test?
preguntas.subtema: Stool from a diaper · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.2 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(3) / (2)(e) · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A stool specimen for parasites is needed from a child in diapers. How should the parent collect it?
opciones: Line the diaper with plastic wrap placed so urine and stool stay apart, then move the stool to the container
Scrape the stool directly from the absorbent diaper into the container, avoiding the wet areas
Apply an adhesive collection bag over the perianal area, as is done for infant urine samples
Place plastic wrap loosely over the toilet bowl, held by the seat, as for an older child
preguntas.explicacion: For a child in diapers the diaper is lined with plastic wrap positioned to keep urine and stool from mixing, which gives a better sample; the stool is then transferred to the clean container and returned as directed. Plastic wrap over the toilet bowl is the method for patients who use the toilet, and the adhesive bag is a urine device. The container is labeled with name, date and time.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.500(a)-(c), Applicability; 45 CFR 164.502(e); StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", To Whom Does HIPAA Apply
preguntas.subtema: Covered entities and business associates · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k33
preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following is a HIPAA covered entity?
opciones: A health care provider that transmits claims electronically
An outside computer repair company that services the lab's servers
A pharmaceutical sales representative who visits the clinic
An accredited agency that conducts patient satisfaction surveys
preguntas.explicacion: The Privacy Rule binds covered entities, which are health plans, health care providers that transmit health information electronically, and clearinghouses, and it binds business associates as regards a covered entity's PHI; a clearinghouse acting as a business associate follows a narrower set of sections. Outside computer repair firms, survey agencies, equipment companies and pharmaceutical representatives are examples of third parties who reach PHI only through business associate arrangements, which require written satisfactory assurances.

preguntas.pregunta: Which sections of a safety data sheet are meant to be read first, for quick general information about a chemical?
opciones: Sections 1 through 8, from identification to exposure controls
Sections 9 through 11 and 16, the technical and scientific ones
Sections 12 through 15, the ones OSHA does not enforce at all
Sections 4 and 5 alone, on first aid and on fighting the fire
preguntas.explicacion: The sheet is built in blocks. Sections 1 through 8 carry the general information: identification, the hazards, what is in the product, how it is handled safely, and the emergency control measures such as fire fighting; they are written for someone who needs the answer fast. Sections 9 through 11 and 16 hold the technical and scientific detail, and sections 12 through 15 are there for consistency with the international system, their content left to other agencies.

preguntas.pregunta: What did comparison of dedicated phlebotomy teams with staff who have broader duties show?

The teams reached higher rates of contamination, despite equal training
The two groups performed identically once both had the same training
The teams drew more tubes per hour but hemolyzed more specimens
preguntas.explicacion: Laboratory staff and members of phlebotomy teams reach lower contamination rates than staff whose responsibilities are broader, even where the training received is the same. It is one of the arguments for formal training and supervised practice in this procedure.

preguntas.pregunta: A nurse inoculates a blood culture bottle straight from the syringe used for the draw, then fills the second bottle with 1 mL. Which two points of technique were missed?
opciones: Changing the needle before inoculating the bottle, and inoculating about 10 % of the medium volume (3 mL into 30 mL)
Cleaning the bottle bung with alcohol only after inoculation, and inoculating about 50 % of the medium volume
Warming the bottle to 37 °C before inoculation, and inoculating at most 1 mL so that the medium is not diluted
Drawing the culture after the first antibiotic dose, and inoculating 10 mL into each bottle regardless of medium volume
preguntas.explicacion: For blood cultures the syringe needle is swapped before the bottle is inoculated, so skin flora do not ride in; the rubber bung is wiped with iodine both before the injection and again afterwards; and the volume drawn runs to roughly 10 % of the medium, 3 mL into a 30 mL bottle for instance. Ask the laboratory which media suit the organism suspected, and take the set before antimicrobials start whenever that is possible.

preguntas.pregunta: Which information must appear on the label of a reagent, control or calibration material under CLIA?

The CLIA number of the laboratory and the initials of the person who opened it
The manufacturer's lot number and the date of the last calibration verification
The name of the test, the reportable range and the critical values for the analyte
preguntas.explicacion: Reagents, solutions, culture media, control and calibration materials must be labeled with their identity and, when it matters, titer, strength or concentration; their storage requirements; their preparation and expiration dates; and any other information needed for proper use. Materials past their expiration date, deteriorated or of substandard quality must not be used. Writing the date opened on a new vial is the waived-site habit that supports this.

preguntas.pregunta: Under the ISO 22367 definition preferred in the literature, over what span can a laboratory error occur?
opciones: Anywhere in the laboratory cycle, from the ordering of the examination to reporting, interpreting and reacting to the result
Only between receipt of the specimen in the laboratory and release of the result by the analyst who ran it
Only during the analytical phase, since collection and reporting errors are classified as clinical errors
From collection of the specimen to reporting of the result, excluding the clinician's interpretation of it
preguntas.explicacion: ISO 22367 calls a laboratory error either a planned action that is not carried through as intended or a wrong plan chosen to reach the aim, arising anywhere in the laboratory cycle, from the ordering of examinations to the reporting of results and the interpreting of and reacting to them; a more recent wording is any defect between the ordering of tests and the reporting, interpretation and reaction. The older jumble of terms, mistakes, blunders, defects, outliers, quality failures, did not help discussion, so this one is preferred.

preguntas.pregunta: A colleague asks where to place the stethoscope for a blood pressure reading. Where is the brachial pulse felt?
opciones: Just medial to the biceps tendon
Just lateral to the biceps tendon
Directly over the median cubital vein
Just medial to the pronator teres muscle
preguntas.explicacion: The brachial artery crosses the fossa medial to the biceps tendon, and that is where the pulse is palpated and where the stethoscope goes when blood pressure is measured. Knowing the line matters at the bedside, because the artery lies under the same small triangle used for venipuncture.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Microbiology, 16.3 Modes of Disease Transmission, Reservoirs and Carriers
preguntas.subtema: Carriers · CPT D1 1K k11 · PBT VI.G.4.a · CCMA 3C k94 · CMA I.B.3 · RMA III.A.2.a · NCMA 2A.1
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist skips hand hygiene after a patient with an infection and carries the organism to the next patient without becoming infected herself. In epidemiologic terms she is which of these?
opciones: A passive carrier, contaminated but not infected
An active carrier, infected but without symptoms
A biological vector, in which the pathogen reproduces
A nonliving reservoir, like contaminated water
preguntas.explicacion: A carrier is someone who can pass a pathogen on without showing symptoms. A passive carrier is contaminated and can move the pathogen mechanically to another host without being infected, and the microbiology text uses exactly this example: the health worker who does not wash her hands after seeing an infected patient. An active carrier is infected, symptoms or not, and may transmit during incubation or convalescence. Vectors are animals, usually arthropods, and a reservoir is where a pathogen normally lives.

preguntas.pregunta: What can poor infection control during a draw produce, besides risk to the worker?
opciones: Bacterial infection where the needle went in, and contaminated specimens
Bacterial infection where the needle went in, and a lost tube vacuum
Hemolysis of the specimen, and degradation of the tube additive
A prolonged clotting time, and a falsely low platelet count reported
preguntas.explicacion: Weak infection prevention and control practices can lead to bacterial infection at the site where the needle was inserted and to contamination of the specimens themselves. It is one reason the cleaned site is not touched again and single-use devices are never shared between patients.

preguntas.pregunta: What information belongs on the label of each forensic sample container?
opciones: A unique code, the location, the date and time, and the collector's signature
A unique code, the patient's diagnosis, and the ordering provider's signature
The requested analysis, the courier's name, and the receiving clerk's signature
The unique code alone, so that the container carries no identifying detail
preguntas.explicacion: Each container label carries a unique identification code, the place, the date and time it was collected, the collector's name and signature, and a witness's signature where there is one. What analysis is wanted and who receives it belong on the chain of custody form instead, and each evidence bag needs a form of its own.

preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2F 2M k43 · PBT II.B · CCMA 3E1 · NCMA 2C.1
preguntas.pregunta: Before agreeing, the patient asks when the results will be back. How does that question relate to obtaining consent?
opciones: Answer it; consent follows once all questions, including result timing, are addressed
Decline to answer; discussing results in any form is the physician's role alone
Proceed with the draw and refer the question to the front desk afterwards
Ask the patient to sign first, then answer the question while preparing the tubes
preguntas.explicacion: Informed consent is obtained after a comprehensive explanation and discussion, once the patient has acknowledged the procedure-related information and all potential inquiries, including the time it will take for results to return, have been fully answered. Signing before answering, or deferring the question to others, reverses that order.

preguntas.pregunta: What 1-hour value is reported as normal on the glucose screening test used in pregnancy?
opciones: 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or less
155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) or less
180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) or less
95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L) or less
preguntas.explicacion: A blood sugar equal to or below 140 mg/dL an hour after the screening drink is a normal result and means no gestational diabetes; anything higher sends the patient on to the oral glucose tolerance test. Thresholds of 130 and 135 mg/dL are also in use, and the choice is left to the clinician. The 95, 180 and 155 figures are abnormal values of the 3-hour test, not of the screen.

preguntas.pregunta: A 3-year-old needs venipuncture and the mother asks whether she should hold him. What does the WHO guidance say?
opciones: Yes, if she wishes; give full instructions on how and where to hold
No; only trained staff may immobilize a child for a blood draw
No; a child must be immobilized with a mechanical restraint device
Yes, and with the mother holding no second adult is needed
preguntas.explicacion: Chapter 6 has the parent asked whether she would like to help by holding the child; if she does, she is given full instructions on how and where to hold, and if she does not, a second phlebotomist assists instead. One person works as technician while a second adult, parent or phlebotomist, immobilizes the child from the far side of the table. Mechanical restraint devices are a last resort in psychiatric care.

preguntas.pregunta: A patient due for a draw is on several blood thinners. Which team member is suggested as a resource?
opciones: The pharmacist, over the medicines that could complicate the draw
The radiographer, over imaging of the arm before the puncture
The dietitian, over the fasting the patient was asked to observe
The phlebotomy supervisor, over which stopper color to select
preguntas.explicacion: Where a patient is taking blood thinners or other medicines that could bring on unwanted complications, the pharmacist is the person to consult. For difficult venous access the case goes instead to a certified phlebotomist, and everyone involved is expected to know the medical history.

preguntas.pregunta: At which point in the life of a needle do sharps injuries most commonly happen?
opciones: Between the use of the device and its disposal
While the needle is being pushed into the vein
While the packaging is being opened at the tray
After the container has been sealed for collection
preguntas.explicacion: Injuries from sharps commonly occur between the use of a needle or similar device and its disposal, which is the window that recapping, disassembly and a distant sharps container all lengthen. Discarding into a puncture-resistant container straight away markedly reduces these injuries.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Therapeutic drug levels (003430), Normal Results
preguntas.subtema: Timed drug levels · CPT D2 k45 · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139 medication levels · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: A lithium level is ordered for a patient with bipolar disorder. How long after the dose should the blood be drawn, and what is the target range?
opciones: 12 hours after the dose, for a target of 0.5 to 1.2 mEq/L
12 hours after the dose, for a target of 5 to 10 mEq/L
2 hours after the dose, for a target of 0.5 to 1.2 mEq/L
24 hours after the dose, for a target of 1.2 to 2.0 mEq/L
preguntas.explicacion: Lithium is reported with the sample taken 12 hours after the dose, and the target range is 0.5 to 1.2 mEq/L (0.5 to 1.2 mmol/L). The same 12-hour rule applies to cyclosporine, tacrolimus and sirolimus. Ranges of 5 to 10 belong to aminoglycoside levels in mcg/mL, and 0.8 to 2.0 ng/mL is digoxin: mixing the units is what makes these figures easy to confuse.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.6 Blood Typing, Antigens, Antibodies, and Transfusion Reactions
preguntas.subtema: PBT I.B.4 · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.h(4) (2027: I.C.6.g(4)) · RMA I.A.2.a · NCMA 1.1 EKB 1 · CPT Core k5
preguntas.pregunta: A patient receives ABO-incompatible blood. What happens to the transfused red cells, and which organ is at risk of failing?
opciones: Antibodies clump them; hemolysis then overloads the kidneys with hemoglobin
They sickle and lodge in narrow capillaries, starving the brain of oxygen
They are phagocytized by macrophages in the spleen, which fails under the load
Platelets coat them and form thrombi that occlude the coronary arteries
preguntas.explicacion: In a transfusion reaction, antibodies bind the foreign antigens on the donated erythrocytes and clump them together, a process called agglutination; the clumps block small vessels, and as they are degraded (hemolysis) their hemoglobin floods the blood. The kidneys cannot clear that load and the patient can rapidly develop kidney failure. Sickling and thrombi are other disorders entirely.

preguntas.fuente: FDA, Medical Devices with Sharps Injury Prevention Features, Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff (2005), Table 1, Active features
preguntas.subtema: Needle safety devices · CPT D3 3M k66 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k97 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.11
preguntas.pregunta: A safety needle requires the user to activate its shield after the draw. How does the FDA say an active feature should be designed to work?
opciones: It can be activated with one hand, with the hands staying behind the exposed sharp
It can be activated with two hands, so that the shield locks firmly over the needle tip
It activates on its own as the needle leaves the vein, with no user action
It is activated after the needle has been placed in the sharps container
preguntas.explicacion: For active features, those the user must trigger, FDA Table 1 recommends that activation be possible with a single-handed technique that lets the user's hands remain behind the exposed sharp. A two-handed action brings a hand toward the point. Automatic activation describes a passive feature, and the feature is meant to protect during handling before and through disposal, not after.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.1 An Overview of Blood, Plasma Proteins and Blood Plasma; and 18.5 Hemostasis, Common Pathway
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k4 (applied D5) · PBT I.B.3 · CCMA 3E k122 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: Which plasma protein is essential for clotting and is therefore no longer present in serum?
opciones: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Transferrin
Immunoglobulin
preguntas.explicacion: Fibrinogen is the third major plasma protein group, made by the liver and required for coagulation; in the common pathway thrombin turns it into insoluble fibrin. Because serum is plasma with the clotting factors removed, fibrinogen (factor I) is gone from serum. Albumin and the immunoglobulins are not clotting factors, and transferrin is the plasma carrier of iron.
