preguntas.subtema: Labeling · CPT D3 3R k22 · PBT III.B · CCMA 3E12 · NCMA 2C.14 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist collects three patients' tubes and labels them all at the desk afterwards. When and where should tubes be labeled?
opciones: Tube identification and labeling are done in the presence of the patient to avoid misidentification
Labeling at the desk is acceptable if the tubes were kept in separate racks per patient
Labels are applied before the draw, at the desk, so that the tubes are ready when the patient arrives
Labeling may wait until the laboratory receives the tubes with the matching requisitions
preguntas.explicacion: Identifying the tube and labeling it are both done with the patient present, so that a tube is far less likely to be misidentified, and identification data and labeling are double-checked before the blood is withdrawn. Its complications section adds that identifying the patient and labeling the tube are where the likeliest errors of the job happen.

preguntas.pregunta: Tissue typing, a paternity study and a DNA study are requested on the same patient. How many different tube types does the table assign?

preguntas.pregunta: How is therapeutic communication defined, following van Servellen (1997)?
opciones: A verbal and non-verbal exchange meant to help the patient overcome emotional distress
A verbal exchange meant to obtain a complete and accurate medical history quickly
A written and verbal exchange meant to document that informed consent was given
A non-verbal exchange used mainly with patients who are unable to speak
preguntas.explicacion: Van Servellen's now widely accepted definition runs like this: an exchange carried on between provider and patient by both verbal and non-verbal means, whose ultimate aim is to help the patient get past distress of an emotional or psychological kind. Taking a history and obtaining consent are settings where it is used, not the definition itself, and it is not confined to non-verbal channels.

preguntas.pregunta: A clinic in a low-resource setting cannot afford safety-engineered devices. What does the guidance accept?
opciones: A needle and syringe used with skill is accepted in that situation
Draws should be postponed until safety devices can be purchased
Needles may be reused between patients if they are sterilized first
Only capillary sampling should be offered until devices arrive
preguntas.explicacion: Cost drives what a low-resource service can buy, and where safety-engineered devices cannot be had, a needle and syringe used with skill is accepted. What is not negotiable is that every patient gets a sterile needle and syringe, which is why enough supplies have to be stocked.

preguntas.pregunta: An ESR rack sits on a shelf that leans a few degrees away from vertical. How much can that change the result?
opciones: Three degrees off vertical can raise the value by as much as thirty percent
Three degrees off vertical can lower the value by as much as thirty percent
Thirty degrees off vertical can raise the value by as much as three percent
Tilt has no measurable effect once the tube has been standing for an hour
preguntas.explicacion: Tube orientation is one of the technical factors that alters this measurement: tilt and vibration both push the value up, and an angle of three degrees from vertical can raise it by up to thirty per cent. Elevated room temperature and direct sunlight also raise the reading.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Elbow Cubital Fossa", sections Introduction and Clinical Significance
preguntas.subtema: Antecubital anatomy · CPT D3 3F k61 k62 · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: In which layer of the cubital fossa does the median cubital vein actually lie?
opciones: In the roof, superficial to the tendon sheet that reinforces it
In the floor, deep to the brachialis and supinator muscles below
Beside the brachial artery, between the two heads of pronator teres
Under the biceps tendon, which shields it from the skin above it
preguntas.explicacion: The roof of the fossa is skin and fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, and the median cubital vein runs within that roof, which is why it can be reached with a short needle. The floor is formed by brachialis above and supinator below, well away from any superficial vein.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5I k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E k135 k138 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c)
preguntas.pregunta: A light blue citrate tube for PT and aPTT arrives filled to about two-thirds of its nominal volume. Applying the acceptance criteria of the emergency laboratory, what is done?
opciones: It is rejected: under-filled citrate tubes below 80 % of target volume fail acceptance because the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio is wrong
It is accepted for both tests, because prothrombin time remains reliable at 67 % fill and aPTT is only slightly affected
It is accepted for the prothrombin time only, and the aPTT is canceled with a note asking for a properly filled tube
It is topped up with blood from the lavender tube of the same patient to restore the nominal volume before testing
preguntas.explicacion: Insufficient volume gives an inadequate blood-to-anticoagulant ratio, and in citrate tubes that lengthens PT, aPTT and thrombin time and lowers fibrinogen; a clinically significant bias appears below 89 % of fill for aPTT and 78 % for fibrinogen, so the laboratory rejects any citrate tube under 80 % of target. Prothrombin time alone stays fairly reliable down to 67 %, but that does not rescue a tube ordered for both tests, and blood is never moved between tubes.

preguntas.pregunta: A medical assistant phones the provider with a critical fingerstick glucose. What must be documented for that report?
opciones: The result, when it was reported and to whom, and any action taken
The result only; a verbal report to the provider needs no written follow-up
The result and the strip lot number, but not who received the call
The result alone until the referral laboratory has confirmed the value
preguntas.explicacion: A testing site should build a system that says which tests carry critical values, makes sure staff know how to reach the physician quickly, and records when each critical value was reported and to whom; anything communicated verbally is documented and a written report follows. Whenever a critical value comes up, the result and the actions taken both go on the record, since such results often change management on the spot.

preguntas.pregunta: Which two problems have studies found to be the most likely errors in phlebotomy?
opciones: Getting the patient wrong and labeling the tube badly
Nerve injury and increased pain from poor technique
Hematoma formation and prolonged tourniquet time
Contamination between tubes and short draws in citrate tubes
preguntas.explicacion: Nerve injury and increased pain can result from improper technique and hematoma from inadequate pressure, but other studies found identifying the patient and labeling the tube to be where the likeliest errors sit, which is why the chapter insists on identifying the patient and labeling the tubes in the patient's presence. The other options are real risks, not the ones the chapter ranks first.

preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical factors · CPT D3 k9 · PBT II.F · CCMA 3E1 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: A patient scheduled for fasting morning blood work says she had only black coffee and water since dinner 13 hours ago. Is the fasting acceptable?
opciones: No; water is allowed during the fast, but coffee is not permitted that morning
Yes; black coffee has no calories, and 13 hours exceeds the 12-hour minimum fast
No; the fast must be at least 24 hours, the same interval set for alcohol
Yes, provided she also avoided physical activity for the previous 24 hours
preguntas.explicacion: Morning sampling should follow a fast of not less than 12 hours after the last solid meal; water is acceptable during the fast, but other drinks, energy drinks and coffee among them, are not allowed on the morning of the draw. Alcohol is avoided for 24 hours, and outpatients should avoid excessive physical activity for 24 hours; neither turns coffee into an acceptable drink.

preguntas.subtema: Identification and labeling · CPT D3 3R k22 · PBT III.B · CCMA 3E12 · NCMA 2C.14 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: The date of birth on the requisition does not match what the patient states. What should the phlebotomist do?
opciones: Defer the blood sampling until the discrepancy is resolved
Draw the blood and note the discrepancy on the tube label
Use the date of birth on the requisition, since it comes from the record
Use the date the patient states, since the patient is the primary source
preguntas.explicacion: If there is any discrepancy in the identification data, any blood sampling should be deferred until the issue is resolved, and identification and labeling are double-checked before the draw. Drawing first and sorting it out later is the pattern behind the misidentification errors the chapter describes as the most likely mistakes in phlebotomy.

preguntas.pregunta: An outpatient arrives at 8 a.m. for a diagnostic OGTT and mentions eating a sandwich at 3 a.m. What should you do?
opciones: Reschedule; the test needs a 10- to 16-hour fast, and at least 8 hours
Proceed; five hours is enough because the glucose load resets the baseline
Proceed, but skip the fasting sample and draw only at 2 hours
Proceed with a 100-g load instead, to compensate for the meal
preguntas.explicacion: The diagnostic OGTT is done in the morning after an overnight fast: StatPearls gives 10 to 16 hours for ambulatory outpatients and MedlinePlus at least 8 hours with nothing to eat or drink. Five hours meets neither, so the test is rescheduled. The fasting sample cannot be skipped because the 2-hour value is read against it, and the load for a nonpregnant adult stays at 75 g regardless of what was eaten.

preguntas.subtema: CPT D3 3O k71 site by age and weight · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E8 · NCMA 2C.10 · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(e)
preguntas.pregunta: A 14-month-old who already walks and weighs 12 kg needs a skin-puncture sample. Which site is indicated, and why?
opciones: A finger: over 6 months and above 10 kg the finger is indicated, and a walking child's feet may have calluses
The heel: the plantar surface remains the site of choice until the child weighs more than 15 kg
The heel: finger punctures in children under 2 years carry the nerve damage the WHO describes
An ear lobe: the WHO reserves finger-pricks for adults and heel-pricks for neonates and infants
preguntas.explicacion: In a pediatric patient the heel or finger is selected by age and weight: the finger-prick applies over 6 months and above 10 kg. Once a child is walking, the feet may have calluses that hinder blood flow. Nerve damage is listed as a complication of puncturing the fingers of neonates, not of toddlers, and ear lobes are used only rarely, in mass screening or research.

preguntas.pregunta: What does a conventional blood culture set consist of?
opciones: One aerobic bottle and one anaerobic bottle
One aerobic bottle and one gray fluoride/oxalate tube
One anaerobic bottle and one non-additive tube
Two aerobic bottles from two different sites
preguntas.explicacion: A set is one aerobic and one anaerobic bottle, filled from the same venipuncture; the CDC's procedure has the collector draw the first set that way and then repeat the whole sequence for a second set from another site. The gray fluoride tube and the non-additive tube are neighbours in the order of draw, not parts of a culture set, and two bottles from two sites are two incomplete sets, not one.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 20.1 Structure and Function of Blood Vessels, Table 20.1 Comparison of Tunics in Arteries and Veins; and SEER Training Modules, Anatomy & Physiology, Cardiovascular System, Classification & Structure of Blood Vessels
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k6 (applied D3 k62) · PBT I.A.2 I.A.3 · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: Both arteries and veins have three tunics. Which tunic is normally the thickest in an artery, and which in a vein?
opciones: Tunica media in arteries; tunica externa in veins
Tunica externa in arteries; tunica media in veins
Tunica intima in arteries; tunica media in veins
Tunica media in both, since both carry blood under pressure
preguntas.explicacion: The layers from inside out are tunica intima, tunica media and tunica externa. The media, rich in smooth muscle and elastic fibers, is normally the thickest layer in arteries, while in veins the media is thinner than the externa, which is the thickest layer there. Veins have less smooth muscle and connective tissue overall, which is why their walls are thinner than those of arteries.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.157(d)(2), (4), (5) and (6), Selection and distribution; OSHA, Laboratory Safety Guidance (OSHA 3404), Fire safety
preguntas.subtema: Extinguisher placement · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.2 · CMA I.B.8.c / 2027 I.B.7.c · RMA II.B.7.c · NCMA 2A.9
preguntas.pregunta: How far may a worker have to travel to reach an extinguisher for Class A hazards, and for Class B hazards, under 29 CFR 1910.157?
opciones: 75 feet for Class A; 50 feet for Class B
50 feet for Class A; 75 feet for Class B
75 feet for both classes
25 feet for Class A; 50 feet for Class B
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (d) of 29 CFR 1910.157 distributes extinguishers by class of fire: for Class A fires the travel distance to any extinguisher is 75 feet, 22.9 meters, or less; for Class B the distance from the hazard area is 50 feet, 15.2 meters, or less; Class C units follow the pattern of the Class A or B hazard present; and Class D agents are within 75 feet of combustible metal working areas. OSHA's laboratory guidance repeats the 75 and 50 foot figures and notes that solvents and compressed gases make Class B the high-risk category in laboratories.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Vascular Spasm; Extrinsic Pathway; Intrinsic Pathway; Disorders of Clotting
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k8 (applied D3 k74) · PBT I.C · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: How long does the vascular spasm that follows a vessel injury usually last, and what triggers it?
opciones: Up to 30 minutes, at times hours; triggered by endothelins
A matter of seconds, the time the extrinsic pathway needs
A few minutes, the time the intrinsic pathway needs
About 3 hours, until bradykinin dilates the vessel again
preguntas.explicacion: When a vessel is injured the smooth muscle in its wall contracts sharply; the response is thought to be set off by endothelins released by the lining cells and by pain receptors, and it typically lasts up to 30 minutes but can go on for hours. Seconds and minutes are the completion times of the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways, and 3 hours is the window for thrombolytic drugs after a stroke.

preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory measures its stat turnaround time from the moment the specimen is received to the moment the result is reported. Which phases of the total testing process does that interval leave out?
opciones: The collection and transport steps before receipt, and the clinician's review after the report
The analytical phase, because instrument run time is not counted in any turnaround definition
The post-analytical phase, because reporting happens only after the measured interval has ended
None, since receipt-to-report is the complete turnaround time by the usual definition
preguntas.explicacion: Turnaround can be counted collection-to-reporting or receipt-in-laboratory-to-reporting; the second version excludes everything before the specimen arrives, and clinicians commonly use a wider definition that runs from test request to their own review of the result. Turnaround potentially spans all three phases, so the receipt-to-report version is a partial measure, not the complete one.

preguntas.pregunta: Blood cultures are ordered along with routine tubes. What is the glove requirement for this draw?
opciones: Sterile gloves are mandatory when blood cultures are being obtained
Non-sterile gloves are sufficient, as the culture bottle is sealed
Gloves may be omitted if the hands were washed with soap and water
Double gloving is required for cultures to reduce blood transfer in a needlestick
preguntas.explicacion: A new, unused pair of gloves with careful hand washing before and after each patient is recommended for every draw, and wearing sterile gloves is mandatory when planning to obtain blood cultures. Double gloving is mentioned in the needlestick chapter as a way to reduce the volume of blood transmitted in an injury, not as a culture requirement.

preguntas.pregunta: The explanation is done and the patient has agreed. Before the tourniquet, what does the preparation guidance say to ask?
opciones: Which collection sites they would like to see prioritised
Which tube colors the last phlebotomist ended up using
Whether they would rather have a capillary sample instead
Whether they want the results sent to a second clinician
preguntas.explicacion: Informed consent without patient resistance is obtained after the full explanation, and only once every question, including when the results will come back, has been answered. The patient is also asked which collection sites have been convenient before, so those can be prioritised, and at the same point those afraid of testing or with a vagal history are identified.

preguntas.pregunta: A new shipment of glucose strips arrives with an insert that looks identical to the one on file. What should the site do with it?
opciones: Compare it with the current insert, file the new one if anything changed, and tell the other operators
Discard it unread, since the insert already on file is the version the site validated
Keep it sealed in the box so the shipment can be returned if the strips fail control
Post it in place of the quick-reference card, which is no longer needed once inserts are current
preguntas.explicacion: Instructions change without notice and differ between manufacturers of the same test, so the insert is checked with each new lot and shipment, the old version is replaced and filed when changes appear, and the changes are communicated to testing staff and to whoever supervises testing. Quick-reference cards only supplement the complete instructions and may need updating too. In surveys, 21 % of sites never checked.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Characteristics of Leukocytes; and 18.2 Production of the Formed Elements
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k3 (applied D3) · PBT I.C · RMA I.B.2.a · NCMA 1.2 EKB 3 · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4))
preguntas.pregunta: The process by which leukocytes squeeze between the cells of a vessel wall to enter the tissues is called what?
opciones: Diapedesis
Chemotaxis
Phagocytosis
Hemopoiesis
preguntas.explicacion: The exit of white cells through the wall of capillaries and other small vessels is called emigration or diapedesis, from roots meaning to leap through. Chemotaxis is the movement of leukocytes toward chemical signals once they are in the tissue; phagocytosis is the engulfing of pathogens or debris; and hemopoiesis is the production of the formed elements in the marrow.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Blood Glucose Monitoring", section Clinical Significance (Hypoglycemia)
preguntas.subtema: Hypoglycemia levels · CPT D5 5G k93 · PBT IV.A.4 · CCMA 3D3 k116 · CMA I.C.10.c.(1) · RMA III.C.4.d
preguntas.pregunta: An alert patient with diabetes who feels shaky has a meter glucose of 48 mg/dL (2.7 mmol/L). Under the classification used for hypoglycemia, what level is this?
opciones: Level 2, below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), the threshold where neuroglycopenic symptoms begin and immediate action is required
Level 1, between 54 and 70 mg/dL (3.0 to 3.9 mmol/L), the threshold for the adrenergic counter-regulatory response
Level 3, because any glucose below 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) is defined as a severe event regardless of the symptoms
Not hypoglycemia, since the meter's capillary sample reads about 10 % lower than a venous plasma sample would
preguntas.explicacion: The ADA scheme has three levels: level 1 is a glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) but at or above 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L); level 2 is below 54 mg/dL, the point at which neuroglycopenic symptoms begin and immediate action is required; level 3 is a severe event defined by altered mental or physical functioning that needs another person's help, whatever the glucose value. At 48 mg/dL an alert patient is at level 2.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.524(b)(1) and (b)(2), Requests for access and timely action
preguntas.subtema: Right of access deadline · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k220 · CMA II.E.1.c · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3C k36
preguntas.pregunta: A patient asks for a copy of her lab results. Under HIPAA, how long does the covered entity have to act on the request?
opciones: No later than 30 days after receipt, with one possible 30-day extension explained in writing
No later than 60 days after receipt, the same limit as breach notification
No later than 15 days after receipt, the same limit as the OSHA written opinion after exposure
No later than 10 working days, with unlimited extensions if the record is large or on paper
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.524(b)(2) requires action on an access request no later than 30 days after receipt, either granting access or giving a written denial; if the entity cannot act in time it may take one extension of no more than 30 days, provided it tells the individual in writing, within the original period, the reason and the date it will finish. The entity may require requests in writing if it says so. Sixty days is the breach notification limit and 15 days the OSHA written opinion; neither governs access.

preguntas.pregunta: A mobile phlebotomy team works at several sites during one shift. Where may the safety data sheets for its chemicals be kept?
opciones: At the primary facility, if the worker can get the information at once
Only in the vehicle, where a paper copy has to travel with the team
At the site being visited, with a copy left behind after each visit

preguntas.explicacion: The general rule is that the employer keeps the sheets in the workplace and makes them readily accessible during each work shift while employees are in their work areas; electronic access is fine as long as it puts no barrier in the way. preguntas.pregunta: A survey of clinical biochemists asked which quality practices their laboratories actually had in place. Which of these was the weakest area?
opciones: A written critical limits list, held by just over half of them
An electronic handbook, held by just over half of them
Advice on interpreting results, offered by just over half of them
Turnaround time discussions with clinicians, held by half of them
preguntas.explicacion: Among 335 respondents, 84 % had an electronic handbook, 80 % gave help interpreting laboratory data and 75 % talked turnaround times over with the clinical staff, but only 58 % kept a written list of critical limits. That is a striking gap, given that the handling of critical results is one of the two priority areas the accreditation criteria single out.

preguntas.subtema: Needle safety devices · CPT D3 3M k66 · D1 1G k30 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C8 k108 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: How much of the percutaneous injury burden can safety-engineered devices avoid, and what undoes that gain?
opciones: Up to seventy-five percent; disassembly, recapping, or not activating the feature
Up to twenty-five percent; disassembly, recapping, or not activating the feature
Up to seventy-five percent; using them on pediatric rather than adult patients
Up to ninety-nine percent; storing them in a tray rather than in the packaging
preguntas.explicacion: Replacing conventional devices with engineered ones can avoid as much as seventy-five percent of percutaneous injuries. The gain is lost when the device is taken apart, when the needle is recapped by hand, or when the safety feature is simply never activated, and exposure to blood then follows.

preguntas.subtema: Tubes and additives · CPT D3 k57 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E k135 k136 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A coagulation test (prothrombin time) is ordered. Which tube does it require, and what is the additive?
opciones: A light blue top tube with sodium citrate, always filled completely
A purple top tube with EDTA, which also removes calcium, filled completely
A red top clot activator tube, spun so the serum can be tested
A light gray fluoride/oxalate tube, which also requires a full draw
preguntas.explicacion: The WHO table lists the light blue coagulation tube for tests such as protime and prothrombin time. Its additive is sodium citrate, which binds calcium as calcium salts and so keeps the blood from clotting, and the table marks it as one of the tubes that needs a full draw. EDTA works the same way on calcium, but the table assigns it to hematology and cross-match, not coagulation; the red top carries a clot activator and gives serum, which a clotting test cannot use; and the gray fluoride/oxalate tube, which also needs a full draw, is the glucose tube.

preguntas.pregunta: A provider orders a routine urinalysis for a patient coming in tomorrow. Which specimen should the medical assistant ask the patient to bring, and why?
opciones: The first void of the morning, because urine that collected overnight is more concentrated
A random specimen collected two hours after breakfast, because food raises the analyte levels
A 24-hour collection, because a single void cannot be dipped reliably for protein or glucose
A specimen collected after drinking a liter of water, because dilute urine is easier to read
preguntas.explicacion: First-void or morning urine is considered the best specimen for routine testing: the urine that accumulates in the bladder overnight is more concentrated, which reflects the kidneys' ability to concentrate and lets the strip detect trace substances that a dilute sample would miss. Random, postprandial and 24-hour collections exist, but each is ordered for a specific purpose, not for the routine dipstick.

preguntas.fuente: ADA.gov, ADA Requirements: Effective Communication, Use of Accompanying Adults or Children as Interpreters
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k16 · PBT II.B · CCMA 6D k195 · CMA F.1.c(2)(4) / 2027 F.1.d(1)(3) · RMA I.D.1.c · NCMA 2B.2
preguntas.pregunta: The deaf patient's 11-year-old daughter offers to interpret the pre-draw questions. Under the ADA guidance?
opciones: Not permitted; a minor may interpret only in an imminent-threat emergency
Permitted, provided the patient requests it and the child agrees to help out
Permitted, because the pre-draw questions are short and simple
Permitted, as long as a staff member witnesses the exchange
preguntas.explicacion: Using people's children as interpreters has proved particularly problematic. The ADA's two exceptions differ by age: where an emergency involves a threat that is imminent, an adult or a minor child may be relied on if no qualified interpreter is at hand; outside an emergency only an accompanying adult may, and only where the patient asks, the adult agrees and it is appropriate.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1241(c)(3), Standard: Test request
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5F · PBT III.B · CCMA 3D k112 · NCMA 2C.1 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.a
preguntas.pregunta: A requisition lists the patient's name and the tests ordered but nothing else about the patient. Which of these does CLIA require the requisition to solicit?
opciones: The patient's sex and age or date of birth
The patient's address and insurance number
The patient's weight and current medications
The patient's room number and attending nurse
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR 493.1241(c) lists what the test requisition must ask for: the authorized person requesting the test with a contact for alert values, the patient's name or unique identifier, the sex and the age or date of birth, the tests to be performed, the specimen source when appropriate, the date and, if appropriate, the time of collection, and any further information needed for accurate testing. Insurance data, weight and location are not on that list.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Peripheral Line Placement", section Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
preguntas.subtema: Needle safety devices · CPT D3 3M k54 k66 · PBT II.J VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3E3 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: Which drawbacks have users reported with safety cannulae compared with standard ones?
opciones: Slower flashback, more friction, and harder threading of the line
Faster flashback, less friction, and a lower price for each device
Slower flashback, less friction, and no possibility of blood splatter
Faster flashback, more friction, and a needle that cannot be shielded
preguntas.explicacion: Users report feeling safer with these devices, but they cost more and can make insertion harder: the flashback appears more slowly, there is greater friction as the cannula is advanced, and threading it into the vein is more difficult. Firing the mechanism may also raise blood splatter.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.6 Blood Typing, ABO Transfusion Protocols
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k5 (applied D4 4D) · PBT I.B.4 · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: An emergency patient is typed AB positive. Which blood types could he theoretically receive, and why?
opciones: Any type, since his plasma carries neither anti-A nor anti-B
Only AB+, since both antigens must match the donor exactly
Only O−, since that is the type of the universal donor
Any Rh− type, since Rh+ cells would sensitize the patient
preguntas.explicacion: The AB positive patient is the universal recipient: with both A and B antigens on his own cells he makes neither anti-A nor anti-B, and as an Rh positive person he can take Rh positive or Rh negative blood. Matched blood is still preferred, because the donor's plasma brings its own antibodies. An Rh positive recipient is not sensitized by Rh positive cells; that risk belongs to Rh negative people.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Prothrombin Time", section Interfering Factors
preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical error · CPT D3 3N k9 k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: Which single fault explains both an unreliable clotting result and the loss of the specimen that produced it?
opciones: A clot in the tube, which uses up the very factors being measured
A tube filled to its line, which leaves the anticoagulant in excess
A tube inverted six times, which shears the fibrin strands apart
A tube kept at room temperature, which activates factor VII early
preguntas.explicacion: When a specimen clots, the clotting factors are consumed inside the tube and whatever the analyser then measures cannot be trusted. Clots follow a traumatic puncture, activation inside the device or poor mixing. Room temperature is the correct storage; it is refrigeration that activates factor VII.

preguntas.fuente: NIA, Talking With Your Older Patients, Compensating for hearing deficits
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k15 k16 · CCMA 6D k195 · CMA F.1.c(2) / 2027 F.1.d(3) · RMA I.D.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: You are moving from the fasting question to the allergy question with a patient who has hearing loss. How should that shift be signalled?
opciones: Pause briefly, speak a little louder, or gesture towards the new topic
Repeat the last sentence twice before beginning the new question
Write out the whole of the new question before speaking any of it
Wait until the patient asks what is going to be discussed next
preguntas.explicacion: The advice is to signal that the subject is changing: pause a moment, lift the voice slightly, gesture toward the new subject, touch the patient gently, or put a question. A notepad is kept to hand for the important points, diagnoses, treatments and terms, and amplification devices are used where the clinic has them.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Chain of Custody", sections Custody of the Evidence and Importance of the Chain of Custody
preguntas.subtema: Chain of custody · CPT D5 5C k91 · PBT III.A.4 · CCMA 3E k127 chain of custody
preguntas.pregunta: What has to be entered on the chain of custody form every time the charge of a specimen changes hands?
opciones: A signature, the date and the time of the transfer
A signature and the reason the transfer was needed
The initials of a witness and the storage temperature
A photograph of the seal and the receiving room number
preguntas.explicacion: Every change of charge is entered with a signature and the date and time, so the paper trail shows who held the specimen at any moment and can put that person on the stand. Each handover from one person to the next is documented, and that is what establishes that nobody else could have reached it without authorization. There is no cap on the number of transfers, but keeping them few is crucial.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 2.3, Recommended order of draw
preguntas.subtema: Order of draw · CPT D3 3J k59 · PBT II.H.1 · CCMA 3E6 k132 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.7
preguntas.pregunta: A chemistry panel is ordered in a plain red clot activator tube and a serology test in a gold serum separator tube. Which is filled first according to the WHO table?
opciones: The red clot activator tube, then the gold serum separator tube
The gold serum separator tube, then the red clot activator tube
Either one, since both yield serum and share the same position
The gold tube first, because its gel must be reached by more blood
preguntas.explicacion: Table 2.3 separates the two serum tubes: the red top with clot activator is position 4 and the serum separator tube, red-gray tiger or gold, is position 5. Both produce serum after centrifugation, but the table does not merge them into one position, and it gives no rule about gel volume. The red tube is drawn before the gold one.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Taking a step back from testing: Preanalytical considerations in molecular infectious disease diagnostics" (Clin Biochem 2023, PMC9729171), section 5 Specimen processing
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A 5D · PBT III.C
preguntas.pregunta: Reagents are short and a laboratory proposes pooling specimens for a widespread infection instead of running each one. Which two drawbacks are raised against that?
opciones: False negatives from dilution, and a longer turnaround when a pool must be broken up and re-run
False positives from carry-over, and a longer turnaround when a pool must be broken up and re-run
False negatives from dilution, and the loss of the internal control each specimen would carry
False negatives from inhibitors, and the extra reagent the pooling was supposed to be saving
preguntas.explicacion: Pooling is routine in blood banks and was adopted more widely as an answer to exponential demand with unreliable supply. For a prevalent infectious disease it carries two costs: dilution can push a positive out of reach and yield a false negative, and turnaround grows because the individual samples of a reactive pool have to be run again to confirm who is infected.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, Section 16: Other Information
preguntas.subtema: SDS section 16 · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k106 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A clinic wants to know whether the safety data sheet in its binder is the current version. Which section settles that?
opciones: Section 16, which gives the date of preparation or of the last revision
Section 1, which gives the product identifier and the supplier's address
Section 15, which gives the regulations in force for that product
Section 3, which gives the composition and the concentration ranges
preguntas.explicacion: Section 16 is where the sheet says when it was prepared or last revised, and it may also point out where the changes were made compared with the previous version; the supplier can be asked to explain them. Any other useful information goes here as well. Section 15, the regulatory section, is one of the four that OSHA does not enforce, and neither the identification nor the composition section carries a revision date.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Clean catch urine sample (007487), After Collecting the Sample; and PMC, PMC3936984 Delanghe & Speeckaert, Preanalytical requirements of urinalysis (2014), Transport and preservation
preguntas.subtema: Home clean-catch storage · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.1 / V.D.3 · CCMA 3D5 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(2)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.i · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A patient collected a clean-catch specimen at home at 7 a.m. and cannot bring it to the office until noon. What should she have been told to do with it?
opciones: Screw the lid on tightly, put the cup in a plastic bag and keep it in the refrigerator until she brings it in
Leave the cup capped on the kitchen counter at room temperature, since refrigeration would alter the cells
Keep the cup in an inside coat pocket so the specimen stays at body temperature during transport
Freeze the specimen at home and let the office thaw it later, since freezing preserves it better than cold
preguntas.explicacion: After collecting, the patient closes the lid tightly without touching the inside of the cup or lid; when the sample is collected at home it goes into a plastic bag in the refrigerator until it can be delivered. Room temperature lets bacteria multiply, freezing is not an accepted substitute for refrigeration in urine preservation, and body-temperature transport in a coat pocket is the instruction for a semen sample, not urine.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(f)(4)(ii), Information Provided to the Healthcare Professional
preguntas.subtema: What the evaluator receives · CPT D1 1H k33 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k109 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.c III.C.5 · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: After a needlestick, which information must the employer send to the healthcare professional who evaluates the exposed employee?
opciones: The employee's duties in the incident, the route and circumstances, and the source results
The employee's job title, the brand of the device, and the department where it happened
A summary of the annual training and the names and qualifications of the trainer
The signed declination form and the dates of the employee's last three exposures
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (f)(4)(ii) lists five things the evaluating professional receives: a copy of the regulation, a description of what the employee was doing when the exposure happened, documentation of the route and the circumstances, the source individual's blood results if they exist, and the medical records the employer keeps that matter for treatment, vaccination status included. The device brand and the work area are what the sharps injury log records under (h)(5)(i); training content and trainer qualifications belong to the training record in (h)(2)(i).

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, How to Understand Your Lab Results, section What can affect my results
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K k46 k48 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 k128 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following is a common factor that can affect the accuracy of test results?
opciones: Exercising hard before the test
Sitting for 15 minutes before the draw
Drinking plain water during the fast
Having the draw done in the morning
preguntas.explicacion: The common confounders are eating or drinking certain things, certain medicines and supplements, hard exercise shortly before the test, being on a menstrual period, and whether the preparation instructions, fasting among them, were actually followed. Sitting beforehand, plain water and a morning appointment are all things the other sources recommend, not confounders.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Tests: Prothrombin Time Test and INR (PT/INR), What happens during a PT/INR test?; StatPearls, "Prothrombin Time", section Specimen Collection
preguntas.subtema: Fingerstick PT/INR · CPT D4 4G · PBT IV.A.3 · CCMA 3D2 · CMA I.C.10.b.(5) INR (2027: b.(8)) · RMA III.C.4.b
preguntas.pregunta: What sample does a fingerstick PT/INR meter use?
opciones: A drop of capillary whole blood placed directly on the test strip
Citrated plasma separated from a light-blue-top tube by centrifugation
Serum from a clotted red-top tube after the clot has been removed
Anticoagulated whole blood transferred from a lavender-top tube
preguntas.explicacion: With a fingertip method, in the office or at home, a small needle punctures the finger, a drop of blood is placed on a test strip or special instrument, and the strip goes into a small device that calculates the result. Laboratory coagulation tests, by contrast, are run on citrated plasma, never on serum, because the clotting factors are consumed when serum forms. Patients on long-term warfarin may be trained to self-test this way.

preguntas.fuente: NIOSH, Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risk Factors (Feb. 13, 2025), Prevention: Reporting
preguntas.subtema: Information to report · CPT D1 1N k39 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k97 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.11
preguntas.pregunta: Which information does NIOSH say to collect when reporting a needlestick?
opciones: Date and time, the procedure, the device with brand and model, and the department
The source patient's diagnosis and insurance, and the worker's vaccination card
The lot number of the gloves worn and the brand of disinfectant on the counter
The names of all patients drawn that shift and the time each was seen
preguntas.explicacion: NIOSH lists what to gather: the date and time of the exposure, the procedure or action being performed, specific details such as profession, department or unit, shift and whether the injured person was the device user, and the specific type of device with brand and model when known. These details feed the sharps injury log, which records the device type and brand, the work area and how the incident occurred, including depth of injury and whether a safety feature was activated. Patient insurance and glove lot numbers are not on the list.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Taking a step back from testing: Preanalytical considerations in molecular infectious disease diagnostics" (Clin Biochem 2023, PMC9729171), section 3.5 Inhibitors: Endogenous and exogenous
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A 5B · PBT III.A.2
preguntas.pregunta: A markedly hemolyzed EDTA specimen is sent for a molecular assay and the laboratory is worried about inhibition. Which substances present in blood are listed as endogenous inhibitors?
opciones: Immunoglobulin G, hemoglobin and its heme metabolites, lactoferrin, and antivirals such as aciclovir
Immunoglobulin M, albumin and fibrinogen, and antibiotics such as vancomycin given before the draw
Citrate and EDTA carried over from the tube, plus the separator gel and the surfactant on it
Urea and polysaccharides, plus the bile salts and glycolipids that reach the blood from the gut
preguntas.explicacion: In whole blood, serum and plasma the endogenous inhibitors named are lactoferrin, hemoglobin, heme metabolites, immunoglobulin G and antivirals such as aciclovir. Hemoglobin and hematin lower the activity of DNA polymerase and quench free fluorescent dyes, while hemin and bilirubin compete with the template. Urea, polysaccharides and bile salts belong to urine and stool.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A k87 · PBT III.C · CCMA 3E11 k136 · NCMA 2C.6 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(d)
preguntas.pregunta: An emergency department keeps sending serum samples that reach the laboratory with fibrin after a very short wait. Which tube change did the study laboratory plan to make?
opciones: Switch to rapid serum tubes, which speed up clotting and shorten processing while improving serum quality
Switch to heparin plasma tubes, which contain no clot activator and so cannot form any fibrin at all
Switch to serum separator tubes with gel, which trap the fibrin below the barrier during centrifugation
Switch to citrate tubes filled completely, which keep the fibrinogen in solution until testing
preguntas.explicacion: To prevent fibrin formation the laboratory planned to use rapid serum tubes, described as tubes that accelerate coagulation, reduce processing time and increase serum quality, a fit for emergency departments and intensive care units. Gel separator tubes do not solve early spinning and are refused for therapeutic drug monitoring; heparin and citrate tubes give plasma, which is a different specimen.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Transmission-Based Precautions (April 3, 2024), Airborne Precautions
preguntas.subtema: Airborne Precautions in transport · CPT D1 1I k34 k36 · PBT VI.G.4.c · CCMA 3C3 k100 · CMA I.B.4.b / 2027 I.B.3.b · RMA III.A.2.b · NCMA 2A.3
preguntas.pregunta: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis must be taken to radiology. What does the CDC say about the escort's respiratory protection during transport?
opciones: No respirator is needed in transport if the patient wears a mask and infectious lesions are covered
A fit-tested N95 is always required for the escort, whether or not the patient is masked
A surgical mask on the escort is sufficient, because the patient is out of the isolation room
Transport is prohibited; imaging must be done inside the airborne infection isolation room
preguntas.explicacion: Inside the room, Airborne Precautions require a fit-tested, NIOSH-approved N95 or higher respirator for personnel. For transport, which the CDC limits to medically necessary purposes, the patient wears a surgical mask if possible and observes cough etiquette, and the CDC states that staff transporting such a patient do not need a mask or respirator during the move when the patient is masked and any infectious skin lesions are covered. The rule is specific to transport; it does not replace the respirator at the bedside.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Preparation
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2C 2M k42 · PBT II.A II.B · CCMA 3E1 3E2 · NCMA 2C.1
preguntas.pregunta: Before the draw, which points does the phlebotomist double-check and then share with the patient?
opciones: Identity, the purpose of the draw, the tests to be run, and the exact volume to be taken
Identity, the expected results, and the reference ranges for each test ordered
Identity, the tube colors needed, and the order of draw that will be followed
Identity, the diagnosis code, and the physician's working differential diagnosis
preguntas.explicacion: The patient's identification, the purpose of the procedure, whether diagnostic sampling or therapeutic phlebotomy, the specific tests to be run and the exact amount of blood are all double-checked; telling the patient each of those makes them more comfortable and sets a professional tone. Results and diagnoses are not the phlebotomist's to discuss.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Semen Analysis", Specimen Requirements and Procedure; and MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Semen analysis (003627), How the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Semen collection container · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.B.1 / V.D.2 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a
preguntas.pregunta: A patient cannot produce a semen sample by masturbation and asks about collecting it during intercourse. What must he be told?
opciones: A nontoxic collection condom supplied by the provider is used; ordinary latex condoms are not acceptable
An ordinary latex condom is acceptable as long as it is rinsed with sterile saline before it is used
Collection during intercourse is never acceptable, because the first fraction is always lost that way
A nontoxic collection condom is used, and the specimen is then frozen until it reaches the laboratory
preguntas.explicacion: When masturbation into a clean, wide-mouthed container is not possible, semen may be collected in a special condom given by the provider. Latex is excluded because the chemicals in those condoms damage sperm viability and motility. Whatever the method, every fraction of the ejaculate has to be collected and any loss reported to the laboratory, and the specimen is held between 20 and 37 degrees Celsius, never frozen.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Blood Glucose Monitoring", section Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings, Oral Glucose Tolerance Test
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K k46 · PBT II.D II.G · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: Before an oral glucose tolerance test a patient asks about the old advice to load up on carbohydrate for three days. What is the current position?
opciones: Updated evidence suggests it may not be needed for every patient
It stands as a firm requirement of 150 g daily for three days
It was replaced by a 24-hour fast in place of the eight-hour one
It applies now only to patients who are already taking insulin
preguntas.explicacion: Individuals were traditionally told to take at least 150 g of carbohydrate a day for three days beforehand, to avoid a false-positive result. Newer evidence indicates that eating carbohydrate freely in the days before makes no significant difference to the outcome in most clinical situations, so that preparation may not be needed for everyone. The eight-hour fast stands.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Ready?: Who Should Perform QC Testing and How Often?; CDC, MMWR RR-54(13) (2005), Frequency of control testing
preguntas.subtema: When to run external controls · CPT D1 1F · PBT IV.B.3 · CCMA 3D k115 · CMA I.C.9.c · RMA III.C.3.d
preguntas.pregunta: A clinic receives a new shipment of rapid strep kits with a different lot number, and a newly hired assistant will start running the test. At a minimum, when should external controls be run?
opciones: With the new shipment, with the new lot number, and by the new operator before patient testing
Once with the new shipment; a lot change and a new operator do not call for controls
Only when the manufacturer's insert makes external controls mandatory for that kit
Each day patient samples are tested, with two levels of control, as for all waived tests
preguntas.explicacion: The site must test controls at least as often as the manufacturer's instructions say, and good practice adds three minimum triggers: each new shipment of reagents or kits, any change in lot number, and each new testing person. Frequency is then adjusted for the stability of the test, environmental upsets such as power outages or temperature swings, and how experienced the staff are. Two levels every day is the nonwaived rule.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Influenza Specimen Collection guide (2024), Nasopharyngeal Swab; and StatPearls, "Overview of the Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", Throat and Nasal Swabs
preguntas.subtema: Transport medium · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.D.3 · CCMA 3D5 k113 · CMA I.C.8.c · NCMA 2C.15
preguntas.pregunta: After a nasopharyngeal swab is withdrawn, what happens to it?
opciones: Its tip goes into a tube of viral transport medium and the applicator stick is snapped off
Its tip goes into a dry sterile tube and the applicator stick is left long for handling
Its tip is rolled onto a glass slide, air dried, and sent with the applicator attached
Its tip goes into a tube of normal saline and the applicator stick is snapped off
preguntas.explicacion: The swab tip is placed into a sterile tube holding 1 to 3 mL of viral transport medium and the applicator stick is snapped or cut off so the cap can seal. Rolling a specimen onto slides for smears is what is done with the nasal swab collected for direct microscopic examination, and plain saline is what is instilled during a nasal wash, not the medium the swab travels in.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.3 Erythrocytes, opening paragraph and Shape and Structure of Erythrocytes
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k4 (applied D5) · PBT I.B.4 · CCMA 3E k122 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: A CBC on a man reports 5.4 million red cells per microliter. How does that compare with the reference values?
opciones: It matches the typical male value; women average about 4.8 million
It is high; men average about 4.8 million and women about 5.4 million
It is high; the reference count is 5,000 to 10,000 per microliter
It is normal only if reticulocytes are under 25 percent of the count
preguntas.explicacion: A man averages roughly 5.4 million red cells in every microliter and a woman about 4.8 million, so this result is ordinary for him. A count of 5,000 to 10,000 per microliter belongs to the white cells instead. Reticulocytes run 1 to 2 percent of the red cells; the 25 percent figure is the share of all the body's cells that are red cells, not a ceiling for reticulocytes.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.508(b)(4), Prohibition on conditioning of authorizations; 164.508(a)(3)
preguntas.subtema: Conditioning treatment on authorization · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k220 · CMA II.E.2.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3C k36
preguntas.pregunta: May a clinic refuse to draw a patient's blood unless she signs an authorization releasing her results to a marketing company?
opciones: No: treatment may not be conditioned on an authorization, with narrow exceptions
Yes: a covered entity may set any condition it discloses in its notice
Yes, if the marketing company has signed a business associate agreement
No, unless the patient pays out of pocket and in full, which removes the restriction
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.508(b)(4) forbids making treatment, payment, enrollment or the eligibility for benefits hang on the individual signing an authorization. The exceptions are narrow: research-related treatment conditioned on a research authorization, a health plan's enrollment or underwriting authorization sought before enrollment, and care given solely to create PHI for a third party. Marketing needs an authorization of its own under 164.508(a)(3), and a business associate agreement covers services performed for the covered entity, not marketing by an outside company.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Does Pneumatic Tube System Transport Contribute to Hemolysis in ED Blood Samples?" (West J Emerg Med 2016, PMC5017839), Methods, Sample Analysis; and PMC, "Preanalytical phase - a continuous challenge for laboratory professionals. Biochemia Medica 2012 (PubMed Central PMC4062337, acceso abierto)" (PMC4062337)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5G k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E13 k138
preguntas.pregunta: A potassium sample is flagged by the analyzer as mildly hemolysed (HK) rather than grossly hemolysed (GHEMO). How was this handled in the hospital that measured the hemolysis index on every potassium?
opciones: The numerical result was reported with a cautionary comment; only grossly hemolysed samples were rejected
Both categories were rejected and a redraw was requested, since potassium is the analyte most affected
The result was corrected with a formula based on the index and reported without any comment
Only tube-transported samples were flagged, since hand-carried ones cannot pick up hemolysis
preguntas.explicacion: In that laboratory the hemolysis index is measured on every plasma and serum sample sent for potassium, whichever way it traveled; when hemolysis is detected the record shows either grossly hemolysed and rejected, or mildly hemolysed with a cautionary comment attached to the numerical result. Correction formulas for the degree of hemolysis have been shown unreliable and potentially misleading, because the release of cell components into the serum is not homogeneous.

preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomy service cut its needlestick rate from 1.5 to 0.2 per 10,000 venipunctures. What was behind that drop?
opciones: Training, changed work practices, safety devices, and encouraging reporting
Fewer draws per shift, and a bonus for each month without an injury
Double gloving for every draw, and a second worker at each bedside
Replacing every vacuum tube holder with a syringe and transfer device
preguntas.explicacion: In the reported case the service brought its rate down over three years, against a national median of about 0.94 per 10,000 venipunctures, through a bundle rather than a single change: worker education, changes in work practices, devices with safety features, and active encouragement of injury reporting, on top of the published guidelines and the bloodborne pathogens standard. preguntas.pregunta: A clinic switches to a tube manufacturer whose stopper colors do not match the chart on the wall. What does the WHO advise about color codes and additives?
opciones: Verify the recommendations with the local laboratory, since codes can differ
Follow the colors of the previous manufacturer, since the additive sequence is standard
Draw the coagulation tube first in every case, because it needs a full draw
Apply the WHO table as printed, because it fixes the color for every manufacturer

preguntas.subtema: Complications: petechiae · CPT D3 3L k68 · PBT II.I II.K · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: After the tourniquet is released, a patient's forearm shows a scatter of red dots about 1 mm across that do not fade when pressed. What are they called?
opciones: Petechiae
Purpura
Ecchymosis
Erythema
preguntas.explicacion: Petechiae are pinpoint non-blanching spots under 2 mm affecting skin and mucous membranes, caused by bleeding into the dermis; a non-blanching spot over 2 mm is purpura. A very large bruised area is an ecchymosis, and erythema, unlike bleeding into the skin, does blanch when pressed. Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, coagulation disorders and loss of vascular integrity are the underlying causes.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Informed Consent", section Clinical Significance and section Function
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2F k43 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.a (both outlines) · RMA I.C.1.a · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: How is the weight of the patient's signature in informed consent described today?
opciones: Its value as proof of understanding is questioned, and communication is favored
It is the single element the accreditation body checks when it reviews a record
It is needed only for procedures that carry a risk of serious bleeding
It moves responsibility for a bad outcome from the clinician to the patient
preguntas.explicacion: Adequate informed consent counts as a patient safety issue, and leaning on a signature as proof that the patient understood is increasingly doubted; the process is moving toward communication and away from signatures. The elements still have to be documented, whether on a form, in progress notes or elsewhere in the record.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Detection of haemolysis, a frequent preanalytical problem in the serum of newborns and adults" (EJIFCC 2020, PMC7109500), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E k138 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: In a neonatal unit many samples are icteric. Why does this make visual screening for hemolysis even less dependable?
opciones: The high bilirubin colors the serum and leads to underestimation of hemolysis by eye
Bilirubin binds free hemoglobin, so the hemolysis index reads falsely low on the analyzer
Icteric serum cannot be centrifuged fully, so the red cells stay suspended in the sample
Bilirubin makes the serum turbid, which is mistaken for lipemia rather than hemolysis
preguntas.explicacion: Neonatal samples usually carry a high bilirubin, and that biases the eye further towards missing hemolysis when the judgment is visual; it is one more argument for assessing hemolysis, icterus and lipemia automatically and objectively. The index itself is a spectrophotometric measurement the paper treats as the reliable reference, and turbidity marks lipemia, not bilirubin.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Influenza Specimen Collection guide (2024), Nasopharyngeal Swab and Deep Nasal Swab
preguntas.subtema: NP swab depth · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.C.2 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(5)(c) · NCMA 2B.20
preguntas.pregunta: How far should a nasopharyngeal swab be inserted?
opciones: To a depth equal to the distance from the nostril to the outer opening of the ear
To a depth of less than one inch, until resistance is felt at the turbinates
To a depth equal to the distance from the nostril to the outer corner of the eyelid
To a depth of about two inches, or until the patient begins to cough or gag
preguntas.explicacion: The head is tilted back 70 degrees, the swab goes in until it has reached a depth equal to the distance from the nostril to the outer opening of the ear, and it is left several seconds to soak up secretions before being withdrawn slowly while rotating. Less than one inch, to the turbinates, is the deep nasal swab instead. Both nostrils are done with the same swab.

preguntas.subtema: Sharps disposal · CPT D1 1G k30 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C8 k108 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: What features does the FDA describe for a cleared sharps disposal container?
opciones: Puncture-resistant plastic, leak-resistant sides and bottom, and a tight puncture-resistant lid
Transparent flexible plastic with a wide open top so the fill level is always visible
A lined cardboard box marked with the biohazard symbol, emptied by hand when three-quarters full
Any closable metal can, provided it is labeled and kept away from the patient
preguntas.explicacion: FDA-cleared sharps containers are built of plastic a needle cannot pierce, with sides and a base that do not leak and a tight lid that a needle cannot go through, and used sharps go into them immediately. When no cleared container is available, a stout plastic household container, a laundry detergent bottle for instance, is the alternative given; an open top, a cardboard box or hand emptying contradict those features.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Medical Ethics", Issues of Concern
preguntas.subtema: PBT VI.E Professional Ethics · CPT D1 1D k26 ethical standards · CCMA 7C codes of ethics · RMA I.C.4.a proper ethics in practice
preguntas.pregunta: A patient refuses the draw after the procedure has been explained, and the phlebotomist stops. Which ethical principle is being honored?
opciones: Respect for autonomy, the patient's ability to decide free of outside control
Beneficence, the duty to act in what is judged to be the patient's best interest
Nonmaleficence, the duty to avoid causing the patient any harm that is avoidable
Distributive justice, the duty to treat patients equitably when resources are short
preguntas.explicacion: Four principles dominate the ethics codes: beneficence, advocating what serves the patient; nonmaleficence, not harming; distributive justice, equal or equitable treatment when more than one patient is involved; and autonomy, preserving the patient's ability to decide independently of outside control. A refusal that stops the procedure is autonomy overriding the clinician's own view of what would be good.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Does Pneumatic Tube System Transport Contribute to Hemolysis in ED Blood Samples?" (West J Emerg Med 2016, PMC5017839), Results and Conclusion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.D.4 · CCMA 3E k144 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A hospital compared hemolysis in 15,851 ED specimens sent by pneumatic tube with 92 hand-carried during system downtime. What did it find, and what did the authors advise?
opciones: No significant difference (13.6 % vs 13.1 %); each system is unique, so every facility should examine its own
A large increase with the tube system (13.6 % vs 3.3 %); hospitals should hand-carry all ED specimens
Less hemolysis with the tube system (10.3 % vs 13.1 %); faster delivery protects the red cells
No difference, which proves that pneumatic tube systems can never contribute to hemolysis anywhere
preguntas.explicacion: The proportions of hemolysed specimens were 13.6 % by pneumatic tube and 13.1 % hand-carried, with no statistical difference, and the result held for gross and mild hemolysis separately. Because other hospitals have seen large increases after installing a system, and features such as speed, distance and packing differ, the authors encourage each facility to consider whether its own transport method contributes to hemolysis rather than generalising.

preguntas.pregunta: In which respects does phlebotomy practice differ most between countries and institutions?
opciones: Technique, training, safety devices, disposal, device reuse and hepatitis B vaccine
Technique, tube color codes, room lighting, chair design and staffing levels
Training, laboratory opening hours, courier routes and analyser brands used
Safety devices, billing codes, appointment systems and record retention rules
preguntas.explicacion: Drawing blood is one of the commonest invasive procedures in health care, yet practice varies widely from country to country, and between institutions and individuals inside one of them. The differences named are technique, training, use of safety devices, disposal, reuse of devices and hepatitis B vaccine.

preguntas.pregunta: Under the Hazard Communication standard, which of these is classified as a health hazard rather than a physical hazard?
opciones: Skin corrosion or irritation
A flammable liquid such as a solvent
A gas under pressure in a cylinder
An oxidizing liquid or solid
preguntas.explicacion: The eTool splits the classifications into two families. On the health side: acute toxicity; corrosion or irritation of the skin; serious eye damage or eye irritation; sensitization of the airways or of the skin; germ cell mutagenicity; carcinogenicity; toxicity to reproduction; target organ toxicity; and aspiration hazard. On the physical side: explosives; gases under pressure; flammables and oxidizers; substances that are self-reactive, pyrophoric or self-heating; organic peroxides; anything corrosive to metal; and substances that release flammable gas on contact with water.

preguntas.pregunta: Speaking clearly at eye level has still not got the post-draw instructions across to a patient with hearing loss. Which two further measures does the guidance name?
opciones: Write the points that matter on a notepad, and use an amplification device if the clinic has one
Write the points that matter on a notepad, and book the follow-up in a quieter room later on
Print the points in large type on the discharge sheet, and use an amplification device if there is one
Have the patient repeat the points back, and use an amplification device if the clinic has one
preguntas.explicacion: Two things sit in the guidance alongside the tone of voice and the face at eye level. Keep a notepad within reach and write down what has to survive the visit — the diagnosis, the treatment, the terms that matter — and reach for an amplification device where the clinic or the hospital has one. Enlarged print belongs to the measures for poor eyesight, not for poor hearing, and while the change of subject is meant to be signalled clearly, nothing there asks the patient to recite the instructions back.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Formation of the Platelet Plug

preguntas.pregunta: Bleeding from a small puncture stops within minutes, before any fibrin has formed. Which step of hemostasis is doing the work, and which plasma glycoprotein stabilizes it?
opciones: The platelet plug, stabilized by von Willebrand factor
The fibrin mesh, which factor XIII cross-links and stabilizes
The vascular spasm, which serotonin from platelets maintains
Fibrinolysis, which plasmin made from plasminogen carries out
preguntas.explicacion: In the second step of hemostasis, platelets meet the exposed collagen, become spiked and sticky and clump together, helped by a plasma glycoprotein called von Willebrand factor that stabilizes the growing plug. The plug can temporarily seal a small opening and buys time for coagulation. Factor XIII stabilizes fibrin, serotonin keeps the vessel constricted, and plasmin dissolves the finished clot.

preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist fills the light gray fluoride tube before the purple EDTA tube. What is the main risk?
opciones: Additive carried from one tube into the next, giving unreliable results
Loss of the vacuum in the purple tube as soon as it is pushed on
A short draw in the gray tube, which can haemolyse that specimen
Clotting in the purple tube, because its additive was left unmixed
preguntas.explicacion: A fixed sequence exists so that the additive of one tube is not carried into the tube filled next, and falsely raised or lowered values can follow in chemistry, hematology, serology and microbiology. A short draw and unmixed additive are real faults, but they come from filling and mixing, not order.

preguntas.subtema: Order of draw · CPT D3 3J k59 · PBT II.H.1 · CCMA 3E6 k132 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.7
preguntas.pregunta: Which tube in the WHO order of draw is filled immediately before the purple EDTA tube when a full set is collected?
opciones: The light green PST with lithium heparin and gel
The dark green sodium heparin tube
The pale yellow acid-citrate-dextrose tube
The red-gray tiger top or gold serum separator tube
preguntas.explicacion: EDTA is position 8 in Table 2.3, and position 7 is the light green plasma separator tube with lithium heparin and a gel separator. The dark green sodium heparin tube is position 6, the serum separator tube position 5, and the pale yellow ACD tube comes after EDTA at position 9. Reading the table by neighbours is the surest way to reconstruct the whole sequence.

preguntas.subtema: Syringe transfer · CPT D3 k54 k9 · PBT II.F · CCMA 3E7 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.9
preguntas.pregunta: Blood from a syringe has to go into a sample tube that has no rubber stopper. How is it transferred?
opciones: Injected extremely slowly, keeping pressure and speed to a minimum
Injected as briskly as possible so the tube fills before it can clot
Poured down the inner wall of the tube after the needle is removed
Injected only after the needle has been recapped for the transfer
preguntas.explicacion: Where there is no rubber stopper to pierce, the blood is injected extremely slowly, because keeping the pressure and the velocity of the transfer low is what limits hemolysis. The instruction that closes that step is not to recap and remove the needle afterwards.

preguntas.subtema: Tube inversions · CPT D3 3N k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: After a blood culture bottle is filled, how many times should it be mixed?
opciones: 8 to 10 times
3 to 6 times
1 or 2 times
15 to 20 times
preguntas.explicacion: A culture bottle is mixed 8 to 10 times after the blood is added so that the contents combine properly. The 3 to 6 inversions belong to the light blue citrate tube in the coagulopathies review, done immediately after the draw. One or two turns is the kind of under-mixing the review links to small clots, and 15 to 20 is not a figure given for any tube.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Preparation
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2L k48 · PBT II.D II.I · CCMA 3E1 k126 k128 · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.3
preguntas.pregunta: Why is a history of a vagal attack during earlier draws sought out before the needle comes out?
opciones: So the team is ready with the means to act should a faint happen
So the draw can be logged as high risk and handed to a nurse
So the tourniquet time can be cut to under thirty seconds
So the patient can be given a sugary drink to break the fast
preguntas.explicacion: Particular attention goes to spotting the patient who is frightened of blood testing, or who has a positive history of a vasovagal attack during an earlier procedure of the kind, so that every means of acting on a vagal syncope is ready beforehand. Simple steps such as counting down may cut anxiety a great deal, and a severe history of panic attacks may call for lying the patient down.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1291(h), Standard: Test report
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5E 5H · PBT VI.B VI.F · CCMA 3E15 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: The chemistry analyzer goes down and a stat troponin ordered from the emergency department will not be reported within the laboratory's established time frame. What does CLIA require?
opciones: The laboratory decides, based on the urgency of the test, whether to notify the appropriate person of the delay
The laboratory must notify the ordering person of every delayed result, regardless of the urgency of the test
The laboratory must refer the specimen to another CLIA-certified laboratory within 30 minutes of the failure
The laboratory may wait until the analyzer is repaired, since delays are addressed only by its accreditor
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR 493.1291(h) says that where the laboratory cannot get patient results out inside the time frames it has set for itself, it has to weigh the urgency of the tests ordered and decide whether the appropriate individuals should be told about the delay; a stat cardiac marker is the sort of request where that decision leans toward notifying. The rule neither demands notice for every delay, nor sets a referral deadline, nor lets the laboratory say nothing.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Contraindications
preguntas.subtema: Contraindications and palpation · CPT D3 k61 k62 · PBT II.E II.I · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.3
preguntas.pregunta: On palpation, a vein feels hard and cord-like from previous punctures. Which contraindication does this represent?
opciones: Venous fibrosis on palpation
A vascular graft in the arm
Cellulitis or abscess
Ipsilateral radical mastectomy
preguntas.explicacion: Venous fibrosis on palpation is one of the local contraindications, alongside a site attempted before that has been left with scar tissue. A vascular graft, cellulitis or abscess and a history of radical mastectomy on the same side are separate entries in the same list, each with its own history or appearance rather than a fibrotic feel of the vein itself.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Bacteria Culture Test, Wound Culture; and MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Skin or nail culture (003762), How the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Wound culture collection · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.C / V.D.1 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(5)(b) · NCMA 2B.20
preguntas.pregunta: How is a specimen taken for a wound culture?
opciones: A special swab picks up cells or pus; for a deeper wound a syringe draws fluid or a biopsy is taken
A special swab picks up cells or pus; for a deeper wound the drainage is squeezed onto a glass slide
The wound is irrigated with sterile saline and the runoff is caught in a sterile container
A dry dressing is left on the wound overnight and then sent to the laboratory in a sealed bag
preguntas.explicacion: Wound cultures look for infection in open wounds or burns. A swab collects cells or pus from the surface, and when the wound is deeper a syringe is used to draw out fluid or a piece of tissue is biopsied. Most disease-causing bacteria are ready to read in one to two days, though some need five days or more. A skin or nail culture is collected with a swab or blade instead.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Lactose tolerance tests (003500), How the Test is Performed; StatPearls, "Lactose Intolerance", section Evaluation: Diagnostic Tests
preguntas.subtema: Lactose testing · CPT D4 4H lactose tolerance · PBT V.C.3 breath testing
preguntas.pregunta: Which method is preferred for diagnosing lactose intolerance?
opciones: The hydrogen breath test
The lactose tolerance blood test
The stool acidity test
A small bowel biopsy
preguntas.explicacion: Measuring hydrogen in exhaled air is the method of choice: the patient breathes into a balloon-type container, swallows a flavored liquid holding lactose, and samples of breath are taken at set times to follow the hydrogen level. Very little of it is normally exhaled, so a rise points to lactose that was neither broken down nor absorbed. A biopsy is invasive and is kept for ruling out other causes such as celiac disease.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Latex Allergy", sections Introduction, Pathophysiology and History and Physical
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2L k48 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k128 · RMA III.C.4.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: A 'true' latex allergy is which type of reaction?
opciones: Type I, IgE-mediated, with symptoms within minutes of exposure
Type IV, delayed, caused by the chemical antioxidants added in processing
Irritant contact dermatitis from friction or chemical contact
Type IV, delayed, caused by inhaling the cornstarch powder on gloves
preguntas.explicacion: A true latex allergy is a type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE antibodies bound to the rubber proteins; within minutes the patient may develop hives, wheezing, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, and systemic reactions up to anaphylaxis are possible. The processing chemicals cause a delayed type IV reaction, and irritant dermatitis is a non-immune reaction, neither of them a true allergy.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Antiepileptic Drug Monitoring", section Other Issues, Trough Versus Free Levels; and section Function
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k45 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e
preguntas.pregunta: For which antiepileptic drugs is the trough level said to matter most?
opciones: Those with short half-lives, since the trough marks the between-dose minimum
Those with long half-lives, since the level then reflects long-term usage
Those given intravenously, since the peak arrives with the infusion
Those newly substituted between a brand and a generic preparation
preguntas.explicacion: A trough is the concentration at its lowest, typically just before the next dose falls due, and it matters most for an antiepileptic whose half-life is short, since the trough marks the minimum reached between doses. Phenytoin's long half-life is why its level reflects long-term usage, and monitoring can guide dosing where a substitution cannot be avoided.
