preguntas.subtema: Additives · CPT D3 k57 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E3 k136 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(d) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: What does the light green PST contain, and what kind of sample does it provide?
opciones: Lithium heparin plus a gel separator; plasma for chemistries
Sodium heparin without gel; plasma for lithium and ammonia levels
A clot activator plus a gel separator; serum for chemistries
Potassium oxalate plus sodium fluoride; plasma for glucose
preguntas.explicacion: Table 2.3 describes the PST as a light green tube holding lithium heparin as anticoagulant plus a gel separator, whose gel separates the plasma at the bottom of the tube; its use is chemistries. The dark green tube holds sodium or lithium heparin without gel, the serum separator tube has gel but no anticoagulant and gives serum, and oxalate with fluoride is the gray glucose tube.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, PMC5580822, Hall et al., Influence of Hematocrit and Total-Spot Volume on Performance Characteristics of Dried Blood Spots for Newborn Screening, Introduction and Conclusions
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4C k81 filter paper technique · PBT III.A.4 newborn screening acceptability
preguntas.pregunta: Why are the printed circles on a newborn screening card sized as they are?
opciones: A 12 to 13 mm circle is just filled by 75 µL, so it guides the collector to an adequate volume
A 12 to 13 mm circle holds exactly one 3.2 mm punch, so each printed circle equals one laboratory test
A 12 to 13 mm circle is the diameter of a newborn heel drop, so one drop fills one circle
A 12 to 13 mm circle prevents the hematocrit from changing the volume in each punch
preguntas.explicacion: By the CLSI standard for collection cards, printed circles have an inner diameter of 12 to 13 mm, 75 µL of blood just fills the area and 100 µL fills slightly beyond the print, so the circles guide the collector to neither too little nor too much blood. Laboratories can see at a glance when a spot falls well short of the 75 to 100 µL target. Hematocrit still alters the punch.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Dialysis Fistula", sections Clinical Significance and Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
preguntas.subtema: Contraindications · CPT D3 3F k62 · D2 k49 · PBT II.E II.I · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: A dialysis patient's arm carries a fistula with a palpable vibration under the fingertips. What does that vibration mean, and what is avoided on that arm?
opciones: A thrill, meaning the fistula is patent; draws, venous access and cuff readings are avoided
A thrill, meaning the fistula has clotted; draws and cuff readings may go ahead as usual
A pulsation, meaning the fistula is patent; only intravenous fluids are avoided on that arm
A pulsation, meaning steal syndrome has begun; the arm is used only for capillary sampling
preguntas.explicacion: Laying the fingertips lightly over a fistula picks up a thrill, a vibration that means the fistula is open, and a thrill is distinguished from a merely pulsating fistula. To protect veins for dialysis, peripheral access, blood draws and blood pressure readings are kept off that side.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Hematocrit", section Testing Procedures
preguntas.subtema: Microhematocrit centrifugation · CPT D4 4G · PBT IV.A.2 · CCMA 3D2 · CMA I.C.10.b.(1) · RMA III.C.4.b.i
preguntas.pregunta: For a spun microhematocrit, at what speed and for how long is the sealed capillary tube centrifuged?
opciones: 11,000 to 12,000 rpm for 4 to 5 minutes
Roughly 3,000 rpm for 25 to 30 minutes
11,000 to 12,000 rpm for 10 to 15 minutes
1,500 to 2,000 rpm for 4 to 5 minutes
preguntas.explicacion: The microhematocrit method fills a capillary tube some 75 mm long and 1 mm across, seals both ends with clay or heat, and spins it at 11,000 to 12,000 rpm for 4 to 5 minutes before it is read against the holder scale or a card reader. The 3,000 rpm, 30-minute spin belongs to the older macrohematocrit method with a Wintrobe tube, which the capillary method has largely displaced.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.1 An Overview of Blood, Characteristics of Blood
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k4 (applied D3) · PBT I.B.4 · CCMA 2A k38 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: How does the viscosity of blood compare with that of water, and what does that viscosity affect?
opciones: Roughly five times that of water; it raises resistance to flow
Roughly twice that of water; it raises resistance to flow
Roughly five times that of water; it lowers resistance to flow
Roughly the same as water, since plasma is 92 percent water
preguntas.explicacion: Blood is viscous and sticky, with a viscosity about five times that of water, owing to the plasma proteins and the formed elements. Viscosity is resistance to flow, and it has a dramatic effect on blood pressure and flow: honey resists flow more than water, and blood behaves the same way relative to water. Plasma being mostly water does not make whole blood flow like water.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Sputum Culture, Will I need to do anything to prepare for the test?; and MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Urine culture (003751), Considerations
preguntas.subtema: Antibiotics before sputum culture · CPT D2 k48 · PBT V.D.2 · CCMA 3D k117 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A patient about to give a sputum culture mentions he is on an antibiotic. What is the correct response?
opciones: Record it and tell the provider, since antibiotics can affect bacterial growth in the culture
Tell him to skip today's dose, since antibiotics can affect the bacterial growth in the culture
Ignore it, since antibiotics reach the bloodstream and not the airway secretions
Postpone the collection for 4 weeks, the interval used before a urea breath test
preguntas.explicacion: Antibiotics can suppress the growth the culture depends on, so the medication is documented and reported; the patient is told not to stop anything unless the provider says so. That is the same rule as in urine culture, where recent antibiotics can produce a false negative. The four-week hold belongs to the urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Glucose screening tests during pregnancy (007562), What Abnormal Results Mean; StatPearls, "Gestational Diabetes", Evaluation
preguntas.subtema: Gestational OGTT values · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139
preguntas.pregunta: Which set of values is read as abnormal on the 3-hour, 100 g glucose tolerance test in pregnancy?
opciones: Fasting 95, 1 hour 180, 2 hours 155, 3 hours 140 mg/dL
Fasting 92, 1 hour 180, 2 hours 153, 3 hours 140 mg/dL
Fasting 95, 1 hour 155, 2 hours 180, 3 hours 140 mg/dL
Fasting 99, 1 hour 200, 2 hours 140, 3 hours 126 mg/dL
preguntas.explicacion: The 100 g test is abnormal at 95 mg/dL or more fasting, 180 or more at one hour, 155 or more at two hours and 140 or more at three hours. The 92 / 180 / 153 trio belongs to the one-step 75 g test, which stops at two hours and has no third value. Fasting 60 to 99, under 200 at one hour and under 140 at two hours are the nonpregnant reference figures, a different scale altogether.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Chain of Custody", section Custody of the Evidence
preguntas.subtema: Chain of custody · CPT D5 5C k91 · PBT III.A.4 special sample types · CCMA 3E k127
preguntas.pregunta: Under chain of custody rules, when is a sample considered to be in custody?
opciones: In the authorized custodian's own possession, in a secured place
In a locked laboratory refrigerator, whoever holds the key to it
In the courier's vehicle, once the transport form has been signed
In the collector's work area, as long as the seals stay unbroken
preguntas.explicacion: A sample counts as in custody when the authorized custodian physically has it, holds it somewhere secured, no unauthorized person can reach it and no opening for tampering exists. Both halves matter: a specimen left unattended in a room others can walk into is not in custody, and neither is one held by somebody who never signed for it on the form.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 1.1.1
preguntas.subtema: Fill level and ratios · CPT D3 k9 k51 k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: How does underfilling a tube contribute to hemolysis?
opciones: The ratio of anticoagulant to blood ends up greater than one to nine
The ratio of anticoagulant to blood ends up smaller than one to nine
The vacuum left in the tube pulls the red cells against the stopper
The additive settles at the bottom and never reaches the red cells
preguntas.explicacion: Among the recognized causes of hemolysis is underfilling a tube so that the proportion of anticoagulant to blood rises above one to nine. It is the same arithmetic that lengthens clotting times in a short-drawn citrate tube, where the plasma is outnumbered by the anticoagulant.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Glucose Tolerance Test", sections Testing Procedures and Interfering Factors
preguntas.subtema: OGTT preparation · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.D II.B pre-collection instructions · CCMA 3E k139 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: A patient has followed a strict low-carbohydrate diet for a week before an OGTT. Why is that a problem?
opciones: The test requires 3 days of unrestricted diet with at least 150 g of carbohydrate a day
The test requires 3 days of fasting so that glycogen stores are emptied first
The test requires a low-carbohydrate diet only on the day before, not for a week
The test requires the same diet the patient will follow after diagnosis
preguntas.explicacion: For at least three days before the OGTT the patient must eat an unrestricted diet containing 150 g or more of carbohydrate per day, keep normal activity and avoid unusual or vigorous exercise; a week of carbohydrate restriction invalidates the conditions of the test. The only fast is the 10- to 16-hour one immediately before the morning of the test. MedlinePlus puts it simply: eat normally for several days beforehand.

preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K k46 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: Which activity should patients avoid while fasting for a blood test?
opciones: Chewing gum during the fasting hours
Drinking plain water during the fasting hours
Taking a medicine the provider said to continue
Brushing teeth within 30 minutes of the draw
preguntas.explicacion: Besides not eating or drinking anything but plain water, there are three things not to do while fasting: chew gum, smoke, or exercise. Plain water is allowed, and usual medicines are continued unless the provider says to stop. The 30-minute rule about brushing and flossing belongs to the cortisol saliva test, not to a blood draw.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion; PMC, "Critical Limits of Laboratory Results for Urgent Clinician Notification" (EJIFCC 2003, PMC6178782), introductory text
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E k138 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.b
preguntas.pregunta: A blood sample for potassium and glucose was drawn from the arm carrying a dextrose infusion, through the IV catheter as it was placed. Which two problems does the literature attach to this practice?
opciones: Higher hemolysis from flow through the narrow catheter, and contamination by the infusion fluid
Formation of fibrin clots in the serum, and dilution of the anticoagulant in the tube
Falsely low potassium from the catheter material, and bacterial contamination of the tube
Air bubbles that lower the blood gas values, and loss of vacuum in the evacuated tube
preguntas.explicacion: Blood taken from an indwelling catheter, or while an IV is being started, hemolyses more often than a straight venipuncture, which the study puts down to flow through the narrow tubing; samples contaminated by an intravenous infusion made up 2.2 % of that laboratory's rejections. The critical-limits paper adds the classic case: a glucose drawn through a line running glucose gives a falsely critical figure that a properly collected sample clears up.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Microbiology, 16.3 Modes of Disease Transmission, Contact Transmission and Vehicle Transmission; and StatPearls, "Universal Precautions" (NBK470223)
preguntas.subtema: Droplet vs airborne · CPT D1 1I k34 · PBT VI.G.4.a · CCMA 3C k94 · CMA I.B.3 · RMA III.A.2.a · NCMA 2A.1
preguntas.pregunta: What distance separates direct droplet transmission from airborne transmission in the microbiology definition?
opciones: About one meter: droplets travel a meter or less; airborne goes farther
About three meters: droplets travel three meters or less
About six feet: droplets travel six feet or less; airborne travels farther
There is no distance; the difference is whether a mask was worn
preguntas.explicacion: When a person coughs or sneezes, droplets of mucus that may carry pathogens are ejected; direct droplet transmission covers distances of one meter or less and is treated as a form of contact transmission, while transmission over more than one meter is called airborne and is classed as vehicle transmission through the air. Fine droplets can stay suspended, travel far, and dry into droplet nuclei; tuberculosis is the classic airborne example, needing as few as 10 organisms to infect. The 3 to 6 feet figure is the clinical rule of thumb for Droplet Precautions, a different framework.

preguntas.fuente: SAMHSA, Urine Specimen Collection Handbook for Federal Agency Workplace Drug Testing Programs (2024)
preguntas.subtema: Drug screen temperature · CPT D4 4J k86 · PBT V.C.5 · CCMA 3E k127 · RMA III.C.4.a.i · CMA I.C.7.a(2)(f)
preguntas.pregunta: A urine specimen for a federal drug test reads 27°C three minutes after the void. What does the collector do?
opciones: Collect a second specimen under direct observation and send both for testing
Warm the container in the hand and read the temperature again in four minutes
Discard the specimen and start over with the ordinary collection procedure
Accept it and write the reading on the remarks line of the custody form
preguntas.explicacion: A reading outside 32° to 38°C is marked out of range on the form, and the collector then takes a second specimen under direct observation, sending both of them to a laboratory certified by HHS rather than to an instrumented initial test facility. A comment goes on the remarks line too, but the comment alone does not make the specimen acceptable, and rewarming it is not an option.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(f)(3)(iii)(A) and (B), Post-exposure Evaluation and Follow-up
preguntas.subtema: Baseline sample and consent · CPT D1 k33 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k97 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.c III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.11
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist stuck by a used needle agrees to have her blood drawn but refuses HIV testing that day. What does the standard require of the sample?
opciones: Keep it at least 90 days so the employee may still choose to have it tested for HIV
Test it for HIV anyway, since consent to the blood draw covers the serologic testing
Discard it, since HIV testing requires a fresh sample drawn after consent is given
Keep it 30 days, the period in which the written opinion has to be provided
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (f)(3)(iii)(B) separates the two consents. If the employee agrees to baseline collection but not, at that moment, to HIV serology, the sample is preserved for at least 90 days; should she decide within those 90 days to have it tested, the test is run as soon as feasible. Testing without her consent is not allowed, and throwing the sample away would defeat the purpose of the rule. The written opinion has its own deadline, 15 days, and is unrelated to the storage period.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Needlestick", Epidemiology: Impact of Safety Devices on Needle Stick Injuries
preguntas.subtema: A device is not a program · CPT D1 1A k12 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k123 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.e · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A hospital brings in safety-engineered devices and its injury rate does not fall. Which two problems have been reported in that situation?
opciones: Trouble working the safety mechanism, and needles still discarded improperly
Shortage of sharps containers, and gloves supplied in only one size
Poor lighting at the bedside, and tubes filled in the wrong order
Late reporting of injuries, and no written exposure control plan
preguntas.explicacion: Safety-engineered devices are in wide use, yet the drop in injuries has not always followed. One study saw the rate move from 1.9 to 2.2 injuries for every 100 workers once the devices were in place, and two explanations came up most often: staff had trouble operating the safety mechanism, and needles went on being discarded improperly. Both are matters of training and work practice, which is why buying a device is only one piece of a prevention program.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Lactose Intolerance", section Evaluation: Diagnostic Tests
preguntas.subtema: Lactose tolerance protocol · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139 timed specimens
preguntas.pregunta: In the protocol for the lactose tolerance blood test, what load is given and when are the glucose measurements taken?
opciones: 50 g of lactose, with glucose measured at 0, 60 and 120 minutes
75 g of lactose, with glucose measured at 0, 60 and 120 minutes
50 g of lactose, with glucose measured at 0, 30 and 60 minutes
100 g of lactose, with glucose measured at 0, 120 and 180 minutes
preguntas.explicacion: The test gives 50 g of lactose and measures glucose at 0, 60 and 120 minutes; a rise of less than 20 mg/dL points to intolerance, with 75% sensitivity and 96% specificity. The 75 g and 100 g loads are glucose, not lactose, and belong to the oral glucose tolerance tests. False negatives turn up in diabetes, in small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and with delayed gastric emptying.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Prothrombin Time", section Interfering Factors
preguntas.subtema: Fill level and ratios · CPT D3 k51 k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A trainee asks how much blood a commercial citrate tube should receive. What is the answer?
opciones: A line printed on the tube marks the volume of blood to be drawn
The vacuum stops the flow well before the tube can be overfilled
The color of the stopper sets the volume for every manufacturer
The laboratory calculates it from the patient's hematocrit result
preguntas.explicacion: Blood for these assays is collected into commercially prepared tubes that already hold their trisodium citrate, and each carries a line showing the volume of blood that should go in. Drawing short of that line leaves too much anticoagulant and lengthens the clotting time measured.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Chain of Custody", section Chain of Custody in Clinical/Medical Drug Testing
preguntas.subtema: Clinical versus legal testing · CPT D5 5C k91 · PBT III.A.4 · CCMA 3E k127 · RMA III.C.4.a.i · CMA I.C.7.a(2)(f)
preguntas.pregunta: A urine drug screen is run on a patient in the emergency department for medical management only. Is a chain of custody required?
opciones: No: a purely clinical result is confidential and cannot be used against the patient
Yes: every drug screen carries the same documentation, regardless of purpose
No: chain of custody applies only to blood specimens, never to urine specimens
Yes: emergency department specimens always travel under a custody form
preguntas.explicacion: A medical drug test result is confidential and cannot be turned against the person in a disciplinary or a penal proceeding, which is why no chain of custody is required for it. It becomes essential once an initial positive immunoassay has to be confirmed for use in court, as after an accident or where the case may go to trial. The matrix is not what decides it.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Sections 1.1.1 and 2.1.4
preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical error · CPT D3 3B k9 k58 · PBT II.J VI.G · CCMA 3E3 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A clinic short of tubes refills used ones by hand with anticoagulant. Why is that listed as a hazard?
opciones: Refilled tubes carry inappropriate amounts of anticoagulant and haemolyse
Refilled tubes carry too little vacuum and stop drawing after a few drops
Refilled tubes carry the wrong stopper color and confuse the sequence
Refilled tubes carry a broken gel barrier and mix serum back into cells
preguntas.explicacion: Reusing tubes refilled by hand with the wrong amount of anticoagulant appears among the causes of hemolysis. It is the practice that stocking enough tubes is meant to prevent, along with decanting blood from one tube into another to make the supply stretch.

preguntas.fuente: HHS OCR, Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (page as of January 31, 2025)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2A k17 k18 · CCMA 7A k214 · CMA E.1 / 2027 E.4 · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: Section 1557 of the ACA, as enforced by HHS OCR, prohibits discrimination in covered health programs on which grounds?
opciones: Age, race, color, disability, national origin or sex
Race, color, religion, national origin or marital status
Sex, disability, insurance status or preferred language
Age, national origin, income level or immigration status
preguntas.explicacion: Section 1557 bars discrimination, in a covered health program or activity, on grounds of age, race, color, disability, national origin or sex, and sex is read to take in sex characteristics, gender identity, sexual orientation and pregnancy, subject to the court stays the page lists as of January 2025. Religion, insurance status, income and immigration status are not on the list.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure (Fecal Samples)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A 5B · PBT V.B III.D.1 · CCMA 3D5 k121 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A stool specimen arrives for viral studies and the processor is told to prepare it before it goes into storage. Which sequence matches the published procedure?
opciones: About 1 mL of stool into 9 mL of sterile buffered saline, spun 30 minutes, supernatant below −40 °C
About 1 mL of stool into 9 mL of alkaline peptone water, spun 30 minutes, supernatant at 2 to 8 °C
About 1 mL of stool into 10 mL of sterile buffered saline, spun 10 minutes, whole tube at −20 °C
About 5 mL of stool into 9 mL of sterile buffered saline, spun 30 minutes, pellet frozen below −40 °C
preguntas.explicacion: For suspected viral infection the feces go into sterile buffered saline, roughly 1 mL into 9 mL, and the mixture is then spun for half an hour. What is kept is the supernatant, not the pellet, and it is frozen and stored below −40 °C until testing. Alkaline peptone water belongs to a different set-up: it is the enrichment broth used when cholera is suspected.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Fibrinolysis; and Plasma Anticoagulants
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k8 (applied D3 k74) · PBT I.C · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: A week after a venipuncture the small clot at the site has disappeared. Which enzyme broke down its fibrin, and from what precursor was it made?
opciones: Plasmin, from plasminogen
Thrombin, from prothrombin
Fibrin, from fibrinogen
Heparin, from basophils
preguntas.explicacion: The gradual removal of a clot is called fibrinolysis: the inactive plasma protein plasminogen is converted into active plasmin, which slowly breaks down the fibrin, while bradykinin dilates the vessel again. Thrombin is the enzyme that builds fibrin, not the one that removes it; fibrin is the clot material itself; and heparin is an anticoagulant from basophils that opposes prothrombin.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Annex C, Table C.1, Winged steel needles (butterfly)
preguntas.subtema: Order of draw with a butterfly · CPT D3 3J k59 k54 · PBT II.H.1 II.J · CCMA 3E6 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.7
preguntas.pregunta: A winged (butterfly) set is connected to evacuated tubes and the first tube to be filled is a light blue citrate tube. What does the WHO device table say must happen first?
opciones: A tube without additive is drawn or discarded, because of the air in the tubing
The tubing is flushed with the light blue tube, which is then sent as the specimen
The tourniquet is tightened until the tubing fills, then the citrate tube goes on
A red clot activator tube is drawn first so that the serum tests are not delayed
preguntas.explicacion: Table C.1 lists, as a disadvantage of winged steel needles used with vacuum tubes, that the air in the tubing means the first tube has to be either a tube with no additive or a discard tube. Sending the citrate tube that was used to fill the tubing would defeat the point, and the table says nothing about tightening the tourniquet or starting with a red tube.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, Section 6: Accidental Release Measures
preguntas.subtema: SDS section 6 · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k107 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A bottle of disinfectant concentrate breaks on the processing room floor. Which section of its safety data sheet guides the cleanup?
opciones: Section 6, on containment and cleanup after an accidental release
Section 4, on the first aid to give after contact with the chemical
Section 13, on disposal of the chemical and of its own container
Section 12, on what the chemical does if it reaches the environment
preguntas.explicacion: Section 6 covers the response to spills, leaks and releases: personal precautions such as removing ignition sources or ventilating, the protective equipment that keeps the chemical off skin, eyes and clothing, emergency steps including evacuation and when to call an expert, methods for containment such as covering drains, and the cleanup technique itself. It may distinguish a small spill from a large one. Sections 12 and 13 are among those OSHA does not enforce, and section 4 treats the person, not the floor.

preguntas.subtema: Daily QC for nonwaived quantitative tests · CPT D1 k28 · PBT VI.A quality assurance · CCMA 3D k115 · CMA I.C.9.c · RMA III.C.3.d
preguntas.pregunta: For a nonwaived quantitative test, what control testing does CLIA require at a minimum each day patient specimens are run?
opciones: Two control materials at different concentrations
One negative and one positive control material
A single control material at the medical decision level
Three controls: low, mid-range and high, every 8 hours
preguntas.explicacion: At least once on each day of patient testing, a quantitative procedure needs two controls of different concentrations, while a qualitative procedure needs a negative and a positive control. Graded or titered procedures and tests with an extraction phase have their own variants. The three-level minimum, mid-point and maximum set belongs to calibration verification, not daily quality control.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure; and WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), section 2.2.3, Step 9
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k41 k42 · PBT II.C · CCMA 3E12 k124 · NCMA 2C.1
preguntas.pregunta: Which items does the ordering guidance call essential on every specimen label?
opciones: Name and age, test requested, date, collection site
Name, age, requested test, ward and ordering doctor
Name, sex, requested test, date and storage temperature
Name, age, diagnosis code, date and collection site
preguntas.explicacion: Every specimen is labeled with the patient's name and age, the test requested, the date and the collection site, and that is what makes reliable analysis and traceability possible. The WHO label for a blood tube is worded a little differently: the two names, the file number, the birth date, and the moment at which the tube was actually drawn.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Results and Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5E 5I · PBT VI.B · CCMA 3D9 k117 · RMA III.C.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: An emergency laboratory compares specimen rejections by shift over one year. What did the published audit find, and what does it suggest for training?
opciones: Two-thirds of rejections (66 %) came from the night shift, pointing training at the staff who collect at night
Two-thirds of rejections (66 %) came from the day shift, when volume is highest, pointing training at day staff
Rejections were evenly split between shifts, so training was aimed at the units with the most samples instead
Night-shift rejections were higher only for coagulation tubes, so training focused on citrate fill levels
preguntas.explicacion: Over a year of auditing, 66 % of specimen rejections fell in the night shift and 34 % in the day, even though the night runs with fewer laboratory staff. The laboratory answered by documenting rejected samples monthly in more detail and by training the personnel of the departments with the worst rejection rates at regular intervals, aiming to pull the overall rate from 6 % down below 2 %.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Does Pneumatic Tube System Transport Contribute to Hemolysis in ED Blood Samples?" (West J Emerg Med 2016, PMC5017839), Introduction
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5I · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3D9 k117 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A ward asks why the laboratory presses so hard on hemolysis when redrawing a tube takes two minutes. What consequences does the literature attach to it?
opciones: Delayed decisions, a longer stay in the department, and extra needle sticks
Loss of the quality control run and a forced recalibration of the analyser
A mandatory report of the quality failure to the accrediting organization
A penalty against the laboratory's proficiency testing performance that year
preguntas.explicacion: A hemolysed sample usually means drawing and testing a second one. Repeats hold up treatment and the clinical decisions that depend on it, stretch the patient's stay in the emergency department, and leave the patient unhappy at having been stuck more than once. The cost lands on the patient, not on the analyser, which is why the collection step gets the attention.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 2.3, Recommended order of draw
preguntas.subtema: Order of draw · CPT D3 3J k59 · PBT II.H.1 · CCMA 3E6 k132 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.7
preguntas.pregunta: Blood cultures, a prothrombin time and a complete blood count are ordered on one venipuncture. Which specimen is collected third?
opciones: The purple EDTA tube for the complete blood count
The light blue citrate tube for the prothrombin time
The blood culture bottle for the microbiology order
A non-additive tube drawn ahead of the citrate tube
preguntas.explicacion: Of the three, the culture bottle sits at position 1, the citrate tube at position 3 and EDTA at position 8, so the EDTA tube is the third one filled. A non-additive tube does hold position 2, but the footnote reserves it for when tissue fluid or thromboplastin contamination is a concern.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Urine Culture", Specimen Requirements and Procedure; and PMC, PMC4771218 LaRocco et al., Effectiveness of Preanalytic Practices on Urine Cultures (2016), Summary of findings
preguntas.subtema: Urine culture delay · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.D.3 · CCMA 3D5 k117 · CMA I.C.8.c · RMA III.C.4.a.i · NCMA 2C.15
preguntas.pregunta: A clean-catch urine for culture cannot reach the microbiology laboratory for about 6 hours. What keeps the culture result valid?
opciones: Refrigerating it or placing it in a boric acid preservative tube, either of which holds it for up to 24 hours
Keeping it at room temperature, which is acceptable for up to 24 hours as long as the cup stays capped
Freezing it, since freezing stops bacterial growth more completely than refrigeration does
Adding a formaldehyde preservative, the additive that best protects bacteria for later culture
preguntas.explicacion: Urine for culture must be plated within 2 hours unless it is refrigerated or placed in a preservative; both boric acid and refrigeration hold the specimen adequately for up to 24 hours. Urine left at room temperature for more than 4 hours shows overgrowth of both pathogens and contaminants. Formaldehyde is used to preserve cells and causes false-positive strip reactions, and freezing is not an accepted substitute for refrigeration.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Plasma Anticoagulants
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k8 (applied D3 k57 heparin tubes) · PBT I.C · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: Which natural anticoagulant is released by basophils, opposes prothrombin, and is also given as a drug to surgical patients at risk of clots?
opciones: Heparin
Protein C
Thrombin
Plasmin
preguntas.explicacion: Several plasma anticoagulants keep clotting confined to the injury: the protein C system, TFPI, antithrombin and heparin. Heparin comes from basophils, is short-acting, opposes prothrombin and also sits on the cells lining the vessels; a pharmaceutical form is given, for example, to surgical patients at risk of clots. Thrombin builds fibrin and plasmin dissolves it; neither is an anticoagulant.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: CPR - adult and child after onset of puberty, First Aid and When to Contact a Medical Professional
preguntas.subtema: Lone rescuer sequence · CPT D1 1L k38 · CMA I.B.9.c / 2027 I.B.8.c · RMA III.I.1.b · NCMA 2A.10
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist working alone finds an unresponsive adult who is not breathing. What is the first step?
opciones: Call 911 (or the local emergency number), get an AED if one is known to be nearby, then start CPR
Give 2 rescue breaths, then check the pulse for 10 seconds before calling
Start compressions for 2 minutes, then leave to look for an AED anywhere in the building
Place the person in the recovery position and monitor breathing until help arrives
preguntas.explicacion: After checking responsiveness by tapping and shouting, a lone rescuer calls 911 or the local emergency number as soon as the person is found unresponsive, retrieves an AED only if one is known to be nearby, and then begins CPR with 30 compressions and 2 breaths; the rescuer should not leave the person to search for an AED whose location is unknown. With help available, one person calls while another starts CPR. The recovery position is for a person who has started breathing again, and pulse checks are left to health professionals.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Latex Allergies - for Hospital Patients, How to Avoid Exposure to Latex in the Hospital
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2L k48 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k128 · NCMA 2C.3
preguntas.pregunta: An inpatient with a known latex allergy is admitted for several days of blood work. Which measure applies?
opciones: Post a sign on the door, note the allergy in the chart, and remove latex items from the room
Use powdered latex gloves, which release fewer allergenic proteins onto the skin
Keep the latex gloves in the room but double-glove with vinyl over them
Notify only the surgical team, since gloves matter most in the operating room
preguntas.explicacion: Hospital patients with latex allergy should ask for a sign on the door and notes in the chart, for latex gloves and other latex items to be removed from the room, and for pharmacy and dietary staff to be told so they do not handle medicines or food with latex gloves. Cornstarch powder on latex gloves is a leading source of inhaled allergen, the opposite of a safeguard.

preguntas.fuente: FDA, Medical Devices with Sharps Injury Prevention Features, Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff (2005), Table 1, Design Recommendations
preguntas.subtema: Needle safety devices · CPT D3 3M k66 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k97 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.11
preguntas.pregunta: Under the FDA's design advice for needle-safety features, what must be true once the feature has fired?
opciones: It cannot be deactivated and stays protective through disposal
It can be reset once so the device can be used on the same patient
It stays protective until the device reaches the sharps container
It may be released by a second single-handed action if needed
preguntas.explicacion: Table 1 of the FDA guidance lists, for all feature types, that the user should be able to tell easily whether the feature is activated, and that once activated it cannot be undone and should keep protecting right through disposal. Resetting or releasing the feature is the opposite of that recommendation, and protection that ended at the container would not cover the disposal step.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Syncope", section Treatment / Management
preguntas.subtema: Responses to complications · CPT D3 3K k69 · D1 k37 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: A seated patient becomes pale and sweaty and says he is about to faint. What should happen right away?
opciones: He should sit or lie down quickly with the legs elevated, and stay horizontal afterwards
He should stand up and walk slowly to a couch, since the movement restores the venous return
He should be given a sugary drink, since hypoglycemia is the most common cause
He should keep still and upright while the last tube finishes filling
preguntas.explicacion: Patients are told to sit or lie down at once during an acute episode, legs raised, to help recovery from reflex postural hypotension, and should be kept horizontal afterwards and prevented from standing too soon; any injury from a fall needs immediate attention. Standing up is the opposite of the advice, and hypoglycemia is listed as a mimic of syncope, not its usual cause.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA, Hospitals eTool, Hospital-wide Hazards: Electrical Safety, 29 CFR 1910.334(a)(2)(ii) and 1910.303(b)(1)
preguntas.subtema: Damaged electrical equipment · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G · CMA I.B.8.a / 2027 I.B.7.a · RMA II.B.7.d III.C.5
preguntas.pregunta: A centrifuge's power cord has a frayed section exposing bare wire. What does OSHA's electrical standard require?
opciones: Remove it from service until repaired and tested; do not use it meanwhile
Wrap the frayed section in tape and continue using it until the next inspection
Plug it into a GFCI receptacle, which makes the damaged cord safe to use
Keep using it if the equipment is grounded and the operator wears gloves
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph 1910.334(a)(2)(ii) takes portable electric equipment out of service, cord-and-plug equipment and extension cords included, the moment a defect or a sign of damage appears that could injure an employee; it goes back into use only after the repairs and tests needed to make it safe. Frayed cords, damaged enclosures and plug prongs bent or missing are the examples the eTool gives of what can put voltage on a metal enclosure. A GFCI softens the consequence of a ground fault; it does not license using damaged equipment.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 2
preguntas.subtema: Equipment assembly · CPT D3 3A · D2 2N · PBT II.F · CCMA 3E5 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: What is placed under the patient's arm before the draw begins?
opciones: A clean paper or towel
A warm compress pack
A rolled cloth tourniquet
A sterile drape with a window
preguntas.explicacion: Preparing the patient includes making the person comfortable, supine where that is possible, and laying a clean paper or towel under the arm that is going to be used. Warming the limb is a measure kept for veins that are hard to find, not a routine part of setting the patient up.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, CLIA Test Complexities: Test complexity categorization; Nonwaived testing; Related terms
preguntas.subtema: Three CLIA complexity categories · CPT D1 k29 · PBT VI.F / VI.F · CCMA 3D k114 · CMA I.C.9 · RMA III.C.1 · NCMA 4.12
preguntas.pregunta: Under CLIA, laboratory tests are sorted into how many complexity categories, and which are they?
opciones: Three: high complexity, moderate complexity and waived
Two: waived and nonwaived, with no further split
Four: waived, PPM, moderate and high complexity
Three: home use, point-of-care and laboratory
preguntas.explicacion: The regulation grades every test system as waived, moderate complexity or high complexity, from the least to the most demanding. Moderate and high together are called nonwaived testing. Provider-performed microscopy is a subcategory inside moderate complexity, not a fourth category, and point-of-care describes where a test is run, not how it is classified.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Informed Consent", section Other Issues, Human Clinical Studies
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k43 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.a (both outlines) · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: Which three elements must valid informed consent for a research study include?
opciones: Disclosure of information, competency to decide, and a voluntary decision
Disclosure of information, a witness signature, and an approved study budget
Competency to decide, a voluntary decision, and payment for participation
Competency to decide, a signed waiver, and a copy filed with the sponsor
preguntas.explicacion: Valid research consent stands on three elements: the information has to be disclosed; the patient, or the surrogate deciding for them, has to be competent to make that decision; and the decision has to be voluntary. Ethical standards in the design of a study are watched over by an Institutional Review Board, which may waive the consent requirement only where the risk to participants is minimal.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Sections 6.1.1 and 6.2.2
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4B pediatric collection · PBT II.E site selection, II.B age-specific needs · CCMA 3E4 site accessibility by age
preguntas.pregunta: For a term newborn who needs several tests, which sampling method is preferred, and why?
opciones: Venipuncture: it is the first choice in a term newborn and hurts less than a heel-prick
Heel-prick: it is the first choice in a term newborn and hurts less than venipuncture
Finger-prick, which the WHO recommends in term newborns since the finger has no bone risk
Arterial puncture, since capillary blood already resembles arterial blood in oxygen
preguntas.explicacion: In a term newborn the vein is the first choice and it hurts the baby less than the heel does, but it needs a phlebotomist with training and practice; where there is none, the doctor may have to take the sample. A newborn's fingers are left alone because of the nerve damage they can suffer, and the heel is kept for small volumes.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 6; and StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", Technique or Treatment
preguntas.subtema: Anchoring the vein · CPT D3 3H k64 · PBT II.F · CCMA 3E7 k133 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.9
preguntas.pregunta: A trainee steadies the vein by pressing a thumb on the skin just ABOVE the intended puncture point. What is the correct anchoring technique?
opciones: Place the thumb below the site and pull the skin down and slightly away, making it taut
Place the thumb above the site but press down harder, so that the vein cannot roll sideways
Use the index finger over the vein itself to guide the shaft of the needle
Skip anchoring; ask the patient to make a fist, which fixes the vein in place
preguntas.explicacion: Step 6 of the WHO procedure anchors the vein by holding the arm and placing a thumb below the venipuncture site; the free hand then uses the thumb to draw the skin downward and a little away from the site until it is taut. A finger over the vein is what Step 5 explicitly forbids after disinfection, and the fist is an addition that makes the veins prominent, not a replacement for anchoring.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA, Hospitals eTool, Hospital-wide Hazards: Recordkeeping, 29 CFR Part 1904; govinfo, Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act, sec. 2(9)
preguntas.subtema: OSHA 300, 301 and 300A · CPT D1 1N k39 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k110 · CMA I.B.11.c / 2027 I.B.10.c · RMA II.B.7.e · NCMA 4.11 · CMAA 3E k44
preguntas.pregunta: Under OSHA's recordkeeping rule, 29 CFR part 1904, which forms record work-related injuries and illnesses?
opciones: The OSHA 300 log, the 301 incident report and the 300A summary posted each year
The sharps injury log, the training record and the employee medical record
The OSHA 200 log, which the Needlestick Act found sufficient for exposure tracking
The exposure determination, the written opinion and the Appendix A declination
preguntas.explicacion: Covered employers record each recordable injury and illness on the OSHA Form 300 log, prepare a Form 301 incident report with details of each case, and at the end of the year prepare the Form 300A summary and post it in a visible place. The sharps injury log, training records and medical records are kept under the bloodborne pathogens standard; the exposure determination, written opinion and declination are other documents of that same standard. Congress found the old OSHA 200 log insufficient, which is why the sharps log was added.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, CLIA Test Complexities: Related terms ("Point-of-care testing"); and CDC, MMWR Recommendations and Reports 2005;54(RR-13), Good Laboratory Practices for Waived Testing Sites
preguntas.subtema: POCT is a location, not a category · CPT D1 k29 · PBT VI.F · CCMA 3D k111 · RMA III.C.2.a · NCMA 4.12
preguntas.pregunta: A coworker says a rapid test "must be waived because we run it at the point of care." What is the correct reading of the term point-of-care testing under CLIA?
opciones: It describes where testing is done and says nothing about the test's complexity
It is a synonym for waived testing when the operator is not a laboratorian
It is the category for tests cleared by the FDA for home use
It refers to a laboratory licensed by a state whose rules are stricter than CLIA
preguntas.explicacion: Point-of-care is a location: the bedside or near the site of care. Some point-of-care tests are waived, but faster technology also lets nonwaived tests be run near the patient, so a test cannot be assumed waived just because of where it is performed. Home-use clearance is one route to waived status, and the state-licensed laboratory description is the meaning of CLIA-exempt.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(c)(1)(iv), Exposure Control Plan
preguntas.subtema: Exposure Control Plan · CPT D1 1H k31 · PBT VI.G · CCMA 3C k109 · CMA I.B.4.a / 2027 I.B.3.a · RMA III.A.2.c III.C.5 · NCMA 4.11 · CMAA 3A k41
preguntas.pregunta: How often does OSHA require an employer's written Exposure Control Plan to be reviewed and updated?
opciones: At least once a year, and whenever the tasks, procedures or positions with occupational exposure change
Within 10 working days of each new hire with occupational exposure, and otherwise every three years
Once a year together with the annual employee training, and at no other time even if tasks change
Every time an exposure incident is reported, and kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (c)(1)(iv) sets two triggers: a review at least every year, plus a review whenever new or changed tasks, procedures or job positions alter who is exposed and how. The same review has to take in new technology that cuts exposure and document, each year, which safer medical devices were considered and adopted. The other periods belong to other rules of the same standard: 10 working days is the deadline for offering the hepatitis B vaccine, three years is how long training records are kept, and employment plus 30 years is the retention of medical records. An exposure incident triggers follow-up for the employee, not a rewrite of the plan.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Competency and Capacity", section Clinical Significance, When To Access Capacity
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2G k43 k49 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.c (both outlines) · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: A patient with dementia was found to lack capacity two weeks ago. What does that finding mean today?
opciones: Nothing by itself: the finding held for that time and that situation
It carries over until a judge rules that the patient has recovered
It carries over for the whole admission, once it is in the record
It removes the need to explain the draw, but not to ask permission
preguntas.explicacion: A capacity assessment holds good only for the moment, the place and the circumstances in which it was made; it is a snapshot, and it cannot be carried over to another occasion. A history of dementia does not by itself mean the person lacks capacity, and the same patient may be clear enough today to take part in the conversation. Competence is a court's decision.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, MMWR RR-54(13) Good Laboratory Practices for Waived Testing Sites (2005), CLIA requirements that apply to CW sites: follow the product insert without modification
preguntas.subtema: Modified test loses waived status · CPT D1 k29 · PBT VI.F · CCMA 3D k114 · RMA III.C.1.a.v
preguntas.pregunta: To stretch a kit, a testing site cuts each rapid test strip lengthwise so two patients can be tested per strip. What is the regulatory consequence?
opciones: The test is no longer waived and falls under the nonwaived CLIA requirements
It stays waived as long as the manufacturer's reading time is still respected
The site must run external controls with every patient sample from then on
The test remains waived because only the specimen volume was changed
preguntas.explicacion: Physically altering test components, such as cutting cards or strips to multiply the number of tests, and changing the timing of a test are both modifications. A modified test is no longer a waived test and becomes subject to the stricter requirements for nonwaived testing. Running more controls does not restore the waiver; only following the insert without modification does.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1241(c)(6), Standard: Test request
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5F · PBT III.B · CCMA 3D k112 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.a
preguntas.pregunta: Which item on the test requisition allows the laboratory to judge later whether a specimen was transported within an acceptable time?
opciones: The date and, when appropriate, the time of specimen collection
The date the requisition was printed by the ordering office
The time the specimen was logged into the laboratory information system
The expected turnaround time promised to the ordering provider
preguntas.explicacion: CLIA requires the requisition to solicit the date and, if appropriate, the time of collection; combined with the receipt date and time the laboratory must document, this gives the transport interval that decides acceptability for time-sensitive tests. The printing date of the form and the promised turnaround say nothing about when blood left the patient, and the log-in time is the second half of the interval, not the first.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Taking a step back from testing: Preanalytical considerations in molecular infectious disease diagnostics" (Clin Biochem 2023, PMC9729171), Table 2
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5B k89 · PBT III.D.1 III.D.3 · CCMA 3D5 k121 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A stool specimen for a gastrointestinal molecular panel has to travel from a rural clinic. Which transport and storage plan matches the general guidelines?
opciones: Room temperature in stabilising media, or on ice; then 2 to 8 °C for four to seven days
Room temperature without media, or frozen; then 2 to 8 °C for up to twenty-four hours
On ice only, never at room temperature; then at −20 °C from the moment it arrives
Room temperature in stabilising media only; then at room temperature until extraction
preguntas.explicacion: For stool the variables listed are time, transport and storage temperature, stabilisation media and the patient's medications. Transport is either at room temperature when a stabilising medium is used or on ice, and storage runs four to seven days, at 2 to 8 °C or at room temperature if stabilised. Freezing on arrival is not part of that general scheme.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Ready?: What are the Types of Controls? (external controls); CDC, MMWR RR-54(13) (2005), Types of controls
preguntas.subtema: External controls · CPT D1 1F · PBT IV.B.3 · CCMA 3D k115 · CMA I.C.9.c · RMA III.C.3.d
preguntas.pregunta: What is an external control for a waived test?
opciones: A liquid or similar material resembling a patient sample, tested to check the entire process
A built-in line or window on the device that confirms the sample moved through the strip
An electronic check the meter runs on itself at start-up to verify its internal functions
A patient sample previously tested by the referral laboratory and retested on site each month
preguntas.explicacion: External controls stand in for patient specimens and are run exactly as one would be, so they cover everything from applying the sample through to interpreting the result, and they show whether the reading falls inside the ranges printed on the control or its insert. They may come with the kit or be bought apart from it. Built-in lines and electronic self-checks are internal controls: they confirm the device worked, not the operator's whole procedure.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Ready?: Who Should Perform QC Testing?; 42 CFR 493.1256(d)(7)-(8)
preguntas.subtema: QC by the same operators, like a patient sample · CPT D1 1F · PBT IV.B.3 · CCMA 3D k115 · CMA I.C.9.c · RMA III.C.1.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: Who should perform quality control testing at a waived site, and how should the control material be handled?
opciones: The same people who run patient tests, treating the control exactly like a patient sample
The most experienced operator only, using a shortened version of the patient procedure
The laboratory director personally, at the start of each shift, before staff arrive
A manufacturer's representative, who ships the control results back to the site
preguntas.explicacion: Quality control is meant to catch operator error as much as reagent or instrument failure, so whoever runs patient testing day to day is the one who runs it, before or alongside patient samples, and the control is handled and tested exactly like a patient sample. Over time the job should rotate through every operator, which is also how a site sees whether a problem follows one person.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 8; and Table 2.3, Source note
preguntas.subtema: Order of draw · CPT D3 3J k59 · PBT II.H.1 · CCMA 3E6 k132 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.7
preguntas.pregunta: On what is the WHO's illustrative order of draw for vacuum tubes based?
opciones: A 2003 consensus of the US national committee that then set clinical laboratory standards
The 2008 CDC guideline on disinfecting and sterilizing in health-care settings, with its annexes
The FDA classification of blood specimen collection devices in 21 CFR 862.1675
The OSHA standard on bloodborne pathogens, 29 CFR 1910.1030, at paragraph (d)(2)
preguntas.explicacion: Step 8 and the source line of Table 2.3 credit the sequence to the US committee on clinical laboratory standards and to its 2003 consensus, presented as a revised and simplified order for vacuum tubes or syringe and needle. The CDC disinfection guideline, the FDA device classification and the OSHA standard are real documents in the same study material, but none of them sets tube order.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Veins", section Clinical Significance; and "Phlebotomy", Anatomy and Physiology
preguntas.subtema: Antecubital anatomy · CPT D2 k53 · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.9
preguntas.pregunta: Which structure lies beneath the median cubital vein and protects it, helping to prevent hematoma formation?
opciones: The bicipital aponeurosis
The medial cutaneous nerve
The brachial artery
The dorsal venous arch
preguntas.explicacion: The biceps aponeurosis shields the median cubital vein and keeps hematomas from forming, and the phlebotomy chapter describes the vein as superficial and lying over the bicipital aponeurosis of the fossa. The nerve and the artery are the structures that make the basilic vein risky, and the dorsal venous arch is in the hand.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Laboratory Tube Collection", section Definition/Introduction; and StatPearls, "Laboratory Evaluation of Coagulopathies", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure
preguntas.subtema: Tube inversions · CPT D3 3N k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: One draw yields a filled culture bottle and a filled citrate tube. How many mixing movements does each receive?
opciones: Eight to ten for the culture bottle and three to six for the citrate tube
Three to six for the culture bottle and eight to ten for the citrate tube
Eight to ten for both containers, since both hold an anticoagulant
Three to six for both containers, since both are drawn before serum tubes
preguntas.explicacion: Once filled, the culture bottle is mixed eight to ten times, while the citrate tube is inverted three to six times straight after the blood goes in. Vigorous shaking is avoided in both cases, since it can froth or haemolyse the sample and spoil the clotting results.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 3.1.1; and Annex E
preguntas.subtema: Sharps disposal · CPT D1 1G k30 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C8 k108 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.c · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Where does the WHO say the sharps container must be during a blood draw?
opciones: Within arm's reach and clearly visible
Outside the room, away from the patient
On the floor beside the chair
Behind the phlebotomist, by the waste bag
preguntas.explicacion: Section 3.1.1 ends its description of vacuum systems with the rule that the sharps container has to be within arm's reach and in plain sight, so that sharps can be disposed of safely; Annex E says the needle is discarded immediately and the disassembly is done close to the container. A container that is far away, out of sight or behind the operator invites the delay that leads to injuries.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Fainting, Home Care; and StatPearls, "Syncope", Treatment / Management
preguntas.subtema: Responses to complications · CPT D3 3K k69 · D1 k37 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: After fainting, a patient wakes up within a minute and wants to get up and leave. What is the correct advice?
opciones: Keep them lying flat for ten to fifteen minutes at least, ideally somewhere cool and quiet
Let the person stand as soon as consciousness returns, since the episode is over
Seat the person upright at once and offer a hot drink to raise the blood pressure
Keep the person lying down for at least an hour before allowing any movement
preguntas.explicacion: Keep the person flat for ten to fifteen minutes at least, ideally in a cool, quiet space, and, if lying down is impossible, to sit the person forward with the head between the knees. Patients should likewise be kept horizontal after the event and prevented from standing up too soon. No source calls for an hour on the floor.

preguntas.fuente: ADA.gov, ADA Requirements: Effective Communication, Who Decides Which Aid or Service Is Needed? and Use of Accompanying Adults or Children as Interpreters
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k16 · CCMA 7A k214 · CMA F.1.c(3) / 2027 F.1.d(4) · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: A deaf patient arrives without warning and asks for an interpreter. What may the clinic require under the ADA rules?
opciones: Reasonable advance notice, though walk-in requests are honored where possible
Two working days of written notice for any auxiliary aid or service at all
That the patient book a later appointment, since no notice at all was given
That the patient pay the interpreter fee whenever notice was not given
preguntas.explicacion: A covered entity may ask for reasonable notice in advance when someone requests an aid or a service, gauged by how long it takes to arrange one, but it may not impose excessive notice requirements, and a walk-in request is honored so far as that is possible. Responsibility for effective communication sits directly on the entity, which cannot make the patient bring an interpreter.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Fasting for a Blood Test, sections What is fasting for a blood test, and How long do I have to fast; MedlinePlus, How to Prepare for a Lab Test, section How do I prepare for a lab test
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k46 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E k125 · NCMA 2C.2 · RMA III.C.4.e · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a)
preguntas.pregunta: A patient arrives for a fasting lipid panel and mentions having chewed sugar-free gum and smoked a cigarette that morning, but eaten nothing. Does the fast hold?
opciones: No: while fasting for a blood test the patient should also not chew gum, smoke or exercise, so the provider is told
Yes: only food and caloric drinks break a fast; sugar-free gum and tobacco are permitted before a lipid panel
Yes, provided the gum and the cigarette were more than two hours before the draw and the patient drank plain water
No: smoking breaks the fast but chewing gum does not, so only the cigarette needs to be reported to the provider
preguntas.explicacion: Fasting for a blood test means taking nothing by mouth but plain water in the hours before the draw, usually 8 to 12 of them, and the patient is also asked to leave off gum, tobacco and exercise while the fast runs. Where the instructions were not followed to the letter the patient says so to the provider or to the laboratory professional, because even a small deviation can move the result and the test may have to be booked again.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Throat swab culture (003746), How the Test is Performed; and CDC, Influenza Specimen Collection guide (2024), Combined Nasal and Throat Swab
preguntas.subtema: Throat swab technique · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.C.1 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(5)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.iii · NCMA 2B.20
preguntas.pregunta: How is a throat swab culture collected?
opciones: The head is tilted back, the mouth held wide open, and the swab rubbed at the back of the throat near the tonsils
The head is tilted forward, the tongue depressed, and the swab rolled along the inner surface of both cheeks
The head is tilted back, the mouth held wide open, and the swab rubbed over the tongue and under it
The head is tilted back 70 degrees and the swab passed through a nostril until it reaches the throat
preguntas.explicacion: The patient tilts the head back and opens wide while the sterile swab is rubbed along the back of the throat near the tonsils, and the provider may scrape several times to raise the chance of catching the organism. Gagging is expected and the patient has to resist closing the mouth. The tongue is deliberately avoided, the cheek is where a buccal swab goes, and the nostril route is the nasopharyngeal swab.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA, Hospitals eTool, Laboratory: Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders, Hazard; OSHA, Laboratory Safety Guidance (OSHA 3404), Ergonomic Hazards
preguntas.subtema: Ergonomic risk factors · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G · CMA I.B.9 / 2027 I.B.8 · NCMA 2A.6
preguntas.pregunta: Which ergonomic risk factors does OSHA identify for laboratory employees?
opciones: Static postures, repetition, forceful exertion, awkward postures and contact stress
Noise, ionizing radiation, chemical vapors and aerosols from biological specimens
Long shifts, night work, understaffing and fatigue from emergency procedures
Latex exposure, glove powder, hand lotions and frequent handwashing
preguntas.explicacion: The risk factors named are static posture from sitting or standing a long while, repetition when samples are sorted or the computer is used, exertion of force, postures that take a joint out of neutral, and contact stress; back pain, tendonitis, tenosynovitis and carpal tunnel syndrome are the disorders that follow. Pipetting, microscope work and keyboarding are the typical tasks. Noise and radiation are separate physical hazards and latex is an allergy hazard, each with its own OSHA guidance.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(f)(2)(iv), Hepatitis B Vaccination, and Appendix A
preguntas.subtema: Hepatitis B vaccine declination · CPT D1 k31 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k97 · CMA I.B.4.a / 2027 I.B.3.a · RMA III.A.2.c III.C.5 · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: An employee with occupational exposure refuses the hepatitis B vaccine. Which document does the standard require?
opciones: The declination statement in Appendix A of the standard, signed by the employee
A written opinion from the evaluating healthcare professional, kept for 15 days
An entry in the sharps injury log noting the department and the employee's reason
A note in the training record, retained three years, that the vaccine was explained
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (f)(2)(iv) requires the employer to make sure that anyone who turns down the vaccine signs the statement printed in Appendix A. The other documents exist in the standard but serve other purposes: the written opinion of (f)(5) follows a vaccination or an exposure evaluation; the sharps injury log of (h)(5) records injuries from contaminated sharps that pierce the skin; and the training record of (h)(2) lists dates, content, trainer and attendees. None of them documents a refusal.

preguntas.fuente: eCFR, 21 CFR 862.1675(a), Blood specimen collection device
preguntas.subtema: Blood collection devices · CPT D3 k54 k57 · D1 1B k25 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E3 k129 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: Which items fall inside the regulatory definition of a blood specimen collection device?
opciones: Tubes, vials, whole systems, serum separators, trays and vacuum tubes
Collection tubes and vacuum tubes only, since trays hold no specimen at all
Serum separators and centrifuges, since both act on the separated serum
Needles, lancets and tourniquets, since all three touch the patient's skin
preguntas.explicacion: The definition covers devices meant to collect and handle blood specimens, and to part the serum from the cellular components before testing, and the generic type is written broadly enough to take in tubes, vials, whole systems, serum separators, collection trays and vacuum sample tubes.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.1 An Overview of Blood, Characteristics of Blood
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k4 (applied D3) · PBT I.B.2 · CCMA 2A k38 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: A blood gas report shows a pH of 7.40. Where does this fall relative to the normal range for blood?
opciones: Right at the average; normal is 7.35 to 7.45
Slightly acidic; normal is 7.45 to 7.55
At the low end; normal runs 7.40 to 7.50
Slightly alkaline; normal is 7.0, like pure water
preguntas.explicacion: Blood pH averages about 7.4, with a healthy range of 7.35 to 7.45, so a reading of 7.40 sits in the middle of normal. Blood is somewhat more alkaline than pure water, whose pH is 7.0, and it carries many buffers that keep the value steady. A range starting at 7.45 or 7.40 would wrongly turn a normal reading into a low one.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 482.13(e)(8), (e)(9) and (e)(12), Standard: Restraint or seclusion
preguntas.subtema: Restraint time limits · CPT D1 k14 · CCMA 7A k215 · CMA II.E.1.d · RMA I.C.1.e · NCMA EKB 29 · CMAA 3D k32
preguntas.pregunta: For violent or self-destructive behavior, how long may a single restraint order last for an adult before it must be renewed?
opciones: 4 hours for adults 18 and older
2 hours for adults 18 and older
1 hour for adults 18 and older
8 hours for adults 18 and older
preguntas.explicacion: Unless state law is stricter, an order aimed at violent or self-destructive behavior may be renewed only within these limits, to a total of 24 hours: 4 hours for adults 18 or older, 2 hours for children and adolescents from 9 to 17, and 1 hour for children under 9. Past 24 hours a physician or other authorized practitioner has to see and assess the patient before a new order, and the patient is seen face to face within 1 hour of the intervention starting. Restraint for non-violent patients may be renewed as hospital policy allows.

preguntas.subtema: Acceptable QC before reporting · CPT D1 k28 · PBT VI.A · CCMA 3D k115 · CMA I.C.9.c · RMA III.C.1.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: Under CLIA, when may a laboratory report a patient's result from a nonwaived test system?
opciones: Only after the control results meet the laboratory's and the manufacturer's acceptability criteria
As soon as the instrument's internal electronic check has passed for that day's run of specimens
After the result has been confirmed by a second trained operator on the same instrument
Once the result has been compared with the patient's previous value in the medical record
preguntas.explicacion: Before any patient result goes out, control results have to satisfy the criteria for acceptability the laboratory has set, and the manufacturer's where those apply, and every control procedure run has to be documented. Where no control material exists, the laboratory needs a documented alternative for catching errors as they happen and for watching performance over time. Electronic checks on their own do not satisfy the rule.

preguntas.fuente: HRSA, Recommended Uniform Screening Panel; and HRSA, RUSP Core Conditions (as of July 2024)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4C metabolic syndromes screening · PBT III.A.4 newborn screening
preguntas.pregunta: What is the RUSP, and into which two groups does it sort the conditions?
opciones: A national list recommended by the HHS Secretary, split into core conditions and secondary conditions
A federal law that requires every state to screen for the same 35 conditions with the same cut-offs
The CDC's list of conditions its quality-assurance laboratory can produce reference spots for
Each state's legally required list, which the state divides into mandatory and optional tests
preguntas.explicacion: The RUSP is a national guideline listing conditions the Secretary of HHS recommends all newborns be screened for, divided into core conditions, which every program is designed to detect, and secondary conditions, which may be found while screening for a core one. States use it to decide their own panels: most screen for most RUSP conditions, and some add others. Classic PKU and classic galactosemia are core.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "HIPAA Compliance", What healthcare information is protected; StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", Introduction and Definition of PHI
preguntas.subtema: What counts as PHI · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.2 · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k35
preguntas.pregunta: What makes a laboratory result protected health information under HIPAA?
opciones: Any identifier tying the result to one patient: name, phone number or email
Only the patient's Social Security number or medical record number, not the name
Only the result itself, regardless of whether a name is attached
Only electronic storage; a printed result with a name attached is not PHI under the rule
preguntas.explicacion: Health information turns into protected health information once it carries an identifier tying it to one particular patient: a name, a telephone or email address, a street address, a Social Security number. The Privacy Rule lists 18 such elements, and information about relatives, employers or the people who share a patient's household is covered as well. PHI may be written, spoken, on paper or electronic, of any size, inside the facility or outside it. Strip every identifier under the de-identification standard and what is left is no longer PHI.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "HIPAA Compliance", Other Issues: Criminal violations; StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", Criminal Violation of HIPAA Rules
preguntas.subtema: Criminal penalties · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.1.b · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k34
preguntas.pregunta: Which HIPAA violation carries a criminal penalty of up to $100,000 and up to 5 years in prison?
opciones: Obtaining or disclosing identifiable health information under false pretenses
Knowingly obtaining or disclosing identifiable health information
Selling identifiable health information for gain or to cause malicious harm
Failing to correct a violation due to willful neglect within the required period
preguntas.explicacion: The criminal side has three tiers. Knowingly obtaining identifiable health information, or disclosing it, reaches $50,000 and 1 year. Doing so under false pretenses reaches $100,000 and 5 years. Doing so while intending to sell, transfer or use the information for commercial advantage, for personal gain, or to do malicious harm reaches $250,000 and 10 years. These cases belong to the Department of Justice, and they can land on nurses, secretaries, telephone operators and other employees, not only on institutions. Willful neglect left uncorrected is the highest civil tier, not a criminal one.

preguntas.subtema: Tube inversions · CPT D3 3N k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A purple EDTA tube arrives in the laboratory with several small clots inside. Which collection error is associated with this finding?
opciones: The tube was not mixed enough after it was filled
The tube was inverted too many times in the figure-of-8 pattern
The tube was filled after the gray fluoride tube
The tube was drawn through a butterfly without a discard
preguntas.explicacion: Tubes with anticoagulants need adequate mixing, for instance by inverting them in a figure-of-8 pattern, and inefficient mixing can leave small clots. Overmixing is the other extreme and leads to hemolysis, not clots. Drawing out of order risks additive carry-over, and the butterfly discard concerns air in the tubing, not clotting.

preguntas.pregunta: An outpatient ran a half marathon yesterday and is booked for a draw this morning. Which instruction was missed?
opciones: Outpatients should avoid heavy physical activity in the 24 hours before
Outpatients should avoid heavy physical activity in the hour before
Outpatients should rest lying down for 15 minutes before the first tube
Outpatients should avoid heavy physical activity for the whole week
preguntas.explicacion: An outpatient is to be kept away from heavy exercise in the 24 hours before the blood is drawn, and exercise is one of the things ruled out during a fast. Exercising hard before a test also appears among the common factors that spoil accuracy. Fifteen minutes is the rule for holding a seated posture, not for exercise.

preguntas.subtema: OGTT conditions · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.D patient assessment · CCMA 3E k139
preguntas.pregunta: An OGTT is ordered for an inpatient who has been on bed rest with pneumonia for a week. What should the phlebotomist recognize?
opciones: The test is not appropriate for an acutely ill, hospitalized or inactive patient
The test is appropriate if the load is raised to 100 g to offset the bed rest
The test is appropriate if a fingerstick meter replaces the venous samples
The test is appropriate if only the fasting and 2-hour samples are drawn
preguntas.explicacion: Bed rest impairs glucose tolerance, and the OGTT is not for a patient who is hospitalized, acutely ill or inactive, nor for anyone carrying an infection, a traumatic injury or a severe illness; the result could not be interpreted, so the provider is told. Changing the load, the specimen or the number of samples fixes nothing, and venous plasma at fasting and at 2 hours is already the standard protocol.

preguntas.subtema: Treatment disclosures · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k220 · CMA II.E.2.a(5) · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3C k36
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist faxes a patient's lab results to the physician who ordered them. Does HIPAA require the patient's written authorization first?
opciones: No: disclosures for treatment are permitted without authorization
Yes: any disclosure outside the facility requires a signed authorization
Yes, unless the patient signed the notice of privacy practices acknowledgment
No, but only because fax transmissions are outside the Privacy Rule
preguntas.explicacion: No authorization is needed for a covered entity to use or disclose PHI in its own treatment, in payment or in health care operations, nor to disclose it so that any other provider can treat the patient; 45 CFR 164.506 sets that out and 164.502(a)(1)(ii) lists it among the permitted uses. Authorization under 164.508 is needed for uses outside those categories, such as marketing or sale of PHI. The acknowledgment of the notice is a separate duty and does not create or remove permissions, and faxes carry PHI like any other medium.

preguntas.subtema: Antecubital anatomy · CPT D3 3F k61 k62 · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: Which side of the upper limb does each of the two main superficial veins drain?
opciones: The cephalic drains the radial side; the basilic drains the medial side
The cephalic drains the medial side; the basilic drains the radial side
Both drain the radial side, and the median cubital vein drains the medial
The cephalic drains the deep muscles; the basilic drains the skin only
preguntas.explicacion: The cephalic vein takes the radial, or thumb, side of the limb and the basilic takes the medial side; near the elbow the median cubital vein connects the two. Both belong to the superficial system, which drains skin and superficial fascia, while the deep veins drain muscle and bone.
