opciones: Treating all human blood and certain body fluids as if they carried a bloodborne pathogen
Treating as infectious only the blood of patients whose chart shows HIV or hepatitis B
Reasonably anticipated contact of skin, eyes or mucous membranes with blood in the course of one's duties
Controls that isolate or remove the hazard from the workplace, such as sharps containers and safer needles
preguntas.explicacion: In the standard's definitions, Universal Precautions is one approach to controlling infection: every specimen of human blood, and certain other body fluids, is handled as though it were known to carry HIV, HBV or another bloodborne pathogen. Nothing depends on a chart, a test result or a diagnosis, so the same barriers apply to every patient. The other two definitions sit next to it in paragraph (b): reasonably anticipated contact in the course of one's duties is Occupational Exposure, and devices that isolate or remove the hazard are Engineering Controls.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1291(c), Standard: Test report
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5H k94 · PBT VI.F (CLIA) · CCMA 3E15 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: A printed report shows the patient's name and ID, the test, the result with units, and the report date, but not where the test was done. Which CLIA report element is missing?
opciones: The performing laboratory's name and the address of its location
The name and address of the authorized person who ordered the test
The date and time the specimen was received in the laboratory
The identity of the testing personnel who performed the test
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR 493.1291(c) lists what a test report must show: positive patient identification, the name and address of the location where the testing was done, the report date, the test performed, the specimen source when appropriate, the result with its units or interpretation, and any information on the condition and disposition of unacceptable specimens. Receipt time and the identity of testing personnel belong to the test record system under 493.1283, not to the report itself.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k89 · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E k135 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c)
preguntas.pregunta: A new technician shakes each tube vigorously right after collection to make sure the additive mixes. What does the evidence quoted in the rejection study say about this?
opciones: Tubes should be inverted gently several times; instant vigorous mixing may itself produce hemolysis
Vigorous shaking is required for citrate tubes and optional for EDTA tubes, per manufacturers' data sheets
Shaking is harmless for whole blood but must be avoided once the tube has been centrifuged
Tubes must be shaken for one full minute, since gentle inversion leaves fibrin filaments in the plasma
preguntas.explicacion: Manufacturers' data sheets and CLSI documents recommend gentle inversion of vacuum tubes several times to bring blood and additive together; a study cited found that mixing immediately after collection for a minute with 15 inversions may not even be mandatory and that instant mixing can cause hemolysis, and a later trial saw no fibrin or microclots with five gentle inversions, or even with none. Shaking is never the instruction.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Personal Protective Equipment", Suggested Sequence for Removal of PPE
preguntas.subtema: Removing eye protection · CPT D1 1J k36 · PBT VI.G.4.g · CCMA 3C3 k100 · CMA I.B.4.b / 2027 I.B.3.b · RMA III.A.3.d · NCMA 2A.4
preguntas.pregunta: How are goggles or a face shield handled when the equipment is being taken off?
opciones: By the strap or the earpieces, never by the front surface
By the lower rim, which stays clean during a procedure
By the front, folded inward so the outside faces itself
By the strap, and then wiped dry with the gown's sleeve
preguntas.explicacion: Eye protection comes off second, after the gloves. The front of it is the contaminated side, the part that met whatever was sprayed or splashed, so it is handled by the strap or the earpieces and dropped into the right container for reprocessing or disposal. The same idea governs the mask, taken off by the ties or straps behind the head without touching the front or the mouth area.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 2.2
preguntas.subtema: Hand hygiene and gloves · CPT D3 3A · D1 1J k36 · PBT II.F VI.G · CCMA 3C4 k100 · CMA I.B.4 / 2027 I.B.3 · RMA III.A.1 · NCMA 2A.4
preguntas.pregunta: Gloves worn for one draw are still clean to look at. What does the infection control table say?
opciones: One pair per procedure or patient, and gloves are never washed for reuse
One pair per session, and gloves may be washed if they stay unsoiled
One pair per patient, and gloves may be reused after an alcohol rub
One pair per procedure, and gloves are changed only when visibly soiled
preguntas.explicacion: The rule is one pair of non-sterile gloves for each procedure or patient, with two prohibitions beside it: the same pair is not used on more than one patient, and gloves are not washed so that they can be used again. The device itself is single use for the same reason.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Clean catch urine sample (007487), How the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Clean-catch cleansing, female · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.1 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(2)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.i · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A woman asks how to clean herself before giving a clean-catch urine sample. What should the medical assistant tell her?
opciones: Spread the labia and use two wipes, front to back: one for the inner folds, a second over the urethral opening
Spread the labia and use two wipes, back to front: one for the inner folds, a second over the urethral opening
Clean the urethral opening with one wipe after retracting the surrounding skin, as done for the head of the penis
Rinse the area with warm water and soap, then dry, exactly as done before placing an infant collection bag
preguntas.explicacion: For a clean-catch, a woman sits with her legs apart, separates the labia with two fingers and uses the first sterile wipe on the inner folds and the second on the urethral opening, always wiping from the front toward the back. Retracting the foreskin is the instruction for uncircumcised men, and washing with soap and water is the routine before an infant bag. The labia stay separated while she voids.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Preparation
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2K 2L k46 k48 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 k128 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: After identity is verified, which patient factors should be asked about and recorded before the draw?
opciones: Any special diet, medications, supplements and herbal preparations
Insurance plan, the copayment collected and the status of the referral
Blood type, previous transfusions and history of blood donation
Height, weight and the vital signs recorded at the previous visit
preguntas.explicacion: Once identification is confirmed, fasting status and preparation are double-checked, and the patient is asked about the factors documented to affect results, with the answers recorded: herbal preparations, nutritional supplements, the medications taken and any diet out of the ordinary. Patients are likewise told to report vitamins and supplements before a test.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Prothrombin Time", section Interfering Factors
preguntas.subtema: Fill level and ratios · CPT D3 k9 k51 k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A citrate tube for a prothrombin time is filled below its mark. Which way do the clotting times move, and why?
opciones: They lengthen, because the anticoagulant is in excess for the plasma present
They shorten, because the anticoagulant is in excess for the plasma present
They lengthen, because the tube loses part of its vacuum during the short draw
They shorten, because the citrate binds less calcium when the tube is not full
preguntas.explicacion: Citrate tubes come pre-loaded with a fixed amount of anticoagulant and marked with the volume of blood wanted. Draw less than that and the anticoagulant is in excess for the plasma collected, which prolongs the clotting time reported. Full filling is what keeps the nine-to-one proportion intact.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Technique or Treatment; and WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood (2010), Section 2.2.3, Step 6
preguntas.subtema: Tourniquet time and pre-analytical error · CPT D3 3E k60 k9 · PBT II.F · CCMA 3E7 k133 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.9
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist spends three minutes searching for a vein with the tourniquet in place before drawing a chemistry panel. What effect does this have on the specimen?
opciones: Hemoconcentration, which falsely elevates laboratory results
Hemolysis, because the prolonged pressure ruptures red cells in the vein
Dilution of the sample with tissue fluid, as happens when a finger is squeezed
Platelet clumping in the tube, producing a falsely low platelet count
preguntas.explicacion: The tourniquet should come off within 1 minute, because prolonged constriction produces hemoconcentration and falsely elevated results; the WHO gives two minutes as the outer limit, and three minutes exceeds both. Tissue fluid dilution is the WHO's warning about squeezing a finger-prick, and platelet clumping is the EDTA artifact, not a tourniquet effect.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Competency and Capacity", section Clinical Significance and section Issues of Concern
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2G k43 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7B k216 · CMA E.3.c (both outlines) · RMA I.C.1.a · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: A phlebotomist doubts whether a confused patient can agree to the draw. Who may determine capacity?
opciones: A physician, a nurse practitioner or a physician assistant
A registered nurse, or the technician standing at the bedside
A judge, because capacity is settled by the judiciary system
Any adult relative present, once the doubt has been recorded
preguntas.explicacion: Because of licensure, assessing capacity is not work for a nurse, a nursing assistant, a technician or other support staff; any licensed physician can do it, and so can a nurse practitioner or a physician assistant. What a judge settles is competence, the legal question, and medical providers never determine that.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 2.3, Recommended order of draw
preguntas.subtema: Additives · CPT D3 k57 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E3 k136 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: Which additive does the WHO table describe as acting by complement inactivation?
opciones: Acid-citrate-dextrose in the pale yellow tube
Sodium citrate in the light blue coagulation tube
Sodium fluoride in the light gray tube
Lithium heparin in the light green PST
preguntas.explicacion: The mode of action column of Table 2.3 pairs acid-citrate-dextrose with complement inactivation, and the tube is used for HLA typing, paternity and DNA work. Sodium citrate removes calcium by forming calcium salts, sodium fluoride is the antiglycolytic agent that preserves glucose, and lithium heparin in the PST anticoagulates while its gel separates the plasma.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Managing the pre- and post-analytical phases of the total testing process" (Ann Lab Med 2012, PMC3255486), section 2
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 k87 · PBT III.C · CCMA 3D k117 · RMA III.C.2.a
preguntas.pregunta: A serum specimen is centrifuged at the wrong speed and for too short a time. In Plebani's classification of errors, to which phase does this belong?
opciones: Pre-analytical, the phase of sorting, aliquoting, labeling and centrifugation inside the laboratory
Pre-pre-analytical, the phase of test request, identification, collection, handling and transport outside the lab
Analytical, the phase of interference, sample mix-ups, undetected QC failure and equipment malfunction
Post-analytical, the phase of validation, reporting, turnaround time and manual transcription
preguntas.explicacion: Plebani splits the front end in two: the pre-pre-analytical phase covers test requesting, patient and specimen identification, collection, container choice, handling, storage and transport, mostly done by staff outside the laboratory, while the pre-analytical phase proper starts once the laboratory accepts the specimen and includes sorting, pour-off, aliquoting, pipetting, labeling and centrifugation time and speed. Analytical and post-analytical errors come later.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(g)(2)(i), (g)(2)(vi) and (g)(2)(viii), Information and Training
preguntas.subtema: Training conditions · CPT D1 k31 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k109 · CMA I.B.4.a / 2027 I.B.3.a · RMA III.A.2.e · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: Under the standard, bloodborne pathogens training must be provided in which way?
opciones: Free to the employee, and inside working hours
At the employee's expense, but on paid time
During unpaid time, by an OSHA-certified trainer
Free, but only for full-time employees
preguntas.explicacion: Paragraph (g)(2)(i) requires the employer to train each exposed employee, to do it free of charge and during working hours, and to institute a program and ensure participation. Paragraph (g)(2)(viii) asks only that the person conducting the training be knowledgeable in the subject as it relates to that workplace; no OSHA certification of trainers is mentioned. The material must also suit the educational level, literacy and language of the employees, per (g)(2)(vi).

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.5 Hemostasis, Intrinsic Pathway; and Table 18.1 Clotting Factors
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k8 (applied D3 k57) · PBT I.C · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: Blood placed in a plain glass tube clots on its own. Which factor starts that in-vitro clotting, and through which pathway?
opciones: Factor XII (Hageman factor), through the intrinsic pathway
Factor III (tissue factor), through the extrinsic pathway
Factor IV (calcium ions), through the common pathway
Factor I (fibrinogen), through the fibrinolytic pathway
preguntas.explicacion: The intrinsic, or contact activation, pathway is most often started when factor XII, the Hageman factor, touches foreign material, and a blood sample put into a glass test tube is the classic example. Factor XII then activates XI and IX, and VIII with IX activates factor X. Tissue factor belongs to the extrinsic route, calcium acts throughout the cascade, and fibrinogen is the precursor of fibrin.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Glucose screening tests during pregnancy (007562), Why the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Gestational screening indications · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.D patient assessment · CCMA 3E k139
preguntas.pregunta: A 22-year-old of normal weight has never had a high glucose result, has no first-degree relatives with diabetes and had no problems in an earlier pregnancy. What is true of her screening?
opciones: She may be low risk, and low-risk patients may not need the screening test
She must still be screened, since no patient is exempt during pregnancy
She must be screened twice, once at 24 weeks and again at 32 weeks
She may skip the screen only if a fasting glucose is drawn in its place
preguntas.explicacion: Patients at low risk may not need the screening test, but every one of the conditions has to hold: no previous high glucose result, an ethnic group at low risk, no parent, sibling or child with diabetes, under 25 years old and of normal weight, and no poor outcome in an earlier pregnancy. Missing any one of them puts the patient back into the routine 24-to-28-week screen.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Critical Limits of Laboratory Results for Urgent Clinician Notification" (EJIFCC 2003, PMC6178782), Table 1
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5G 5I · PBT III.A.2 · CCMA 3E13 k138 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A platelet count comes back under the 20,000 mark of the notification list on a patient with no bleeding at all. Which possibility does the notification list tell the laboratory to rule out first?
opciones: Thrombocytopenia caused by the EDTA in the tube itself
Dilution of the specimen by an intravenous infusion nearby
A clot in the tube that has trapped part of the platelets
Interference from lipemia on the optical platelet channel
preguntas.explicacion: A platelet count below 20,000 is listed as needing urgent notification because of the bleeding risk, and the note attached to it is a caution rather than a diagnosis: exclude EDTA-induced thrombocytopenia before the call is made. The upper limit on the same line, above one million, is flagged for the opposite reason, the risk of thrombosis.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), section 2.2.1
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2N k52 · PBT II.D · CCMA 3E1 k125 · RMA III.C.4.a.ii
preguntas.pregunta: Which fittings does the WHO ask for in a dedicated outpatient phlebotomy cubicle?
opciones: A clean surface with two chairs, a hand wash basin and alcohol hand rub
A clean surface with one chair, a sharps bin and a lockable drug cabinet
A clean surface with two chairs, a fridge for the tubes and a light box
A clean surface with one chair, a curtain rail and a wall-mounted screen
preguntas.explicacion: In an outpatient department or clinic the cubicle should hold two chairs at a clean surface, one for the patient and one for the phlebotomist; a basin for washing hands, supplied with soap, running water and paper towels; and alcohol hand rub. The blood-sampling room should also have a comfortable reclining couch fitted with an arm rest.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Neonatal Jaundice", section Evaluation; and MedlinePlus, Newborn jaundice, Exams and Tests
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4B pediatric collection, D2 k45 timing of draws · PBT II.G common tests, II.B age-specific needs
preguntas.pregunta: A 30-hour-old newborn's skin bilirubin probe reads high. What comes next?
opciones: A blood sample for total serum bilirubin to confirm the transcutaneous reading
Immediate phototherapy, since the probe is more accurate than a blood test
A repeat probe reading after feeding, which replaces the need for blood
A conjugated bilirubin by probe, which detects cholestasis without a blood draw
preguntas.explicacion: The AAP recommends assessing bilirubin between 24 and 48 hours after birth, first by a transcutaneous device or a blood total serum bilirubin; the transcutaneous estimate is a screening tool that reduces blood tests, but serum is measured when it exceeds the 95th percentile or 75% of the phototherapy threshold, and it cannot read the direct fraction. High probe readings are confirmed by blood.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Ready?: Understanding "Off-Label Use" of Waived Tests and its example
preguntas.subtema: Off-label use = high complexity · CPT D1 k29 · PBT VI.F CLIA · CCMA 3D k114 · RMA III.C.1.a.v
preguntas.pregunta: A clinic modifies a waived glucose meter's procedure so it can test patients whose hematocrit is outside the range in the insert. Under CLIA, what happens to that testing?
opciones: It becomes high complexity and needs a Certificate of Compliance or Accreditation
It stays waived as long as the modification is written into the site procedure manual
It becomes moderate complexity and can continue under the same Certificate of Waiver
It becomes a PPM procedure that only the physician or midlevel practitioner may run
preguntas.explicacion: Using a cleared test outside its intended use is off-label use. Any off-label use of a waived test is treated as high-complexity testing, which brings in proficiency testing, verified performance specifications, quality control, quality assessment and personnel qualifications. A site with only a Certificate of Waiver would have to upgrade to a Certificate of Compliance or of Accreditation first.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Urinalysis", Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings (Blood Cells, Glucose)
preguntas.subtema: Ascorbic acid interference · CPT D4 4G · PBT V.D.2 · CCMA 3D k117 · CMA I.C.10.a.(2) · RMA III.C.4.b · NCMA 2B.19
preguntas.pregunta: A patient taking large doses of vitamin C has a urine reagent strip run. Which pair of pads can read falsely negative?
opciones: The blood and glucose pads
The protein and bilirubin pads
The bilirubin and ketone pads
The ketone and urobilinogen pads
preguntas.explicacion: Vitamin C is listed among the causes of a false-negative blood reaction, alongside captopril, a high specific gravity, acid urine and proteinuria, and among the causes of a false-negative glucose, with high specific gravity and uric acid. It also appears on the nitrite and leukocyte lists, though neither of those pads is paired here. Bilirubin and ketones read falsely low in stale specimens, and urobilinogen after daylight exposure or with formaldehyde.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Hand Hygiene in Clinical Practice", Technique or Treatment: Surgical Hand Antisepsis
preguntas.subtema: Surgical scrub position · CPT D1 1K k35 · PBT VI.G.4.f · CCMA 3C7 k104 · CMA I.B.4.c / 2027 I.B.3.c · RMA III.A.3.b · NCMA 2A.7
preguntas.pregunta: During a surgical hand scrub, how are the hands and forearms held while rinsing, and why?
opciones: Hands above the elbows, so water runs off the least clean part
Hands below the elbows, as in the routine wash at the sink
Hands flat against the sink, so the water reaches the cuticles
Hands at the same height, so the soap is rinsed off evenly
preguntas.explicacion: In a routine handwash the hands stay below the elbows, so the water travels from the less contaminated area toward the more contaminated one. The surgical scrub turns that around: once scrubbed, the hands are the cleanest part and the forearms and the elbows are the dirtier end, so the hands are held up and away from the body and the water runs from the fingertips down toward the elbows. Reverse the position and the forearm gets washed over the hand.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Clinical Drug Testing", section Specimen Requirements and Procedure
preguntas.subtema: Detection windows · CPT D4 4J k86 drug screening · PBT V.C.5 · RMA III.C.4.a.i urine drug screen
preguntas.pregunta: How soon after intake do drugs generally appear in urine, and how long are they detectable after a small dose?
opciones: They appear in 1 to 2 hours and are detectable for 1 to 3 days
They appear in 1 to 2 hours and are detectable for 1 to 3 weeks
They appear in 6 to 8 hours and are detectable for 1 to 3 days
They appear within minutes and are detectable for about 48 hours
preguntas.explicacion: Drugs generally first show up in urine one to two hours after intake, and after a small dose they can be found for one to three days. In plasma the times are shorter, often one to two days. Because metabolism differs from drug to drug, the first and last detection times differ too, and for most substances the metabolite outlasts the parent drug.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 2.3, rows 3, 8 and 10
preguntas.subtema: Fill level · CPT D3 k51 k57 k59 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E7 k135 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.6
preguntas.pregunta: A purple EDTA tube for a complete blood count stops filling at roughly half its volume. What does the order-of-draw table require for this tube?
opciones: A full draw, the same requirement it places on citrate and fluoride tubes
A half draw is acceptable, because EDTA is used in a fixed concentration
A full draw only when a cross-match rather than a blood count is ordered
A full draw only when the tube will be held longer than five days before use
preguntas.explicacion: Three rows of the table carry the note that a full draw is required: the citrate tube, the EDTA tube and the fluoride/oxalate tube. It applies to the EDTA tube whichever of its listed uses is ordered, hematology or cross-match, so a half-filled tube is redrawn.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Cholesterol Screening", section Specimen Collection
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2C 2K k46 · PBT II.A II.D · CCMA 3E2 k125 · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2C.2
preguntas.pregunta: The requisition reads 'lipid panel: family history of premature ASCVD'. The patient ate 3 hours ago. What should happen?
opciones: Fasting is mandatory in this case; the draw should be rescheduled
Non-fasting sampling is acceptable for any lipid panel nowadays
Proceed, since fasting matters only when the triglycerides are of interest
Proceed; fasting is required only to diagnose metabolic syndrome
preguntas.explicacion: Fasting is no longer routine for every lipid profile, but there are settings where it is preferred, and one where it is required: screening and follow-up in a patient whose family history holds genetic hyperlipidemia or premature ASCVD. The others in that group are diagnosing hypertriglyceridemia, judging residual risk in a treated patient, and assessing the risk of pancreatitis. Metabolic syndrome sits on the non-fasting side.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA, Laboratory Safety Guidance (OSHA 3404), Ionizing Radiation, pp. 21-22
preguntas.subtema: Radiation area signs · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.3 · CMA I.B.7.a / 2027 I.B.6.a
preguntas.pregunta: How must an area where radioactive materials are used or stored be marked?
opciones: With the radiation hazard symbol, and access limited to authorized personnel
With the fluorescent orange BIOHAZARD label and a red bag for the waste
With the red-framed GHS pictogram and the signal word Danger on the door
With no sign, so that visitors are not alarmed; film badges track who enters
preguntas.explicacion: OSHA's laboratory guidance has every area where radioactive material is used, or kept, display the radiation hazard symbol conspicuously and restrict entry to authorized personnel; the laboratory itself must hold a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license or one from an agreement state. The protection objectives are to keep the intake of radionuclides and external exposure as low as reasonably achievable, ALARA, and inside dose limits. The biohazard label and the GHS pictogram mark biological and chemical hazards under other standards.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Preparation; and "Peripheral Line Placement", section Preparation
preguntas.subtema: Tourniquet application · CPT D3 3E k60 · PBT II.F II.J · CCMA 3E7 k133 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.9
preguntas.pregunta: After the tourniquet is tightened, the phlebotomist can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. What does this indicate?
opciones: It is too tight; it should stop venous flow but leave arterial flow intact
It is correct; the pulse disappears once the veins are fully engorged
It is too loose; a properly placed tourniquet always abolishes the radial pulse
It is correct, provided it is released within two minutes of placement
preguntas.explicacion: The tightness is managed to halt venous flow while maintaining arterial blood flow, and the peripheral line chapter repeats it: tight enough to swell the veins without shutting off arterial flow. A lost radial pulse means the artery is occluded, so the band is too tight regardless of how quickly it will be released.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Phlebotomy", section Contraindications
preguntas.subtema: Contraindications and palpation · CPT D3 3F k61 k62 · PBT II.E II.I · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.8
preguntas.pregunta: The vein a patient offers lies under a firm pale mark left by repeated punctures. Why is that site avoided?
opciones: Residual scar tissue at a previously attempted site is a contraindication
Scarred skin cannot be disinfected with alcohol and needs povidone iodine
Scarred skin is where the tourniquet must sit, so the vein cannot be seen
Scarred skin bleeds longer, so a pressure dressing would have to be used
preguntas.explicacion: A site attempted before and left with residual scar tissue is listed as a contraindication in its own right. On palpation these veins can also feel fibrosed, which is another entry on the same list, so the arm is examined and a different vein chosen rather than the old track reused.

preguntas.fuente: NIOSH, Alert 2000-108, Activities Associated with Needlestick Injuries; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)(vii)
preguntas.subtema: Needles on tubing · CPT D1 1G k30 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k123 · CMA I.B.4.e / 2027 I.B.3.e · RMA III.A.2.b · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Why are winged-steel needles and other needles attached to tubing singled out as a disposal hazard?
opciones: The tubing makes them hard to place in a sharps container
The tubing holds enough blood to soak through the container
The tubing keeps the shield from sliding over the used needle
The tubing has to be cut with scissors before it is discarded
preguntas.explicacion: A needle on a length of flexible tubing is awkward to get into a sharps container, and that awkwardness is itself an injury hazard. The related habit of parking the needle somewhere convenient, in a drip chamber, an intravenous port or bag, or even the bedding, leaves an exposed sharp behind. Cutting a contaminated needle is not an option either: shearing or breaking one is prohibited by the bloodborne pathogens standard.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Urinalysis", section Interfering Factors (Preservatives)
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5B · PBT III.D.1 · CCMA 3D k117 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a.i · CMA I.C.8.c(3)
preguntas.pregunta: A 24-hour urine was preserved with formaldehyde, and the laboratory is asked to run a dipstick on an aliquot. Which pattern of false results does formaldehyde produce on reagent strips?
opciones: False positives for urobilinogen, glucose, the peroxidase reaction and leukocyte esterase
False negatives for the leukocyte esterase reaction, with the other strip reactions unaltered
False positives for albumin only, with the pH of the specimen shifted toward acidity
False negatives for glucose and ketones, with the specific gravity reading raised
preguntas.explicacion: Preservatives are reached for only now and then, precisely because they distort the reading: with formaldehyde in the pot, strip reactions for urobilinogen, glucose, the peroxidase reaction and leukocyte esterase can all come up falsely positive. Mercury salts push leukocyte esterase the other way, to a false negative; thymol fakes albumin; and hydrochloric acid, used to hold cell structures and for steroid assays, moves the pH.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Lab Tests: Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT) Test, What is it used for?; and WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood (2010), Table 2.3
preguntas.subtema: Common tests · CPT D3 k57 D2 k47 · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E3 k129 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: A hospitalized patient is receiving heparin. Which coagulation test is used to monitor that drug, and in which tube is it collected?
opciones: The partial thromboplastin time, in a light blue sodium citrate tube
The prothrombin time with INR, in a light blue sodium citrate tube
The partial thromboplastin time, drawn in a dark green sodium heparin tube
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate, in a black-top citrate tube
preguntas.explicacion: Monitoring people taking heparin is a use of the PTT (also called aPTT), which measures the seconds the sample takes to clot; the PT/INR is the test tied to warfarin. Like all coagulation studies, the PTT goes in the light blue citrate tube of the WHO table, never in a heparin tube. The ESR measures how fast red cells settle and is a marker of inflammation, not of heparin.

preguntas.fuente: HHS OCR, Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, Resources for Providers
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k16 · CCMA 7A k214 · CMA F.1.c(3) / 2027 F.1.d(4) · NCMA 4.11
preguntas.pregunta: Which notices does HHS OCR say Section 1557 requires covered entities to post?
opciones: Notices of nondiscrimination and of available language assistance
A notice of privacy practices and of patient rights under HIPAA rules
A notice of the two patient identifiers used by the laboratory
A notice of the fee schedule for interpreter services
preguntas.explicacion: Under Section 1557 a covered entity posts two notices: one saying it does not discriminate, and one saying language assistance is available; HHS OCR offers sample notices in nearly 50 languages. Language assistance is free under Title VI and Section 1557, so a fee schedule would be wrong; privacy notices come from HIPAA, and identifiers from The Joint Commission's goal.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Patient Rights and Ethics", Issues of Concern: Informed Consent Prior to Treatment
preguntas.subtema: Elements of informed consent · CPT D1 1D k14 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k211 · CMA II.E.1 · RMA I.C.2 · NCMA 4.2
preguntas.pregunta: Which elements do most state statutes set as the minimum for an informed consent discussion?
opciones: Nature, benefits, risks and alternatives, plus the patient's capacity
Cost, insurance coverage, the referral needed and the appointment date
Diagnosis, prognosis, the physician's credentials and the facility's rating
Names of the staff involved, the equipment used and the disposal method
preguntas.explicacion: In most American jurisdictions the statutory floor covers five things: the nature of the therapy, what it stands to achieve, what it risks, which reasonable alternatives exist, and whether the patient has the capacity to decide. The reasoning behind the list is that patients own their bodies and choose which risks to run, yet cannot weigh a risk or an alternative that nobody has described to them. Consent gathered without those pieces is what tort claims are later built on.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Urine 24-hour volume (003425), How to Prepare for the Test; and StatPearls, "Urinalysis", Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings (Specific Gravity)
preguntas.subtema: 24-hour interfering factors · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.1 · CCMA 3D k117 · CMA I.C.7.a.(2)(c) · RMA III.C.4.e · NCMA 2B.18
preguntas.pregunta: A patient scheduled for a 24-hour urine protein test had a CT scan with contrast dye two days ago. Why does this matter?
opciones: Contrast dye given within 3 days before the collection can affect the results, so the provider should be told
Contrast dye given within 3 hours before the collection can affect the results, so a short delay is enough
Contrast dye can affect the results only if it was given during the 24-hour collection period itself
Contrast dye lowers the specific gravity reading, so the collection should be extended to 48 hours
preguntas.explicacion: Among the factors that can distort a 24-hour urine result is radiographic contrast given within the 3 days before the test, along with dehydration, emotional stress, strenuous exercise, vaginal fluid in the urine and urinary tract infection. Three hours would be far too short a window. Contrast media falsely raise, not lower, specific gravity, and the fix is to inform the provider, not to lengthen the collection.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Table 7.1
preguntas.subtema: Site by age · CPT D3 k55 · PBT II.E · CCMA 3E4 k131 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.5
preguntas.pregunta: For a finger-prick in an adult, which fingers does WHO Table 7.1 recommend, and which does it say to avoid?
opciones: The middle and ring fingers; avoid the thumb and index finger, and the little finger
The thumb and index finger; avoid the middle and ring fingers, and also the little finger
The index and middle fingers; avoid the thumb, the ring finger and the little finger
Any finger except the thumb, provided the lancet is placed on the fingerprint lines
preguntas.explicacion: Table 7.1 recommends the second and third fingers, that is the middle and ring finger. The lancet goes on the side of the pad, set to cut across the fingerprint ridges rather than to follow them. It says to keep off the thumb and the index finger, which callus, and off the little finger, whose tissue is thin. The lancet is not laid ALONG the fingerprint lines: it crosses them.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Bleeding, When to Use a Tourniquet; and eCFR, 49 CFR 173.199, Category B infectious substances (UN3373 Biological substance, Category B; eCFR vigente 2026-09-04)
preguntas.subtema: Tourniquet for hemorrhage · CPT D1 1M k37 · CMA I.B.9.a / 2027 I.B.8.a · RMA III.I.1.b · NCMA 2A.10
preguntas.pregunta: If a tourniquet becomes necessary for life-threatening limb bleeding, where is it placed?
opciones: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, avoiding the joint, noting the time
Directly over the wound, tightened until the bleeding stops
4 to 5 finger widths above the wound, released every 2 minutes
Just below the joint nearest the wound, loosened every 10 minutes
preguntas.explicacion: A tourniquet is used only when continuous pressure has not stopped extremely severe bleeding, and it is applied to the limb 2 to 3 inches, 5 to 7.7 centimeters, above the wound, avoiding the joint and moving above it toward the torso if necessary, preferably over clothing or padding rather than bare skin. The time of application is written down or memorized and told to responders, because a tourniquet left on too long injures nerves and tissue. Four to five finger widths and two minutes are venipuncture tourniquet figures, not first-aid ones.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1283(b), Standard: Test records
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5F k92 · PBT VI.D · CCMA 3E k145 · NCMA 2C.14 · RMA III.C.4.a · CMA I.C.8.a
preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory clearing out its storeroom asks whether the analyser printouts filed with old patient results can be thrown away. What does CLIA require?
opciones: Records of patient testing, printouts included, have to be kept
Printouts may go once the result is reported and verified
Printouts are kept only for tests sent to an outside laboratory
Printouts are kept only when the specimen failed acceptability
preguntas.explicacion: Beyond the four items the record system must contain, the same standard adds a plain sentence: records of patient testing, including instrument printouts where they exist, must be retained. There is no carve-out for tests that were already reported, for referred work, or for problem specimens; the retention rule covers the patient testing record as a whole.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.530(j)(1) and (j)(2), Documentation and retention period
preguntas.subtema: HIPAA documentation retention · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k219 · CMA II.E.2.c · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.4 · CMAA 3B k39
preguntas.pregunta: How long must a covered entity retain its HIPAA policies, procedures and other required documentation?
opciones: Six years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later
Three years from creation, matching OSHA training records
Thirty years, matching OSHA employee medical records
Ten years from creation, matching the period for Medicare claims documentation
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.530(j) requires policies and procedures to be kept in written or electronic form, together with every communication the rule requires in writing and every action, activity or designation it requires to be documented, for six years from the date of creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later. The same section requires a privacy official, a complaints contact, workforce training, safeguards, a complaint process, sanctions, mitigation and no retaliation. Three and thirty years are OSHA periods, not HIPAA ones.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Needlestick", History and Physical; Evaluation
preguntas.subtema: Tetanus after a puncture · CPT D1 1H k33 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C9 k95 · CMA I.B.4.d / 2027 I.B.3.d · RMA III.A.2.b · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Besides the bloodborne pathogens, which vaccination history is reviewed after a puncture wound from a needle?
opciones: Tetanus, since the date of the last dose guides what is given
Influenza, since the season decides whether a dose is due
Measles, since a worker without immunity may be excluded
Hepatitis A, since the wound was contaminated with blood
preguntas.explicacion: A needlestick is a puncture wound, so tetanus is assessed alongside the bloodborne pathogens. Three things decide what is given: the kind of wound, how long ago the last tetanus-containing dose was received, and whether the primary series was ever completed. Hepatitis B status is reviewed at the same visit, because it decides whether immune globulin is needed. Hepatitis C has no vaccine, and measles immunity is a work-restriction question rather than a wound question.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Patient Rights and Ethics", sections History (1973, 1986) and Treatment Refusal
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 k14 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7A k215 · CMA E.1.d (both outlines) · RMA I.C.1.c · NCMA 4.7
preguntas.pregunta: Which 1986 measure made the right to refuse treatment enforceable for patients in facilities using federal insurance programs?
opciones: 42 CFR § 482.13, issued by the executive branch
The AHA's 1973 patient bill of rights
Cruzan v. Director, decided by the Supreme Court
The Norwood-Dingell Bill passed by Congress
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR § 482.13 dates from 1986 and is the founding catalog of patient rights that can actually be enforced in the United States, though its reach extends only to places where federal health insurance programs are used, and it confirmed that a patient with capacity may refuse any treatment. The AHA bill of 1973 had little enforceability, Cruzan came in 1990, and Congress rejected Norwood-Dingell.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Therapeutic Communication", Table (Specific Techniques), Reflecting
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k15 k40 · CCMA 6 k199 k202 · CMA F.1.g / 2027 F.1.d · RMA I.D.1.c
preguntas.pregunta: The patient says, 'Last time they stuck me four times and I nearly passed out.' The phlebotomist replies, 'Four sticks, and you nearly passed out.' Which technique is this?
opciones: Reflecting
Summarizing
Clarifying
Silence
preguntas.explicacion: Reflecting means saying the patient's own words back, at times exactly as they were spoken, to show that the listening is real. Summarizing restates the account in the provider's words to build a shared understanding; clarifying uses guiding statements to draw out more detail; and silence shows attention by not interrupting, which is a different way of listening, not a way of answering.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Urine Culture", Specimen Collection
preguntas.subtema: Method actually used · CPT D2 2P k50 · PBT V.B.1 / V.D.2 · CCMA 3D1 k113 · CMA I.C.7.a.(2)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.i
preguntas.pregunta: Which urine collection method is used most often for culture, even though it is not the one least likely to be contaminated?
opciones: Clean-catch midstream, because it is neither invasive nor uncomfortable for the patient
Straight catheterization, because it is quick and needs no cooperation at all from the patient
Suprapubic aspiration, because it is quick and needs no cooperation from the patient
Sterile bag collection, because it is simple and needs no cooperation from the patient
preguntas.explicacion: Suprapubic puncture gives the cleanest specimen and single catheterization is the next best, but both are invasive, uncomfortable and labor-intensive, so they are kept for patients who cannot collect their own. The clean-catch midstream is therefore the routine method, and its colony counts agree reasonably well with those two. Bag collection is a pediatric option for children who are not toilet trained.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Annex C, Introduction
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2D 2M · PBT II.B · CCMA 3E1 · RMA I.D.1.c · NCMA 2C.1
preguntas.pregunta: The WHO Annex C script for explaining the procedure opens with which three points?
opciones: The worker's name, the facility, and that they are trained to take blood
The worker's name, the tests ordered, and the colors of the tubes needed
The worker's name, the ordering doctor, and when the results are expected
The worker's name, the patient's diagnosis, and the reason for the tests
preguntas.explicacion: Annex C begins with the worker giving their name and saying they work at the facility, then asks the patient's name to check it against the order and any name band, and then states that the worker is trained and experienced in taking blood. The tests and the clinician who will receive the results come later in the script; the diagnosis is never part of it.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Chain of Custody", sections Custody of the Evidence and Importance of the Chain of Custody
preguntas.subtema: Chain of custody · CPT D5 5C k91 forensic studies · PBT III.A.4 · CCMA 3E k127
preguntas.pregunta: At trial, the prosecution cannot show who held a specimen during one stretch of time. What is the likely outcome?
opciones: The chain is deemed broken and the defense may ask to have it annulled
The chain is repaired by having the laboratory re-analyze the specimen
The chain holds, because the tamper-evident seal was never broken
The chain holds, because the analyst can testify to the result obtained
preguntas.explicacion: Where inconsistencies remain and the prosecution cannot show who held the item at a given moment, the chain counts as broken, and the defense may ask the court to annul the evidence that came from it; evidence whose record was not maintained can be ruled inadmissible and have its legitimacy and integrity questioned. Re-analysis cannot fill a gap in possession, and an intact seal does not say who was holding it.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Specimen rejection in laboratory medicine: Necessary for patient safety?" (Biochem Med 2015, PMC4622196), Discussion
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5B 5E · PBT III.A.2 III.D.3 · CCMA 3D9 k117 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: Blood gas samples from a distant ICU keep arriving clotted, and the wards still draw with syringe, needle and container rather than an evacuated tube system. Which two responses did the emergency laboratory adopt?
opciones: Placing point-of-care blood gas analyzers in the ICUs under laboratory control, and teaching use of the evacuated tube system
Adding heparin to every syringe on arrival in the laboratory, and asking the ICUs to send samples only during the day shift
Accepting clotted gas samples with a cautionary comment, and moving all blood gas testing to the core laboratory
Requiring each ICU to centrifuge gas samples before sending them, and doubling the frequency of the courier rounds
preguntas.explicacion: To cut down the blood gas samples that clotted on long transport routes, the laboratory placed several point-of-care blood gas analyzers in the ICUs and emergency departments, kept under laboratory specialists' control; and since collection with the conventional syringe, needle and container system was still going on in the wards and was thought to add to the fibrin-clotted samples, the education seminars covered venipuncture technique, the right additive tubes, the order of tubes, gentle mixing and transport. Rapid serum tubes were the answer for early-spun serum.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Syncope", section Treatment / Management; and MedlinePlus, Medical Encyclopedia: Fainting
preguntas.subtema: Responses to complications · CPT D3 3K k69 · D1 1M k37 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.B.9.l / 2027 I.B.8.l · RMA III.I · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: A patient slid off the drawing chair during a faint and struck the arm of it. What must not be overlooked?
opciones: Injuries from the fall, which need attention straight away
The tube already drawn, which has to be discarded and repeated
The tourniquet, which must be reapplied before the patient moves
The label, which is rewritten because the draw was interrupted
preguntas.explicacion: Any injury sustained in a fall from a faint requires immediate attention, and patients who collapse frequently need a trauma assessment for what they hit on the way down. A fall from a height, or obvious injury and bleeding, is one of the situations in which emergency help is called.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.530(b), Standard: Training; StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", To Whom Does HIPAA Apply and Training Employees
preguntas.subtema: Workforce training · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k33
preguntas.pregunta: Whom must a covered entity train on its privacy policies and procedures?
opciones: All workforce members, as suited to their functions, including new hires
Only clinical staff who document care in the medical record
Only the privacy official and the contact person for complaints
Only paid employees; volunteers and students fall outside the training rule
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.530(b) has every member of the workforce trained on the policies and procedures for privacy, to the degree their own functions make necessary and appropriate: everyone by the compliance date, each new member within a reasonable time of joining, and anyone whose work is touched by a material change in the policies, with the training documented. Clinical guidance applies the rule to interns, volunteers and administrative, food service, clerical and janitorial staff alike, and recommends refreshing it every year.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Taking a step back from testing: Preanalytical considerations in molecular infectious disease diagnostics" (Clin Biochem 2023, PMC9729171), section 4.1
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5B k89 · PBT III.D.1 III.D.3 · CCMA 3D5 k143 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A urine specimen for a molecular assay will sit for several hours before extraction. Why is it either processed at once or refrigerated?
opciones: Its low pH and urea denature the nucleic acid at ambient temperature
Its bacteria multiply at ambient temperature and consume the target
Its bilirubin breaks down in the light and quenches the fluorescent dye
Its specific gravity climbs as it evaporates, concentrating inhibitors
preguntas.explicacion: Urine is worked on at once or held at 2 to 8 °C, for two reasons. Urine tends to a low pH and carries urea, and the pair denature DNA at 25 °C and above. Long storage in the cold, on the other hand, encourages uric acid, calcium oxalate and phosphorus to precipitate, and those precipitates can inhibit the amplification themselves, so neither extreme is harmless.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Patient Rights and Ethics", Issues of Concern: Informed Consent Prior to Treatment
preguntas.subtema: Disclosing a small risk · CPT D1 1D k14 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k211 · CMA II.E.1 · RMA I.C.2 · NCMA 4.2
preguntas.pregunta: How small a risk must still be disclosed to a patient, according to the federal decision that shaped informed consent?
opciones: A risk of one percent, if it means death or a lasting harm
A risk of ten percent, no matter what harm it would cause
A risk of one percent, but only for elective procedures
A risk of five percent, unless the patient asks for more
preguntas.explicacion: A federal court held that a risk as small as one percent still has to be disclosed when what it threatens is death, or a complication that changes the patient's life for good, paralysis being the example given. What decides is the severity of the outcome, not the probability on its own. Because the three branches of government have left the minimum standard vague, these rights tend to be enforced afterwards, through tort claims brought by patients.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, MMWR RR-54(13) (2005), Recommended Practices Before Testing: Waived test specimens; CDC, Ready? Set? Test! (2024), Set?: Collecting the Sample
preguntas.subtema: Unprocessed specimens only · CPT D1 k29 · PBT IV.A.5 · CCMA 3D k114 · RMA III.C.1.a.v
preguntas.pregunta: A group A strep antigen kit's insert describes testing both a throat swab and a colony from a culture plate. Under a Certificate of Waiver, which specimen may the site test?
opciones: Only the throat swab; testing the culture is not a waived use
Either one, because the kit itself is categorized as waived
Only the culture, because the swab requires an extraction step
Neither, because any test with two specimen types is nonwaived
preguntas.explicacion: Waived tests are approved only for direct, unprocessed specimens that need no operator manipulation: whole blood, urine, a throat or nasal swab, stool, saliva. When one insert covers both a processed and an unprocessed specimen, the waiver applies only to the unprocessed one. Group A strep antigen testing is waived on a throat swab and not on a microbiology culture; urine hCG is waived, serum hCG is not.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Blood Culture Contamination: An Overview for Infection Control and Antibiotic Stewardship Programs (2022), Blood Culture Contamination Rate; PMC, Interventions to reduce blood culture contamination (BMJ Open 2018, PMC6267024), Background
preguntas.subtema: Blood culture quality · CPT D4 4A · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139
preguntas.pregunta: What is the maximum overall blood culture contamination rate recommended by the ASM and CLSI, as cited by the CDC?
preguntas.explicacion: Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidance, like the American Society for Microbiology's, puts the ceiling for overall contamination at 3%. Many facilities have driven it below 1%, and the CDC treats 1% as reachable where best practices are followed, but that 1% is a goal, not the ceiling. Rates as high as 12% appear in the literature, which is what the benchmark exists to correct.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Personal Protective Equipment", Suggested Sequence for Removal of PPE
preguntas.subtema: Taking gloves off · CPT D1 1J k36 · PBT VI.G.4.g · CCMA 3C3 k100 · CMA I.B.4.b / 2027 I.B.3.b · RMA III.A.3.a.ii · NCMA 2A.4
preguntas.pregunta: How is the second glove removed once the first one is already off?
opciones: Fingers of the bare hand slide under it at the wrist
The bare hand pinches its outer surface at the fingertips
The bare hand pulls it off by the cuff and turns it over
Both gloves are peeled together before the first is dropped
preguntas.explicacion: The first glove is taken off by grasping the palm surface with the other gloved hand and dropping it into the right container. For the second, the fingers of the now bare hand go underneath it at the wrist, so that bare skin never touches the contaminated outside, and it is peeled off over the first. Gloves come off before everything else, and hand hygiene follows immediately, since a glove is not a substitute for washing.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 1.1.1
preguntas.subtema: Pre-analytical error · CPT D3 k9 k55 k56 · PBT II.J II.I · CCMA 3E3 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: A laboratory reports repeated hemolysis from one phlebotomist. Which needle choices raise that risk?
opciones: A gauge of twenty-three or finer, or one too wide for the vessel
A gauge of twenty-one or finer, or one too short for the forearm
A gauge of sixteen or wider, or one too long for the antecubital
A gauge of twenty-three or finer, or one too short for the vessel
preguntas.explicacion: Both extremes of gauge appear on the list of factors that raise hemolysis: a needle of twenty-three gauge or under, and a needle too large for the vessel it is being put into. The wider figures, sixteen to eighteen, belong to blood donation rather than to routine sampling.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, Section 2: Hazard(s) Identification
preguntas.subtema: SDS section 2 · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k106 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Which safety data sheet section repeats the signal word, the hazard statements and the pictograms that appear on the label?
opciones: Section 2, Hazard Identification, with the hazard classification as well
Section 3, Composition, with the ingredients and their concentrations
Section 8, Exposure Controls, with the limits and the protective gear
Section 11, Toxicological Information, with the routes and the symptoms
preguntas.explicacion: Section 2 carries the hazard classification of the chemical, the signal word, the hazard statements, the pictograms, which may be drawn or simply named, the precautionary statements, a note on any hazard that falls outside the classifications, and, for a mixture holding ingredients of unknown toxicity, what percentage of it they make up. It is the section that matches what the reader has already seen on the container label.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 1.1.1
preguntas.subtema: Complications: haematoma · CPT D3 3L k68 k74 · PBT II.I · CCMA 3E13 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(a) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.12
preguntas.pregunta: In a study of blood donors, how often did bruising and hematoma appear at the puncture site?
opciones: In about twelve percent of the donors studied
In about fifty percent of the donors studied
In under one percent of the donors studied
In about thirty percent of the donors studied
preguntas.explicacion: One study of donors found bruising and hematoma where the needle went in for 12.3 percent of them, which makes it the best documented adverse event of the procedure. In the same study syncope happened in under one percent, and nerve injury occurred infrequently.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Laboratory Tube Collection", section Definition/Introduction, Grey
preguntas.subtema: Tubes and tests · CPT D3 k57 · PBT II.G II.J · CCMA 3E3 k129 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(c) · RMA III.C.4 · NCMA 2C.4
preguntas.pregunta: A lactic acid level is ordered. Which tube is used for this test?
opciones: The gray tube with potassium oxalate and sodium fluoride
The lavender tube with EDTA, which is used for hematologic assays
The green tube with heparin, used for stat chemistry
The light blue tube with 3.2% sodium citrate
preguntas.explicacion: The gray tube, with potassium oxalate as anticoagulant and sodium fluoride as the antiglycolytic agent, is the tube for plasma glucose and for lactic acid. The lavender EDTA tube is the hematology tube, the green heparin tube is used for stat chemistry, and the light blue citrate tube is reserved for coagulation studies.

preguntas.fuente: CDC, Influenza Specimen Collection guide (2024), Packing
preguntas.subtema: Labeling the transport tube · CPT D4 4F k84 · PBT V.D.3 · CCMA 3D4 k113 · CMA I.C.8.a · NCMA 2C.14
preguntas.pregunta: What does the CDC say about writing the label on a viral transport tube?
opciones: Use a barcode or a permanent marker, because pencil and pen rub off or smear
Use a pencil, because permanent marker dissolves in the transport medium
Use a pen and cover the writing with clear tape so the ink cannot smear
Label the outer shipping bag instead, so that the tube itself stays easy to read
preguntas.explicacion: The label goes on the transport tube itself, written with a barcode or a permanent marker, since pencil and pen can rub off or smear in transit; the cap is then checked to be tightly sealed and the paperwork completed to state health department requirements. A frozen cold pack goes in with the specimen, and packing follows the transport regulations for biological substances.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Chain of Custody", section The Relevance of the Chain of Custody Documentation
preguntas.subtema: Forensic packaging · CPT D5 5C k91 · PBT III.A.4 · CCMA 3E k127
preguntas.pregunta: How should forensic specimens be packed for transport?
opciones: Sealed in tamper-evident bags or with tamper-evident tape, one form each
Sealed in tamper-evident bags, grouped under one form for the whole case
Double-bagged in biohazard bags, with the form taped to the outer bag
Boxed with absorbent material, with the form kept at the collection site
preguntas.explicacion: Evidence is packed so transport cannot damage it, and preferably sealed in bags that resist or reveal tampering, or with tape that shows it; each evidence bag travels with its own chain of custody form. Bundling several bags under one form breaks the one-to-one trail, and a form left at the collection site cannot record the transfers that follow.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, "Preanalytical phase - a continuous challenge for laboratory professionals" (Biochem Med 2012, PMC4062337), Preanalytical phase studies published in this issue
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5A 5B · PBT III.A.3 · CCMA 3E10 k138 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.4.a
preguntas.pregunta: A physician asks to add a test to a serum sample collected the previous day and kept refrigerated. What decides whether the laboratory can honor the add-on?
opciones: Whether the analyte is documented as stable for that storage time and temperature in that tube type
Whether the request reaches the laboratory within 30 days of the original oral order for the panel
Whether the original requisition already listed the panel to which the new test belongs
Whether the tube carried a gel barrier, since only gel tubes may be retested after storage
preguntas.explicacion: Add-on acceptability rests on stability data: the study that measured common biochemical analytes in serum separator tubes under various storage conditions exists precisely to define the time and temperature within which a stored sample can be retested. The 30-day rule concerns written authorization of oral orders, the original panel does not fix what may be added, and that same study covered tubes both with and without a gel barrier, so the gel is not what settles the question.

preguntas.fuente: NIA, Talking With Your Older Patients, Compensating for visual deficits
preguntas.subtema: CPT D2 2B k16 · CCMA 6D k195 · CMA F.1.c(2) / 2027 F.1.d(3) · RMA I.D.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: Which steps are advised when a patient's eyesight makes the pre-draw paperwork hard to read?
opciones: Good lighting with little glare, and a check that glasses were brought
Dim the lighting so there is no glare, and hold the page close to her face
Handwritten notes in a small neat script on unlined white paper
A relative reading the paperwork aloud in place of the patient
preguntas.explicacion: For visual deficits the advice is to ensure adequate lighting, including light on your own face, and to keep glare down; to check the patient has brought and is wearing glasses or contact lenses; and to make handwritten instructions clear and printed type large enough. Where low vision blocks reading, audio instructions or large pictures and diagrams are offered.

preguntas.fuente: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 19.3 Cardiac Cycle, Heart Sounds; and SEER Training Modules, Anatomy & Physiology, Cardiovascular System, Physiology of the Heart, Heart Sounds
preguntas.subtema: CPT Core k6 (applied D3) · PBT I.A.1 · CCMA 2A k37 · CMA I.C.6.g(4) (2027: I.C.6.f(4)) · RMA I.A.1 · NCMA 1.1
preguntas.pregunta: A nurse auscultating a patient hears the 'lub' and then the 'dub'. What produces the second heart sound, S2?
opciones: The semilunar valves snapping shut as the ventricles relax
The atrioventricular valves shutting as the ventricles contract
The semilunar valves opening as the ventricles eject blood
The atria pushing blood into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle
preguntas.explicacion: A healthy heart gives two sounds: S1, the lub, when the atrioventricular valves shut as the ventricles contract, and S2, the dub, when the semilunar valves shut as the ventricles relax. Both sounds are vibrations set off by valves closing, and abnormal ones are called murmurs. The atrial push into a stiff ventricle is S4, seldom heard and a sign the left ventricle is failing.

preguntas.fuente: 45 CFR 164.520(c)(2), Specific requirements for certain covered health care providers; 164.520(c)(1)(v)(B)
preguntas.subtema: Notice of privacy practices · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k33
preguntas.pregunta: A new patient arrives at a clinic that treats patients directly. When must the clinic hand over its notice of privacy practices?
opciones: No later than the first service delivery, with a good-faith effort to obtain acknowledgment
Within 60 days of the first visit, by mail to the patient's home address
Only when the patient asks for it, since posting the notice in the office is sufficient by itself
At the first visit, and the patient must sign it before any care may be provided
preguntas.explicacion: Section 164.520(c)(2) has a covered provider that treats patients directly hand over the notice no later than the day of the first service delivery, electronic service included, or as soon as practicable after an emergency; it must then try in good faith to get the patient's written acknowledgment that the notice arrived, and where that fails, document the attempt and the reason; and it must keep the notice available on site and posted prominently. The acknowledgment is sought, never made a condition of care. Sixty days is the window a health plan without a website has to distribute a materially revised notice.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Gestational Diabetes", Evaluation and History and Physical; MedlinePlus, Glucose screening tests during pregnancy (007562), Why the Test is Performed
preguntas.subtema: Gestational screening timing · CPT D4 4H · PBT II.G · CCMA 3E k139 timed specimens
preguntas.pregunta: When is routine gestational diabetes screening performed in an uncomplicated pregnancy?
opciones: Between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation
Between 12 and 16 weeks of gestation
Between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation
At the first prenatal visit, in every patient
preguntas.explicacion: Screening is done between 24 and 28 weeks; ACOG and the USPSTF recommend that window for all pregnant patients, although the method and the cutoffs vary between experts. Testing is moved earlier when urine glucose runs high at prenatal visits or when the patient is at high risk: a 75 g or 50 g test at the first visit is suggested for a BMI of 30 or more plus another risk factor. That is targeted, not routine.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA Brief 3514, Hazard Communication Standard: Safety Data Sheets, Section 10: Stability and Reactivity
preguntas.subtema: SDS section 10 · CPT D1 1A k24 · PBT VI.G.1 · CCMA 3C k107 · CMA I.B.7.b / 2027 I.B.6.b · RMA II.B.7.d.i III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: Which safety data sheet section states whether a chemical is stable in storage and which conditions could set off a hazardous reaction?
opciones: Section 10, which also names the hazardous decomposition products
Section 3, which also names the ingredients and their percentages
Section 5, which also names the extinguishing agents to be used
Section 12, which also names the effects on fish and other species
preguntas.explicacion: Section 10 has three parts: reactivity test data, chemical stability under ordinary temperature and handling conditions, and the rest, which covers whether the chemical could react or polymerize and release heat or pressure, the conditions to avoid such as static discharge, shock or vibration, the classes of materials it is incompatible with, and the hazardous decomposition products it may give off. Combustion products also appear in section 5, because a fire is where they matter.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 7.1.2
preguntas.subtema: CPT D3 3O k71 lancet for premature neonate · PBT II.J lancets · NCMA 2C.5 equipment by age
preguntas.pregunta: Which lancet length is made specifically for premature neonates?
opciones: 1.5 mm
2.2 mm
2.4 mm
preguntas.explicacion: Makers offer lancets from 0.85 mm, the neonatal size, up to 2.2 mm, and the 0.85 mm one is the length kept for a premature baby. Of the other figures, 1.5 mm is the finger depth between 6 months and 8 years, 2.2 mm is the longest lancet in normal adult use, and 2.4 mm is the ceiling for both the finger and the heel.

preguntas.fuente: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(g)(2)(vii)(N) and (g)(2)(viii), Information and Training
preguntas.subtema: Interactive training · CPT D1 1A k31 · PBT VI.G.4.h · CCMA 3C k109 · CMA I.B.4.a / 2027 I.B.3.a · RMA III.A.2.e III.C.5 · NCMA 2A.8
preguntas.pregunta: A clinic's annual bloodborne pathogens training is a video played at the workstation, with nobody available afterwards. What is missing?
opciones: The chance to ask questions of the person conducting the session, which is required
A written test at the end, which the standard says is kept for three years
A copy of the hepatitis B declination form for each attendee to sign
A separate session for each job title named in the exposure determination
preguntas.explicacion: The training program carries a minimum content list in paragraph (g)(2)(vii), and the last item on it is a chance to put questions to whoever gives the session and get answers back; (g)(2)(viii) adds that this person must know the subject as it applies to that workplace. A video with nobody around fails on both counts. The standard never asks for a written test, the declination form belongs to the vaccine under (f)(2)(iv), and a single session may cover several job classifications.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", Definition of PHI and HIPAA and Communication With Patients; StatPearls, "HIPAA Compliance", Questions to Consider
preguntas.subtema: Oral disclosures · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k214 · CMA II.E.1.a · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k35
preguntas.pregunta: Two phlebotomists discuss a named patient's HIV result in a crowded elevator. Under HIPAA this conversation is which of these?
opciones: A violation: oral disclosure of identifiable health information is PHI
Permitted, since both are workforce members of the same covered entity
Permitted, since spoken information is not covered, only written or electronic
A violation only if a patient's relative happens to be in the elevator
preguntas.explicacion: PHI covers written, paper, spoken and electronic information, and the elevator conversation about an identifiable patient is the very example used to illustrate an oral violation; discussions of patient information do not belong in public places, hallways, cafeterias or shared phone lines. Being workforce members does not help, because the disclosure reaches people not involved in the patient's care and exceeds the minimum necessary. State law may add stricter rules for HIV results, and the violation does not depend on who happens to overhear.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Personal Protective Equipment", Issues of Concern: Infection Prevention
preguntas.subtema: Signs at the door · CPT D1 1I k34 · PBT VI.G.4.c VI.G.4.d · CCMA 3C2 k100 · CMA I.B.4.b / 2027 I.B.3.b · RMA III.A.2.d · NCMA 2A.3
preguntas.pregunta: What should tell a phlebotomist arriving at a patient's room which protective equipment that patient requires?
opciones: An easily visible sign posted outside the room or contact zone
The color of the wristband the patient was given at admission
The order in the chart, which names the equipment to be worn
The container by the door, whose contents indicate what to wear
preguntas.explicacion: A sign that is easy to see hangs outside the room, or outside the contact zone, and it names the protective equipment that encounter calls for; that is how a worker arriving from elsewhere gears up correctly before crossing the threshold. It fits the rest of the system, since donning is done outside the room and the precautions in force decide which items are needed: not every component is required for every patient.

preguntas.fuente: PMC, PMC6688222, Whitehead et al., Interventions to prevent iatrogenic anemia: a Laboratory Medicine Best Practices systematic review, Background
preguntas.subtema: CPT D4 4E k83 pediatric volume considerations · PBT II.I complications and considerations
preguntas.pregunta: Why is phlebotomy blood loss considered even more serious in the neonatal ICU than in adult intensive care?
opciones: In their first two weeks they give up 10 to 90% of the blood in circulation to testing
They give up 340 to 660 mL of blood a week to testing, as an adult in intensive care does
They give up about 25% of the blood in circulation each day, mostly to line flushes
Each 50 mL taken raises their risk of anemia by 18%, which is the adult ICU figure
preguntas.explicacion: Babies in a neonatal ICU give up between a tenth and nine tenths of the blood in circulation to sampling in the first fortnight alone, while an adult in intensive care loses something like 340 to 660 mL a week, each 50 mL adding 18% to the risk of anemia. Many end up transfused, with everything that carries, so the sensible move is to stop the anemia from starting.

preguntas.fuente: 42 CFR 493.1291(k), Standard: Test report
preguntas.subtema: CPT D5 5H k94 · PBT VI.F (CLIA) · CCMA 3E15 · NCMA 2C.15 · RMA III.C.1.a
preguntas.pregunta: After a report has gone to the ordering physician, the laboratory discovers a transcription error in one result. What does CLIA require?
opciones: Promptly notify the ordering person, issue a corrected report promptly, and keep duplicates of the original and the corrected report
Issue a corrected report within 30 days and destroy the original so that only the corrected version remains on file
Correct the value in the LIS and rely on the next routine report to carry the corrected result to the physician
Notify the ordering person by telephone with read-back, which replaces the need for a corrected written report
preguntas.explicacion: 42 CFR 493.1291(k) has three parts when a reported result is found to be wrong: the laboratory promptly notifies the authorized person who ordered the test, and whoever uses the result, of the reporting error; it issues a corrected report promptly; and it maintains duplicates of both the original and the corrected report. The original is never discarded, a silent LIS edit notifies nobody, and the read-back procedure belongs to critical results, not to corrections.

preguntas.fuente: MedlinePlus, "CPR - adult and child 9 years and older", First Aid
preguntas.subtema: CCMA 3B11 k83 · CMA I.B.9.c · 2027 I.B.8.c · RMA III.I.1.b · NCMA 2A.10 EKB 15 · CPT 1L k38
preguntas.pregunta: What compression rate is kept during adult CPR?
opciones: 100 to 120 per minute, letting the chest rise fully between compressions
80 to 100 per minute, starting the next push before the chest rises
60 to 80 per minute, matched to the normal resting adult pulse rate
140 to 160 per minute, matched to the resting pulse rate of an infant
preguntas.explicacion: Compressions are fast and hard, in the band of 100 to 120 per minute, and the chest is allowed to come all the way back up after each one. Full recoil between compressions is what maintains coronary artery perfusion pressure, so leaning on the chest defeats the compression that follows. The counted set of 30 is done without pausing.

preguntas.fuente: SAMHSA, Urine Specimen Collection Handbook for Federal Agency Workplace Drug Testing Programs (2024), Chapter 7 collection steps 13 and 23
preguntas.subtema: Chain of custody · CPT D4 4J k86 · PBT V.C.5 chain-of-custody · CCMA 3E k127 witness · RMA III.C.4.a.i · CMA I.C.7.a(2)(f)
preguntas.pregunta: From the moment the donor hands over the specimen until the bottles are sealed, who has to keep it in sight?
opciones: Both the donor and the collector keep visual contact with the specimen
The collector alone, because the donor is no longer part of the process
The donor alone, so that the collector cannot be accused of tampering
A second collector acting as a witness for the whole of the procedure
preguntas.explicacion: Collector and donor both keep the specimen in sight from the moment it changes hands until the seals are on the bottles and they are ready to ship to the laboratory or testing facility. Only then is the donor told the watching is over and allowed to wash their hands. That unbroken line of sight is where the documented chain of custody starts.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Annex C, Table C.1, Safety-engineered devices
preguntas.subtema: Lancets and safety devices · CPT D3 k54 k66 · PBT II.J · CCMA 3E3 k134 · CMA I.C.7.a(1)(b) · RMA III.C.4.a.ii · NCMA 2C.5
preguntas.pregunta: In the WHO classification of safety-engineered devices, how are retractable lancets categorized, and what is their listed advantage?
opciones: Passive devices; they retract and prevent needle-stick injuries
Active devices; the user must slide a sleeve forward over the blade
Passive devices; they prevent reuse but do not reduce needle-sticks
Active devices; the mechanism can trigger during probing and require a new puncture
preguntas.explicacion: Table C.1 places lancets under passive safety-engineered devices with the advantage that they are retractable and prevent needle-stick injuries. The sleeve that slides forward describes the active self re-sheathing needles, and the two remaining descriptions belong to auto-disable syringes, the other passive device, which prevents reuse but offers no needle-stick protection and can trigger while probing.

preguntas.fuente: WHO, Guidelines on Drawing Blood: Best Practices in Phlebotomy (2010), Section 7.1.4 Complications
preguntas.subtema: CPT D3 k74 post-procedural complications · PBT II.I complications · CCMA 3E13 complications · NCMA 2C.10
preguntas.pregunta: Which vascular injury is associated with puncturing the medial aspect of a newborn's heel?
opciones: Laceration of the tibial artery, with collapse of veins
Rupture of the plantar vein, with a spreading hematoma
Thrombosis of the calcaneal branch, with local necrosis
Puncture of the tibial nerve, with loss of the venous branch used
preguntas.explicacion: Heading the list of complications is the collapse of veins that follows when the tibial artery is cut by a puncture on the inner side of the heel. The same list carries osteomyelitis of the calcaneus, nerve injury from sticking a newborn's fingers, hematoma with the venous branch lost, scarring, and necrosis, local or general, as a late effect.

preguntas.fuente: StatPearls, "Patient Confidentiality", Clinical Significance: Clergy and Other Religious Figures
preguntas.subtema: Clergy and the patient list · CPT D1 1C k13 · PBT VI.E · CCMA 7E k213 · CMA II.E.2 · RMA I.C.5 · NCMA 4.3 · CMAA 3B k35
preguntas.pregunta: A hospital chaplain asks for the names of admitted patients of his denomination. What does the privacy rule allow?
opciones: Telling him, provided the patient was informed and did not object
Telling him, since clergy are workforce members of the hospital
Refusing, unless each patient signed a written authorization first
Refusing, because religious affiliation is never disclosed at all
preguntas.explicacion: Clergy and religious figures may be told which patients belong to their denomination, on the condition that the patient was informed first and raised no objection. That is why these preferences, along with who may visit and who should be notified, are asked at admission and put in writing.
